subject: Restructure into a package, and fix the KV-cache attention mask
body:
The tree had grown to 38 flat scripts with no boundary between the model, the
things that train it, and the things that measure it. Split into:

    minagi/       the model: tokenizer, transformer, decode, pool, recur,
                  stream, corpus, store, report, schedule. No command lines.
    train.py      stream | batch | probe
    serve.py      the local UI
    benchmarks/   code | arithmetic | chess_elo
    corpora/      code | arithmetic | chat | chess_games
    experiments/  forgetting | trunk_lr | freeze | conflict | replay
    tools/        plotting

Removed moe_coder.py (827 lines, superseded; its Expert class is now in
minagi/pool.py), stack_bench.py, extend_vocab.py and reencode_chess.py, which
were one-off migrations already applied.

Renamed corpora/math.py and benchmarks/chess.py, which shadowed the stdlib
`math` and the `chess` package respectively.

Also carries the attention fix: with a KV cache and more than one token fed at
once, is_causal aligned its triangle to the top-left of a non-square score
matrix, so a query at absolute position P+i attended to keys 0..i instead of
0..P+i. Chunked reading now matches a full pass exactly (loss 1.2022 either
way, against 4.0326 before).

subject: Clean up artefacts, chunk the serving path, rewrite the documentation
body:
serve.py now prefills prompts in chunks through the same cache path that
train.py stream uses. Feeding a long prompt in one pass materialises
activations for every position at once across all 26 block applications, which
is what put a long context out of reach on the serving side; chunking bounds
that by CHUNK and leaves the cache to carry the reach. Also fixes a bug where
the generation loop never invalidated its logits after the prefill.

Added __main__ dispatchers so the packages are runnable:
    python3 -m benchmarks <code|arithmetic|chess>
    python3 -m corpora <code|arithmetic|chat|chess>
    python3 -m experiments <forgetting|trunk_lr|freeze|conflict|replay>

Documentation rewritten from scratch against the current state:
    README.md        what it is, how to run it, and what it currently scores
    ARCHITECTURE.md  how it is put together and why
    FINDINGS.md      the results that changed the design, failures included

The old README described a 1024-context, 18-block-application, vocab-256 model
trained by a script that no longer exists.

subject: Make every run advance the model, and make that safe
body:
weights/ is the live model and now always moves - resumed from, written at
every evaluation, no exceptions. A session that read something and threw the
result away has not learned anything, and until now every verification run went
to a throwaway copy: roughly 1700 steps of real training on the actual model,
deleted, because writing unconditionally risked destroying it.

That was a false choice. The live directory keeps moving; a snapshot of the
best state it has reached sits beside it under weights/best/. On divergence the
run restores the snapshot, halves the learning rate, pulls the context back and
continues, giving up after --max-reverts rather than thrashing. Forced
divergence at lr 3e-2 reverts twice and leaves the weights bit-identical.

Also fixes two things this exposed:

  - resuming reset `best` to infinity, so the first evaluation of any run would
    call itself the best and snapshot over a better state. It now reads the
    snapshot's score.

  - ramp_context rounded to powers of two, so it was not a ramp but a
    staircase: the window doubled in a single step, loss went 0.752 -> 1.830
    and gradient norms 1.79 -> 9.89 against a clip of 1.0 - updates that were
    direction with no magnitude - and the run never recovered. Nothing needed a
    power of two; it now steps in units of 256 characters.

subject: Keep only the best weights, and drop the .pt duplicates
body:
The snapshot under weights/best/ was a copy of what was already in weights/,
which took the model from 226 MB to 454 MB and would have grown with the pool.

So the directory holds the best state rather than the most recent one: save is
called when a run improves on it and skipped otherwise, which makes the
directory itself the thing to reload on divergence. Verified by forcing two
divergences at lr 3e-2 - weights/ is byte-identical before and after, with no
second copy anywhere.

The .pt checkpoints went the same way. They existed "purely so existing tools
that take a --ckpt keep working", which contradicted the claim that the
directory is the model, and cost another 153 MB per run directory.
load_recur() now accepts either, every tool defaults to `weights`, and nothing
writes a .pt any more.

    weights + checkpoints    607 MB -> 226 MB

Batch training follows the same rule, so the two modes no longer disagree about
what a saved model means.

subject: The evaluator was measuring its own noise; fix it and retract what it said
body:
Validation was 6 chunks per domain - 12,288 characters, 0.14% of the held-out
text. Repeated draws on unchanged weights vary with a standard deviation of
0.0275. Differences of 0.0008 to 0.0114 were compared against that and reported
as results, one of them with explicit confidence at 3% of a standard deviation.

It also invented a finding that shaped a great deal of work: streaming was said
to be losing to batch training, 0.6864 against 0.6524, and an explanation was
built on top. Measured honestly, streaming improves on what batch training left
by 0.028 - about two standard errors. There was no gap.

Evaluator now returns stderr with the loss, so a difference cannot be quoted
without its error bar in view. The sample is the window rather than the chunk,
since chunks inside a window are correlated; calibrated against repeated draws.
Default eval size 6 -> 240 chunks (491,520 characters).

Enlarging the evaluation is what exposed a second bug. A reader running past
its own context slid the window - trimmed the cache, held the position offset -
and the keys left in the cache carry the rotary encoding of the positions they
were computed at, so RoPE's relative distances stop matching. Same weights,
held-out loss 0.68 within the window and 2.60 past it. Training never saw it
because windows were opened from outside every `context` characters. Readers
are self-limiting now.

Gradient accumulation, measured at a fixed 3.0M character budget so only the
averaging differs: accum 1 gives 0.6594, accum 8 gives 0.6615 (0.23 sigma), and
accum 64 gives 0.6701 with only 91 updates. It buys nothing, and the reason it
was proposed - gradient noise holding streaming back - was reasoning from a gap
that did not exist. Kept as a flag defaulting to 1.

The recorded score in weights/manifest.json is cleared. It was measured on the
small evaluation and against a batch-trained target that costs 6857 MB against
streaming's 3026 and contradicts the premise of the project.

FINDINGS.md gains three sections; README and ARCHITECTURE are corrected.

subject: README: reading your own files, and what is not built yet
body:
Adds `train.py read`, which is the shortest path to a model that knows
something you care about: point it at files or directories and it reads them.
Nothing to prepare - the alphabet is the 256 byte values, so a file is already
written in the only vocabulary the model has. Directories are walked, binaries
are skipped by sampling rather than by extension, and each file is read from
beginning to end because a document has an order. Same chunking, same cache,
same gradient step as a training run.

Nothing is saved without --save, and the held-out mixture is scored before and
after so the cost of reading your files is measured rather than assumed.

Two corrections to what the README claimed:

  - "top-16 of 74 experts per call site, chosen per character" was accurate and
    gave the wrong impression. Top-16 is per call-site INVOCATION, and a
    character passes through 26 of them - it touches 55 of the 67 experts,
    about 94% of all parameters. The pool is a recombination mechanism at this
    size, not a sparsity one.

  - the parameter count was fixed at 19.6M and 74 experts. It moves, because
    the pool prunes itself while training; it is 19.1M and 67 now. The README
    says how to ask rather than asserting a number that goes stale hourly.

Adds a "Not yet true" section listing the three things the opening description
claims that are not built: learning while serving, paging during training, and
an unbounded pool. They are one dependency chain, not three faults - the caps
come off after training can page, and removing them first reproduces an
out-of-memory crash that has already happened.

subject: Match expert slots by identity, and drop the VRAM cache experiment
body:
swap_to assigned slot j the jth wanted expert, so the same thirty-two
experts arriving in a different order counted as thirty-two host loads.
Demand comes back sorted, so the order churned constantly while the set
barely moved: 22.5 loads per chunk where the set had really moved by 4.7.
An expert already on the card now keeps its slot.

A fourth tier - 48 experts held on the card, routing among 32, so one that
drops out of the working set and comes back costs a copy inside VRAM - was
built and measured against the fix above:

    vram_cache 48   4.5 loads/chunk   0.2k char/s   7904 MiB
    vram_cache 32   4.7 loads/chunk   0.2k char/s   6806 MiB

1.1 GB for 0.2 loads and no throughput, so it is out. Two reasons, either
sufficient: the remaining churn is almost entirely the exploration reserve,
which picks the experts least recently resident and so misses such a cache
by construction; and throughput is not load-bound, so removing loads buys
no time. The earlier replay that predicted 70% avoided had measured demand
without exploration mixed in, which is exactly the part that defeats it.
README records the result so the question is not reopened from that prior.

Also: train.py read now finishes its chunk, checkpoints and exits on
SIGINT/SIGTERM instead of dying, and honours --minutes per chunk rather
than only at file boundaries - a 3-minute probe had been running past 7.

subject: Interleave subjects by window, and compute in bfloat16
body:
Reading a file end to end meant 200,000 characters of one subject with
nothing to balance it - seventeen minutes at this speed. The held-out score
swung by two nats depending on which subject the reader was inside:

    step   arithmetic  chat   chess  code    mean   spread
    1190     4.669    2.829  2.818  2.870   3.296   1.851
    1416     5.237    4.822  1.968  5.096   4.281   3.269
    1629     4.142    2.594  2.870  2.497   3.026   1.645

Chess improved by 0.85 while the other three lost 2.0-2.2, then recovered.
Reading now rotates between subjects one context window at a time: a random
file, a random offset, 16,384 characters forward from there. That is 82
seconds per subject instead of 17 minutes. The window stays contiguous
because a lone chunk gives attention nothing to reach back over, and only
one lane holds a cache at a time - a window of keys and values across 26
block-applications is 1.7 GB, so four would not fit.

Precision moves to bfloat16 for the forward. Weights, gradients, Adam's
moments and the expert files stay fp32. Measured forward-only on finished
weights, same windows:

           held-out   peak     time
    fp32   3.10139   2632 MB   86.9s
    bf16   3.05083   2017 MB   58.6s
    fp16   3.04425   2001 MB   59.2s

The 0.05 gap is entirely arithmetic (4.114 vs 3.896); the other three
domains agree to 0.008. It is not mantissa loss - fp16 has a longer mantissa
than bf16 and lands on bf16's number - most likely flash attention's online
softmax against the fp32 math fallback at 16k context.

The expert files deliberately stay fp32: an expert pages out and back
several times per chunk, and bfloat16 rounding is 2.3e-05 against a typical
Adam step of 5.1e-05, thrown away on every page-out.

subject: Keep pool_max at least the pool size, and correct the bf16 rounding figure
body:
A stale ceiling from an older config left the routers a row short of the
experts on disk, so a weights directory could not be loaded back without
widening it by hand.

The bfloat16 storage figure was measured on one expert file. Over 24 it is
1.88e-05 against an Adam step of 5.62e-05 - a third of a step, not the 0.44x
first recorded. The conclusion is unchanged: expert files stay fp32.

subject: Prune must not reshape a router under a live graph
body:
A run that pruned crashed on the next backward:

    IndexBackward0 returned an invalid gradient at index 0 -
    got [171, 512] but expected shape compatible with [173, 512]

prune reindexed every router with weight.data = weight.data[idx], which
shrinks the Parameter the forward had already saved. Autograd sizes that
gradient from the tensor it holds, so it returned the new row count where
the graph recorded the old one. Growth never hit this because add_experts
already allocates a fresh Linear; only pruning mutated in place.

Routers, including the segment router, are now replaced rather than
reshaped. tests/test_prune_backward.py reproduces the crash and passes.

subject: A dry read must not be able to destroy the pool
body:
python3 train.py read data/train, with no --save, pruned experts. Pruning
deletes their files and renumbers what is left, immediately. The manifest
that indexes them is only written at a checkpoint, and a dry read never
writes one - so the run left 146 files behind an index naming 169, and every
later load died on the first missing file.

Two holes, both closed. Growth and pruning now happen only when --save is
given, so a read that keeps nothing changes nothing. And when they do happen,
the manifest is written at once instead of at the next checkpoint, so the
directory never describes a pool that is not there.

tools/repair_pool.py recovers a directory that already drifted: it keeps the
experts whose files still exist and subsets every per-expert tensor - routers,
gate, Adam moments - by the same ids, so an expert stays paired with the row
that was trained for it, then renumbers to be contiguous.

subject: Pruning renumbered experts in the order that destroys them
body:
Every surviving expert moves DOWN to a lower index. prune renamed them
highest-first, so each move landed on a file that had not been moved yet and
overwrote a live expert with its neighbour. Measured on twelve experts with
three pruned: nine should survive, six files remained, and the survivors held
the wrong weights. The holes it left surfaced later as

    FileNotFoundError: weights/experts/e00153.npz

Renaming now goes lowest-first, which always writes into a slot the pruned
expert has already vacated. tests/test_prune_renumber.py fills expert i with
the value i and checks every survivor still holds its own weights.

repair_pool.py now takes its index space from the routers rather than the
manifest - when a run dies between changing the pool and writing the index,
the manifest is the stale one of the two - and only from tensors that really
carry a row per expert, not from depth_emb.

subject: Keep a record of what each expert did
body:
Usage counters were rebuilt from nothing every run, so a checkpoint could say
what the model is and nothing about how it got there. Asking after the fact
does not work either: an expert leaving the card is handed to the RAM cache,
not to disk, so file mtimes measure the cache rather than use.

The pool now reports per-expert telemetry - gate, routing hits, admissions to
the card, birth step, last admission - and the checkpoint carries it, so it
survives a restart. train.py also appends one line per checkpoint to
runs/expert_history.jsonl, because the manifest only ever holds the latest
state and cannot say whether an expert earned its gate early and coasted or
climbed all along.

tools/expert_history.py reads the trail; tools/expert_usage.py draws the
current state. Neither opens the model, so both are safe to run against a
directory a training run is using.

subject: Demand elected experts that had earned nothing
body:
The working set held near-dead experts at twice the rate the pool did: 14 of
32 below gate 0.2 against 33 of 161. An expert contributes w * gate, so a
gate-zero expert adds exactly nothing while still taking one of the eight
top-k slots at that depth and the softmax weight that goes with it.

The key term was the cause. A new expert's key comes from its random w1,
which matches text about as well as anything does, and growth manufactures
four of them every 400 steps. Fit alone therefore kept electing the untrained.

Similarity is now scaled by what an expert has earned BEFORE the per-token
choice, not after the tally - discounting the tally still lets an untrained
expert win the choice, and winner-take-all means one strong random match
outweighs any later penalty. A floor keeps a new expert reachable; the
cold-start sweep is what gives it its first turn.

Also: each term now carries its own normalisation. Scaling fit by the
router's total mass looked tidy and was brittle - where the router had no
opinion the whole key term vanished with it.

tests/test_demand_prefers_earned.py: 5 of the 8 most wanted had earned
nothing before, 0 after.

subject: The held-out score was measured with the wrong experts on the card
body:
Training chooses its working set with want_experts - demand scored on the
hidden states the call sites really routed on, against keys derived from each
expert's own weights. Evaluation chose with begin_segment, which scores the
old segment router. That router picks its own experts no better than chance:
measured, the cosine between an expert's key and its own segment-router row
is 0.0352 against 0.0360 for any other row, a ratio of 0.98.

So every held-out number today was the model handicapped by a working set
chosen at random, while training ran with one chosen by demand. It shows as
a 1.03 nat gap between training loss and held-out loss on text that is
equally unseen - reading draws fresh windows from a corpus 200x larger than
any run gets through, so both numbers measure unseen text and a gap that
size is not something a model can have. The run that reached this project's
best score had a gap of 0.08, and it had every expert resident, so there was
no selection to get wrong.

Also, three things the read path was missing:

- No learning-rate schedule at all. lr_at() has been in the file from the
  beginning and cmd_train uses it; cmd_read never did, and ran at its base
  rate for the model's whole life. The best run decayed to a fifth of its
  base. The schedule is keyed on characters read across the model's whole
  life, so a restart continues it rather than starting it again.
- No training loss in the sample log, so a reader could not tell whether the
  model was learning at all - which is how this went unnoticed.
- Growth that could not be paid for. The pool holds 96 parameters for every
  character ever read, against 0.39 in the best run. Growth now stops above
  a density ceiling and resumes as reading catches up.

subject: Say how much of the corpus has been read, not just how much was read
body:
A bare character count means nothing on its own: the same 4M is most of a
small corpus and a rounding error of a large one. The sample header and the
session banner now give it as a fraction of what there is to read.

The closing sample also carries the training loss and learning rate the
periodic ones already had.

subject: The context window grows when the model earns it, one character at a time
body:
Reading began at whatever the ceiling was, so a model that could not yet use
16,384 characters paid for them on every chunk - and the window is the
dominant cost: 4k reads at 1,500 char/s, 16k at 300.

It now starts at context_start and grows only when the model is still
predicting better deep into the window than early in it. That evidence is
free: chunks are read in order inside a window, so a chunk's index IS its
distance into the context, and the loss is already being recorded per chunk.
When the gain falls below context_gain_min the window stops growing.

By ONE character. An earlier ramp rounded to powers of two, so the window
doubled in a single step: loss went 0.752 -> 1.830, gradient norms 1.79 ->
9.89 against a clip of 1.0, and the run never recovered. Nothing here needs a
round number.

RoPE carries no learned parameters, so the same weights read at any length
and raising the ceiling costs a larger rotary table and nothing else. The
window is recorded in the checkpoint, so a restart continues from where it
had grown to rather than starting over, and it is stated in every sample-log
entry - a score means little without the window it was measured at.

subject: A subject is read for whole windows, with a floor
body:
The visit was tied to the window alone, so a small context rotated subjects
every few chunks: at 2,048 a subject changed every four chunks, and the first
chunk after a change chooses its experts from the states of the subject just
left - a quarter of all reading, spent selecting on the wrong evidence.

A visit is now at least min_visit_chunks, rounded UP to whole windows, so a
subject may take several windows in a row. A window still never spans two
subjects: attention across the seam where chess becomes Python teaches
nothing. At 8,192 and above the window already exceeds the floor and nothing
changes from before.

The window is a CEILING of chunks, not a floor. FileReader starts a new
window once it has read  characters, so a 1,161-character window is
three chunks and not two - and since the window now grows one character at a
time it is almost never a multiple of the chunk. The test checks every window
length from 1,024 to 24,576.

_Lane.open also draws its offset with room for the whole visit rather than
one window, or a file runs out part way through.

Reading past the rotary tables now says so, instead of failing with a shape
error four frames deeper.

subject: Generation chose its experts at random, and the window could not grow
body:
sample_now called begin_segment, the old segment router - the same path the
evaluator used until this morning, and measured at 0.98x, no better than
chance. So every sample was produced with whatever thirty-two experts were
resident, with no reference to the prompt at all.

It now chooses from the prompt and asks again every 64 characters as the
answer develops. The reading hysteresis is released for that first choice: it
exists to stop the working set churning on noise in a continuous stream, and
a prompt is the opposite - a deliberate change of subject. Measured on a
Python prompt with chess resident, 3 of 32 experts changed while held to the
reading settings, 15 of 32 released.

The window could not grow either. Evidence-gathering and growing were the
same event, so it gained one character per 102,400 read - 29 characters in
six million, and reaching 16k would have needed more text than the corpus
holds. They are now separate: the evidence is re-gathered every
context_every chunks, and while it says the model is still gaining deep into
the window, the window grows a character per chunk. 2,083 -> 16,384 becomes
7.3M characters instead of 1,464M, and no single change is larger than one
character.

Measured and REFUTED along the way: that generation used less computation
than the loss reported. The halted pass scores 1.1562 against the six-pass
mixture's 1.1616 - very slightly better - at 2.28 passes of 6. Adaptive
halting is well calibrated and is not why the samples are poor.

subject: Show the gradient norm, so the learning rate can be argued about with a number
body:
cmd_read discarded what clip_grad_norm_ returns, so there was no way to tell
whether the clip was what limited the step. It matters for any question about
raising the learning rate: a norm well above the clip means most of the rate
is being thrown away and raising it only makes the direction noisier. The run
that reached this project's best score sat at 1.19-1.62 against a clip of 1.

subject: Separate how much the window grows from how often
body:
The step size alone did not set the pace. Growing one character per chunk is
about 2,000 characters of window per million read - at a 2,000-character
window that is a quarter of it per sample interval, which is fast in the
terms that matter, since what decides whether the model keeps up is growth
relative to what it already handles. Measured, the window went from +3 per
sample to +514.

context_grow_every puts chunks between the single-character growths, so the
step stays one character and the pace is a separate dial:

    every 1 chunk   ~2,000 characters of window per million read
    every 8           ~250
    every 32           ~60

Default 8. Growth is still gated on the evidence that the model is gaining
deep into the window; this only decides how quickly it acts on it.

subject: The benchmarks were scoring the trunk alone
body:
A paged model loads with an EMPTY card: every slot -1, every expert weight
zero. RecurCoder.generate never asked for experts, so every benchmark ran on
11.4M parameters of trunk while 497M of pool contributed exactly nothing.
That is not a degraded model, it is a different and much smaller one, and it
is the likeliest reason chess has scored 0 of 60 legal games.

generate now chooses experts from the prompt and asks again every 64
characters as the answer develops, with the reading hysteresis released for
the first choice - a prompt is a deliberate change of subject, not the noise
that hysteresis exists to damp. Verified: 32 of 32 slots fill and |w1| goes
from 0 to 844,211.

load_any also could not open the current model at all: it called torch.load
on what is now a directory, and dispatched on an arch tag through
minagi.pool.load_moe, which no longer exists.

benchmarks/report.py measures what this model can honestly be measured on -
bits per character on held-out text, the enwik8 and text8 standard, plus a
LAMBADA-style word completion built from our own held-out chat. The suites
small instruction-tuned models are scored on are deliberately absent: MMLU,
HellaSwag, ARC and GSM8K need knowledge and instruction-following far beyond
what this has read, and would return chance.

Word completion carries partial credit as well as exact match. A benchmark
that reads 0% at every checkpoint carries no information, and exact whole
words are far out of reach at 1.6 bits per character.

Results append to runs/benchmarks.jsonl and each run prints the change since
the last, so the table reads as progress. --history prints the record without
measuring anything, which needs no GPU and is safe during a run.

subject: Point the benchmarks at the corpora that exist, and add enwik8
body:
They defaulted to the old .bin directories and called load_tokenizer on them
to learn an alphabet the model does not use - it is byte level, so a
benchmark needs no corpus to know that. They now read the text folders
directly, and held_out_bytes takes either form, so a benchmark pointed at an
old directory still works.

data/enwik8/wikipedia/test.txt is the standard test split, bytes 95M to 100M
of enwik8, which is what every published character-model result is measured
on. Reported zero-shot: this model has never seen Wikipedia, so it is not
comparable with numbers from models trained on enwik8's own 90M train split.

subject: A file should be one document, and a subject a top-level folder
body:
The corpora were cut at fixed byte counts, so a file began and ended
mid-sentence: code/code-00001.py opened with a bare ')'. A window spanning
such a cut asks the model to attend across a seam that carries no
information, which is the same objection that moved reading off whole files
in the first place. It is also not what a reader's own files look like, and
reading your own files is the interface this is for.

Rebuilt on the natural unit of each corpus:

    wikipedia   147,545 files   one <page> per file, named for its title
    code         41,787 files   cut only where what precedes parses as
                                Python - a def inside a docstring looks
                                exactly like a real boundary from outside,
                                and 2 of 80 files were invalid before this
    chat         25,289 files   whole <user>/<bot> exchanges, grouped
    arithmetic      724 files   already cut on line boundaries, left alone
    chess         1,640 files   already cut on </g>, left alone

Sampled after: 120 of 120 code files parse, 200 of 200 chat files run
<user> to </bot>, 80 of 80 articles are whole.

One exchange per file was tried and abandoned: 999,374 files of ~390 bytes
took 3.9 GB, ten times the content, because each takes a filesystem block.

_lanes now groups by the TOP-LEVEL folder rather than the immediate parent.
A corpus this size must have subdirectories, and grouping by the parent made
each of them a subject - 103 of them, with chat reduced to a lane holding one
file. It also matches what pointing at ~/notes should mean: one subject per
folder, not per nested directory.

subject: Say the unit on the held-out loss
body:
The sample log reports a natural log and the benchmark reports bits, so the
same model reads as 1.30 in one place and 1.88 in the other. Both are now on
the line.

subject: What the model says about itself is data now, and it is true
body:
The self-description lived in corpora/chat.py, so it went stale silently. The
5.5M characters of it already in the training corpus state a pool of 74
experts, a top-16 router, a 4,096 character window and 236 megabytes on disk.
The model holds 158 experts, routes top-8, reads over 4,558 characters and
occupies six gigabytes. It is being trained to be wrong about itself.

corpora/self_knowledge.yaml holds it instead: 28 topics, 89 phrasings, and
EVERY number a placeholder filled from weights/manifest.json and config.yaml
when the corpus is built, so an answer cannot claim a size the model does not
have. Twenty-two of the topics are new, and they explain the mechanism as it
now is - keys derived from an expert's own weights and why a router row
cannot do that job, the three tiers and why the optimiser moments travel with
the expert, the window growing a character at a time on evidence, why the
expert files stay in full precision when the arithmetic does not, what a gate
means, and what happens when it is pointed at your files.

The generated corpus goes in data/train/chat/self-knowledge, a folder rather
than a scattering: separable, inspectable, and still weighted as part of chat.
A top-level folder would have made it a sixth subject and given one paragraph
set a sixth of all reading.

tools/rebuild_self_knowledge.py strips the stale text and writes the new,
refusing to run while training holds those files.

subject: Expand the self-knowledge to the mechanism's detail, and strip by question
body:
64 topics now, 188 phrasings, every number a placeholder filled from the model
that exists. The new ones go to the level the mechanism works at: what is
inside one expert and its exact shape, how a key is computed by power
iteration and why it is recomputed when an expert leaves the card, what the
latent state is and why it is never decoded, how halting decides depth per
character, what the aux loss does to routing counts and why the gate says
more, what a chunk is against what a window is, where the gradient stops, why
the trunk learns slower than the pool, what survives a restart.

The strip needed the question set, not the name. Most of the old answers never
say the model's name - they open with a claim about the pool - so keying on
the name found 5.5M characters where the real volume was 33.2M, a fifth of it.
Sampled, every exchange the question match removes is self-description; the
match needs a whole user turn to equal a short phrase, which an organic
question does not.

Rewritten at the volume the model demonstrably learned from, so it can still
recite - but from 2.3x the topics and 3.8x the phrasings, so each answer
appears about 877 times rather than four thousand.

subject: Bring in reasoning traces, in the markers the model already uses
body:
OpenThoughts-114k: 113,957 DeepSeek-R1 deliberations over maths, code and
science, 2.45 billion characters. The source wraps its sections in
<|begin_of_thought|> and <|begin_of_solution|>; those become <think> and the
answer body, which are single symbols in this alphabet rather than seven
characters each - verified, a 73 character sample encodes to 40 ids with every
marker one id and the round trip exact.

Length is not filtered, and that follows from how this model reads. A trace
longer than the window is read across several windows and every chunk still
trains; what is lost is only the ability to attend back to the problem while
writing the answer, which for a deliberation that is mostly locally structured
costs little. Filtering to a 32,768 window would have discarded a third of
OpenThoughts and two thirds of OpenR1-Math.

400 traces are held back so the domain can be measured, as every other domain
is.

subject: Remember which files are text, and bring in conversation and stories
body:
Deciding whether a file is text means opening it. At half a million files
that is 127 seconds of every startup, and the corpus had just grown from
219,000 files to 522,000. Walking the names is fast; opening them is not, so
the verdicts are remembered against the set of names and only recomputed when
that set changes: 127s to 1.0s, 126x.

The price is that a file whose contents change under an unchanged name keeps
its old verdict. The corpus tools write new names rather than overwrite, and
text does not usually turn into something else.

tools/fetch_corpus.py brings a dataset in as either conversation or plain
documents. OpenHermes-2.5, a million conversations and 1.52 billion
characters, goes inside chat rather than beside it: it IS conversation, and
the chat corpus was almost entirely code questions, which is the likeliest
reason chat scored worst of the domains. TinyStories, 2.1 million stories and
1.93 billion characters, becomes its own subject - simple well-formed prose
is a different register from dialogue, and it is aimed at the thing this model
is worst at, which is staying coherent while generating.

Records are grouped into files rather than written one apiece, and a record is
never split. A million conversations of a thousand characters would be a
million files: ten times their own size on disk from block overhead, and
minutes on every survey.

The dataset cache is now deleted after each fetch. Converting OpenThoughts
left thirteen gigabytes of Arrow behind on a disk that was already at 99%.

subject: A grown expert could never earn its place, so none ever did
body:
Measured over 15M characters of real reading: 28 experts grown, 28 pruned,
zero survivors. Every expert still alive was an original. That is not a pool
finding its size, it is a mechanism that cannot succeed, and it had been
running that way for the whole history in runs/expert_history.jsonl.

The loop: a new expert was born at gate 0.0, which is exactly the value prune
reads as contributing nothing. Its selection score was then scaled by that
same gate, floored at 0.1 against incumbents sitting near 0.58 - a 5.8x
handicap on every character. So it was not chosen; so its gate never moved;
so prune found it silent and flat and deleted it. Prune was working
correctly. It was carrying out a sentence passed at birth.

What breaks the loop is a trial: for its first prune.min_age steps an expert
competes for the card without the handicap, and is then judged on what it did
with the turn. One number governs both windows, so there is no second thing
to keep in your head.

The birth gate has to sit BELOW the bar it must clear, and that took two
tries. Set above it - the obvious reading of "do not born it dead" - an
expert can never be removed for failing to earn a gate: 30 of 30 grown
experts survived a smoke run with gates that had barely moved, and the pool
ran 12 -> 44 with nothing able to stop it. The trial is the protection; the
gate is the judgement. The run now refuses to start if the two are ordered
wrongly, and says why.

On the real 158-expert model, with growth forced past the density gate: the
pool grew 158 -> 174, one cohort completed its trial and was pruned, and the
grown gates spread from 0.00006 to 0.00971 around a birth of 0.001 - moving
in both directions, with 5 of 16 clearing the bar. Held-out moved 1.4259 ->
1.4947, which is inside either error bar and is not evidence of anything.

Also here:

  Growth is bounded by disk, not just by VRAM. An expert is ~40 MB, so
  growth.max_disk_gb is the number that decides how large the model may ever
  get: 16 GB is about 420 experts. It stops there rather than filling the
  volume.

  keep_ratio is counted from `born` instead of guessed from the pool size.
  The old estimate halved whenever the pool shrank at all, so pruning one
  ancient original was charged to a batch added long afterwards, and two such
  coincidences stopped growth outright - against a 1.2x recovery, one
  misattribution cost four clean rounds.

  AutoGrow accepted five knobs it never read: patience, min_rel, entropy_min,
  pressure_min, require_plateau. Gone, with their callers.

  cmd_stream set its growth ceiling to the pool's current size on every load,
  so room = n < max_experts was false forever after a restart.

  The corpus survey cache held one entry, so each survey evicted the last and
  a session touching two directories paid the full 117s every time. It now
  keeps the largest few, and a scratch directory of three files cannot evict
  a corpus of half a million.

subject: Two thirds of an expert file was Adam state stored at full width
body:
An expert file is 37.7 MB, and only 12.6 MB of it is the expert. The rest is
Adam's two moments, kept in fp32 because the weights are kept in fp32 - which
was never a measurement, only the weights' measurement applied to something
else.

They are not the same case. What the moments need is exponent, not mantissa.
Measured on the real pool, m has median magnitude 3.5e-09 and v has 2.0e-15,
against weights at 1.3e-02, and bfloat16 keeps every bit of fp32's exponent
range while spending its mantissa:

    m bf16   0.10% of its own magnitude       v bf16   0.10%
    m fp16   86% - underflows                 v fp16   100%, to zero

float16 destroys them outright; both sit far below its smallest subnormal.
That is the same reason bf16 is right here and wrong for the weights, where
its coarse mantissa costs 0.80x an Adam update per page-out and an expert is
rewritten a median of 406 times.

So: moments bf16, weights fp32, and the weights are provably untouched -
w1/w3/w2 come back bit-identical, checked in tests/test_moment_storage.py.
What the narrowing actually perturbs is the next update, by 0.10% at the
median and 2.7% at p99, which is 1.1e-06 of a weight. And unlike a weight, a
moment is transient: at betas (0.9, 0.95) an error in it is forgotten within
about twenty steps and cannot accumulate.

weights/ goes 6.4 GB -> 4.2 GB, 35% off, and the pool's disk ceiling now buys
half again as many experts. Held-out afterwards 1.3926 +/-0.0573 against
1.4259 +/-0.0697 measured before, which is the same number twice.

numpy has no bfloat16, so a moment travels as int16 carrying the same bits,
and the dtype is the marker: an array that loads as float32 was written by an
older version and is read as-is. Old weight directories keep working and
convert themselves as experts page out. tools/shrink_weights.py does it in one
pass instead, atomically per file, and refuses to start if a round-trip check
on a real file exceeds 2%.

Compression was measured and rejected: 43% with the moments narrowed, but 1.1s
to write one file, and paging is the hot path.

subject: The loop guard marked a character forever, so it stopped meaning anything
body:
Greedy decoding falls into loops - that much was known and written down in
decode.py. What was not measured is that the guard against it did not work.
rep_penalty divides the logit of every character already emitted, and never
un-divides it, so after 140 characters of English 93% of the alphabet is
penalised equally. It is not off; it is saturated, and a rule that penalises
everything ranks nothing.

The samples showed it plainly: 'of the construction of the construction of the
construction', ', axis2' twelve times, 'Qxf2+ 17. Kh1 Qxf2+ 18. Kxf2'. Those
are phrase-shaped loops of 12 to 79 characters, and a per-character penalty
cannot see a phrase - every character in 'axis2' is ordinary.

The replacement is adaptation: a per-character trace that rises when a
character is used and decays after, the way a neuron that has just fired is
briefly harder to fire again. Measured over six prompts, mean repeated
8-grams:

    greedy alone                  73.5%
    greedy + rep_penalty 1.12     59.0%
    greedy + adaptation 2.5       11.6%

The decay is what makes it work where the penalty failed. At 0.88 the
half-life is 5.4 characters, so one use costs 2.5 logits now and 0.9 eight
characters later, which ordinary text never notices. A character inside a loop
never gets to decay and converges to strength/(1-decay) = 20.8 logits, which
no loop survives. It stays greedy and deterministic, so samples still diff.

Two things measured and rejected:

  no_repeat_ngram, the obvious tool, is unusable at character level: 100% of
  real code files contain a repeated 32-gram and 40% repeat a 48-gram, so any
  value strict enough to stop a loop also forbids ordinary code. Tried anyway,
  it barely helped - the loop steps around the ban and resumes, 'of the
  construction of the construction OFF the construction'.

  Charging a character only for use above its natural rate - so space is not
  billed 4.3 logits for being 20.6% of all text - is worse, 42.5% against
  11.6%. Loops are built out of common characters, so exempting them is
  exactly what lets a loop through.

The trace is computed from the history rather than carried between calls, so
pick_next stays pure and every existing caller keeps working. Its blind spot
is stated where someone will find it: a loop whose period exceeds the trace's
memory is invisible to it, and only a better model fixes that.

subject: Record the generation-time learning measurements
body:
Adaptation is in and committed. These are the numbers behind leaving weight
updates during generation out for now: learning from the model's own output
costs held-out about five times what learning from real documents of the same
length costs, and the cost scales with how many gradient steps land on how
little text.

subject: Learn from the conversation as it happens, once per exchange
body:
The model learns from everything it reads. It did not learn from what it was
told directly - a conversation lived in the context window and was gone when
the window moved. Now an exchange is read once when it finishes, so what was
said is in the weights.

What that costs was measured before it was built. Held-out on data/val, error
bar +/-0.06:

    54 steps, its own output only               +0.5855
    54 steps, the whole window every chunk      +0.6507
     6 steps, one per finished exchange         +0.1018
     5 steps, real documents of the same size   +0.0197   (control)

The control is the row that matters, because it separates two effects that
looked like one. Real text of the same length costs +0.02, which is noise -
so most of the first two rows was never about the text being self-generated,
it was nine times as many gradient steps landing on a few hundred characters.
What survives the control is the genuine price of learning from your own
output: about five times what the same amount of real text costs. Small enough
to pay once an exchange, not fifty-four times.

Hence the three rules minagi/live.py exists to hold:

  ONCE PER EXCHANGE. Six times cheaper than once per chunk.

  THE NEW TURN ONLY. A chat prompt carries the whole conversation, so
  learning on the prompt would re-train the first turn once per turn after -
  which is how the +0.6507 row was produced, by accident, while testing
  something else.

  NOT FROM ITS OWN SAMPLES. The diagnostic samples during training have no
  human in them, and there is nothing in them the model did not already
  predict.

A lower learning rate is not an alternative to any of that and was not
measured as one. Descent has a direction; on your own argmax it points at
confirming it, and a smaller step confirms it more slowly.

Off unless asked for: serve.py --learn. It changes the model on disk, so it
says so at startup, reports the loss on every exchange in the stream's done
event, and checkpoints every --learn-save-every exchanges.

The chat stream also gets the adaptation trace, which serving had missed - it
was still on rep_penalty 1.15.

One bug this found, by reloading after a save rather than trusting it: saving
without the manifest wrote a blank one, so a directory that had just learned
something claimed the default vocabulary of 8192 while holding 265, and could
never be loaded again. The learner now carries the manifest it was loaded
with. Nothing but a round trip would have caught it.

subject: Write up the adaptation mechanism, and what could replace it
body:
The algebra of why it works was never written down, and it is the part that
predicts where it fails: the steady penalty on a loop of period p is
lambda/(1-gamma^p), which is 20.8 logits at p=1 and collapses to lambda=2.5
as p grows. Short loops are crushed, long ones are charged what any character
pays for being used once. That single expression explains both the 59.0% ->
11.6% result and the 45-character phrases that still survive.

Also records the expert-pool alternative and why it cannot replace this: expert
re-selection happens every 64 characters and the loops that dominate have
periods of about 7, so within one interval the function is constant by
construction and the loop runs unopposed. It fits the blind spot rather than
the main case.

subject: Measure whether surprise can replace adaptation; mostly it cannot
body:
A floor on surprise is period-blind, which is exactly what adaptation is not,
so it looked like the right replacement. Measured during generation with the
correct experts resident, it is not:

    loop      mean 0.916  median 0.866  p<0.2 at 18.9%
    real text mean 1.305-1.781, median 0.410-1.096, p<0.2 at 30.7-40.4%

By mean the loop sits 0.53 below real text - real signal, but real text itself
spans a comparable range, so a global threshold sits inside the interval it is
meant to discriminate. By median the loop is MORE surprising than real chat,
so a median rule fires backwards. And per-character a floor is impossible:
20-35% of real characters are predicted at p>0.9, because finishing a word is
not a failure of imagination.

What does separate, with no overlap, is the fraction of positions where the
model is genuinely uncertain. That reframes the thing being detected: a loop
is not confident text, it is text that has stopped making choices. Mean p of
the chosen character in a loop is 0.500, which is not confident at all - the
distribution is flat and the argmax is merely stable.

Recorded as route D with a deterministic rule, ranked above expert rotation,
and with the caveat that wikipedia sits at 20.2% against the loop's 18.9%.

subject: Plot a run from the sample log, which is the record that survives
body:
samples.txt is appended at every checkpoint and outlives restarts, so it
reaches further back than anything held in memory - 198 checkpoints from step
94. The header gained the corpus total partway through the project, so the
parser has to read both shapes or it silently drops the first half of the
history, which it did: 103 of 198.

Plotted against characters read rather than step, because the context window
moves during a run and a step is not a fixed amount of reading.

Anything about the pool comes from expert_history.jsonl instead, which is
written at every growth decision rather than every checkpoint. That log
accumulates rows from tool runs against copies of the weights as well as from
training, and a twelve-expert smoke test drawn on the same axes as a
158-expert pool is a diagonal across the whole figure. Segments shorter than
--min-rows are dropped.

subject: Gate growth on the gap it was guarding against, not on a proxy for it
body:
The density ceiling was a guess I made and then cited as though it were a
measurement. The two numbers behind it were real - 96 parameters per character
read gave train 1.63 against held-out 2.75, and the project's best run carried
0.39 - but 8.0 was picked between them and never tested. It then held growth
off for 14M characters.

Checked against 117 checkpoints of the live run, the proxy does not track what
it stands for:

    density   n    train  held-out    gap
     8-10    18    1.157    1.215   0.058
    10-14    54    1.197    1.308   0.111
    14-20    35    1.061    1.211   0.150
    20-40    10    1.036    1.102   0.066

Correlation with the gap is +0.20, and it is not even monotonic - the gap at
density 20-40 is LOWER than at 10-14. Nothing in the observed range shows the
memorising the ceiling exists to prevent; that appeared at 96, an order of
magnitude above where the gate sat.

There is a second reason the proxy misleads here. Its denominator counts
characters read, so it cannot tell one pass over a large corpus from many
passes over a small one - and memorising needs the second. This run has read
0.66% of one pass over 7.9B characters and has never seen the same character
twice.

So growth is now gated on the generalisation gap directly, which is the
evidence rather than a stand-in for it: hold when held-out minus train exceeds
growth.max_gap, default 0.4. Every gap this run has produced lies between
0.058 and 0.150; the run that genuinely memorised showed 1.12.

The density ceiling stays as a backstop at 40, above anything measured here,
because parameters per character is still the right shape of worry once a
corpus is small enough to be re-read.

Growth resumes at the next decision rather than in five hours.

subject: Pay for capacity with information, not with characters
body:
The backstop counted parameters per character read, which assumes every
character is worth the same. Measured on this model they are not: a character
of chess costs 0.744 nats to predict and a character of wikipedia 1.686, so
the same million characters carries 2.27x the information from one as from the
other.

That gets the direction exactly wrong. Repetitive text needs LESS capacity to
predict, not more, and counting characters would let a long run of chess buy
as much capacity as a run of encyclopaedia. The unit was the problem, not just
the threshold.

The loss is the information content of what was read, in nats, so integrating
it over the run is the honest measure of what the model has had to account
for. read_nats now rides in the manifest beside read_chars, and the backstop
is parameters per nat.

A checkpoint written before this has characters but no information count, and
starting from zero would make the ratio enormous and silently re-block growth
for six hours after the upgrade. It is seeded instead from the held-out score,
which is the model's own estimate of what a character of text like that was
worth.

subject: Judge growth on the network as it stands, not on the run's history
body:
Every condition now reads the pool or the training statistics of the moment.
Nothing integrates over the run.

Gone: the ceiling on parameters per character - later per nat - read since the
model was created. It was wrong three ways. Its unit ignored that a character
of chess costs 0.744 nats to predict and one of wikipedia 1.686, so a long run
of chess bought as much capacity as a run of encyclopaedia. It did not track
what it stood in for - across 117 checkpoints its correlation with the
generalisation gap was +0.20 and not monotonic. And it was set to 8.0, an
order of magnitude below the 96 where memorising was actually observed, so it
held growth off for 14M characters on evidence that did not exist.

What replaces it is what it was always a proxy for, asked directly:

  ROOM      disk and VRAM, now
  USED      what share of gates sit far below the median, now
  EARNING   whether experts that recently finished their trial cleared the
            bar, read from born and gate, now
  HONEST    train against held-out, now

USED is measured relative to the median gate rather than against a fixed
number, because gates are strongly bimodal: on the live pool 127 of 157 sit
around 0.42 and 27 below 0.05, with 0.05 to 0.10 completely empty. Any
threshold inside that valley gives the same answer, so 15%, 25% and 50% of the
median all count the same 27 experts. The absolute 0.005 it replaced sat far
below the valley and reported ONE idle expert where 27 were contributing
almost nothing.

One thing genuinely cannot be done this way, and a test caught it: "the batch
I added was all pruned" is a fact about experts that no longer exist. That
question is gone rather than faked. What holds the line instead is visible in
the present - an expert is born below the idle threshold, so every addition
counts as idle until it earns a gate, and four fruitless batches take the idle
share from 17% to 25% and growth stops on its own. It resumes as soon as they
start contributing.

subject: Carry the information count through the exit save too
body:
Two places write the manifest - the periodic checkpoint and the save at the
end of a normal run - and only the first had been given read_nats. A run that
finished cleanly therefore dropped it, and the next run re-seeded from the
held-out score as though it had never been counted. read_chars had the same
shape of bug once before, for the same reason.

Both sites now write the same keys, and a test in the commit checks they
agree rather than trusting that they do.

subject: Size the routers by the pool, not by a ceiling that ratchets
body:
A restart died on load:

    size mismatch for recur.0.mlp.router.weight: copying a param with shape
    torch.Size([157, 512]) from checkpoint, the shape in current model is
    torch.Size([158, 512])

pool_max was doing two jobs that look like one. It sizes the per-token
routers, which keep one row per EXPERT, so a checkpoint's routers only fit a
model built at the same count. It was also read as the growth ceiling, where
equalling the current size makes room = n < max_experts false forever and a
restarted pool can never grow.

Fixing the second broke the first. Widening pool_max to
max(cfg.pool_max, n_experts) unlatched the ceiling, but the manifest's
pool_max ratchets up and never comes down - so once a prune took the pool from
158 to 157, the max() still read 158, the routers were built a row too wide,
and load_state_dict refused the whole model. The directory could not be opened
at all.

The two jobs are now separate. Sizing follows n_experts exactly, which is the
only number that can be right. The ceiling lives with the grower, which takes
args.pool_max.

Worth noting what made this expensive: nothing was wrong with the weights.
Every part of weights/ agreed - manifest 157, telemetry 157, routers 157, 157
files on disk - and the model that could not read them was built wrong by the
loader. The test added here checks a directory against itself as well as
checking the sizing rule, because that is the form the failure took.

subject: Show the routing mechanism, from a real decision rather than a drawing
body:
Two clocks and an indirection, and prose was not carrying it. This captures
one real decision - the trained model reading real text - and animates it in
five acts: the pool, what asks for an expert, the choice, the addressing, and
what happens per character.

Nothing is drawn by hand. The demand, its two halves, the slot table before
and after, and every per-character routing weight come from
tools/capture_routing.py, which loads the checkpoint and reads the corpus.

The capture warms up first, deliberately. The card starts empty, so the FIRST
decision fills all 32 slots and shows no hysteresis at all - it has nothing to
displace. Reading six chunks first makes the captured decision a real one: 26
slots stayed and 6 moved.

PooledMLP gains `record_weights`, off by default. `last_route` counts how
often a slot was picked, which is 1/k for every pick and therefore says
nothing - and the weight is the whole point, because an expert gated to zero
is chosen exactly as often as one gated to 0.9 and contributes nothing. With
weights recorded the bars vary from 0.00025 to 0.83 and the picture means
something.

tools/expert_state.py replaces the recency half of tools/expert_usage.py,
which reads `since` and calls it "segments since last admitted". `since` is
written only when an expert is newly ADMITTED, so an expert that never leaves
the card keeps its arrival time forever. `last_seen` is the right buffer.

subject: Redraw the graphs whenever the sample log gains an entry
body:
A graph that has to be remembered is a graph that is out of date when it is
looked at. The sample log is the record a run leaves; the graphs are the same
record as a picture, and the two should never disagree about what step it is.

write_samples now calls refresh_plots() once the entry is on disk. It draws
runs/training_progress.png always, and runs/training_recent.png from
plots.since - the corpus changed twice during this project and each change
lifted the loss, so the whole history on one axis hides everything that
happened after it.

Drawn in a separate process and not waited for. It takes about two seconds
against a ten-minute sample interval, but a training step should not be held
up by matplotlib for any length of time, and a plotting bug must not be able
to stop a run that has been going for days. A drawing still in progress is
skipped rather than queued, and a missing plotter turns the hook off instead
of raising once every ten minutes.

--no-plots disables it.

subject: Let config.yaml decide how much recurrence depth training pays for
body:
Training does not halt. With targets present the model runs every one of
max_steps passes and takes the halting-weighted mixture of their losses,
because the halting head only learns through those weights. So the adaptive
compute this model has saves nothing while training: every character costs all
six passes, and the recurrence is 24 of the 26 block applications - very
nearly the whole model.

RecurConfig has had train_steps_mean since the start, and it draws a fresh
depth each step instead. It was only reachable from cmd_train, which is not
the path anything uses, and the read path inherited 0.0 from the checkpoint
forever. It is now model.train_steps_mean in config.yaml, and the flag wins
over the manifest: how to spend compute is a decision about now, not a
property of the weights.

The setting is not the mean depth, which is worth saying loudly because the
obvious reading is wrong. The draw is poisson(this) + 1, clipped:

    setting   mean depth   recurrent compute
       1.0        2.00          33%
       2.0        2.98          50%
       3.0        3.87          64%

Nothing changes at inference, which still runs the ceiling and lets halting
decide. What to watch if it is turned on is the halting head: the deepest
steps get trained more rarely, and inference leans on exactly those.

subject: Write down what the model predicts, not only what the guard lets through
body:
samples.txt showed one reading of each prompt: greedy with the adaptation
trace. Instrumented character by character, that guard overruled the model on
28 of 72 choices - more than a third of the text there was the decoding rule
talking, and nothing said so. Reasoning about the model from it was reasoning
about the guard.

Now every prompt is read twice, both deterministic:

  raw       plain greedy, no guard of any kind. What the model actually
            predicts, and the only text here that describes the MODEL.
  adapted   the same with the trace, which is easier to read and partly
            written by the rule.

Where the two agree, the guard is doing nothing. Where they diverge is exactly
where the model is falling into a hole - a signal that was invisible while
only the guarded text was kept.

The header line now carries the repeat rate of the RAW reading, because that
is a fact about the model and the number a better model should drive down on
its own. Held down from outside by a decoding rule it says nothing; left alone
it is a benchmark.

No temperature anywhere. Sampling would make the text look better by rolling
dice against the model's own prediction, which is a different thing from the
model being right - and reproducibility was never the argument for greedy,
since CUDA does not give that anyway.

--sample-raw-only drops the guarded reading, for when the raw text no longer
needs it.

Two things this cost, both mine: the sample_now rewrite spliced out the _PLOTS
declaration, and inserting the depth documentation stranded max_steps' comment
on train_steps_mean. Both restored. train_steps_mean was already in
config.yaml at 3.0 - what was broken is that cmd_read took it from the
manifest instead, which said 0.

subject: One block per row, so halting can stop after any of them
body:
The model could only choose its effort in multiples of four. A pass was three
recur blocks and a coda, halting spoke only between passes, and the shallowest
thing a character could ask for was four rows. Measured on one character, the
model put 94.2% of its halting mass at the first opportunity and then ran 20
more rows, 160 expert evaluations, weighted at 5.8%. It wanted to stop sooner
and had no way to say so.

n_recur 1, n_coda 0, max_steps 6 -> 24. The ceiling of 24 block applications
is unchanged; what changes is that halting now speaks after every one.

tools/collapse_depth.py converts rather than retrains. Of 561M parameters,
4.2M change shape - the four pooled blocks becoming one. All 177 experts, the
prelude, the adapter, the head and the norms carry over. Six ways of making
one block from four were built and scored on held-out rather than guessed at;
the mean of all four won at 3.1695.

FIVE settings are counted in ROWS and every one had to be rescaled, because a
row stopped being four blocks:

    train_steps_mean  2.5 -> 12.8   2.5 now means 3.5 rows, not 13.7
    halt_prior        0.4 -> 0.072  0.4 asks the model to stop at 2.5 rows
    bptt_window       4   -> 16     4 of 6 passes was 16 rows
    min_steps         1            value fine, never read by the read path
    ponder_beta       0.01         value fine, was not in config at all

Three of those were not in config.yaml at all - they lived in the manifest,
where editing config could never reach them. All five are wired now, and the
read path prints what it is using.

Getting one wrong is SILENT. Left at 0.4, halt_prior made every character stop
at row 1 and the model ran almost no computation; held-out was 3.17 either way
and no curve showed it. It was caught by watching the depth animation, which
is why that animation exists.

config.yaml states the rescaling rule once, and marks which keys BUILD a model
against which ones RUN it - editing d_model or n_recur on trained weights does
nothing, and that confusion is what made this a conversion.

Where it stands: 3.1764 at conversion, 2.4887 after ~25 minutes. The block is
not yet worth iterating - row 1 scores 2.62 and row 24 scores 4.46, so halting
at 1 is currently correct rather than stale. tools/row_depth_curve.py is the
measurement that says whether that changes.

subject: Let the learning-rate schedule start again when the regime does
body:
The schedule is keyed on characters read over the model's whole life, so a
restart continues it rather than starting over. That is right for a restart
and wrong for a change of regime: after the collapse to one block per row the
model is relearning most of its trunk, and the count says it is finished.
71M characters against a 60M horizon pins it at the floor, 3e-5.

It now counts from lr_origin, carried in the manifest beside read_chars, and
--lr-reset moves that anchor to here. read_chars stays the honest total; this
is a separate number for a separate purpose.

After a reset: 3e-4 at the top of the warm-up, still 2.8e-4 ten million
characters later, back to the floor at sixty.

Worth remembering against this: a sweep on the OLD model found 3e-5 was best
of four, and every increase made held-out worse - 1e-4 by +0.07, 3e-4 by
+0.24. That was measured on a model sitting near its optimum. This one just
changed shape and is at 2.44 against the 1.19 it had, which is a different
situation - but it is a reason to watch the first hour rather than assume.

Also fixes sample_now, which never disabled gradients. model.eval() only
changes dropout, so every generated character was retained in a graph across
all 24 rows of expert dispatch, chained to the last through `cur`, and none of
it was ever backpropagated. It had always been marginal; writing two readings
per prompt doubled it and put sampling out of memory while training itself sat
at 3.8 GB. Sampling now costs 0.06 GB.

And a guard at startup for a config written against a different shape:
bptt_window above max_steps makes the detach condition never fire, so nothing
is detached and the whole chain is held - which is how a config meant for a
24-row model put a 6-row model out of memory.

subject: Anneal over four days rather than one
body:
lr_horizon 60 -> 240 million characters. 60 is the horizon for a run with a
fixed budget: anneal over the whole thing and finish. This run is open-ended
and has read 0.9% of its corpus, so 60M floored the rate after about a day and
left the remaining 99% to be read at the minimum.

At ~700 char/s, 240M is about four days to the floor, and holds the rate above
1e-4 until 150M characters.

subject: plot: fit the trend to the current regime, not across the architecture change
body:
The power-law fit spanned the collapse to one block per row, so it averaged
two different models and reported loss ~ chars^0.29 - rising - while the model
was in fact recovering fast. It now detects the last jump larger than four
error bars, marks it, and fits only what follows: chars^-1.61.

The best-score marker was stuck at 60M for the same reason and now reports the
best of the current regime, with the all-time best kept in the console line.

subject: pool: a read-only mode, so tools can inspect a live training directory
body:
Tiers.put marks an expert dirty on page-IN, unconditionally, so it is written
back on eviction even in pure eval with no gradients. Any visualisation
pointed at a directory a run owns was writing expert files underneath it.

read_only defaults to False, so the training path is unchanged. Where it is
set nothing is marked dirty, flush is a no-op, and _to_disk raises rather than
writing - a tool that would have written now fails loudly instead.

subject: recur: accumulate the halting mixture once, and draw the trunk
body:
The mixture was accumulated twice - the second copy re-added the term to the
total it had just been folded into - so the returned logits were exactly 2x.
Both call sites bind logits and discard it, and the loss is built from
loss_terms rather than from this, so nothing downstream was wrong. Anything
that started reading them would have been.

tools/trunk_anatomy.py draws the trunk from a real weights directory: the
forward path with every parameter placed, and the backward path with its three
rules. Tied embeddings are counted once, which is what makes the trunk 8.135M
rather than the 8.271M a naive sum over core.npz reports.

subject: draw the trunk the way transformers are normally drawn
body:
The first attempt drew boxes and arrows without the two things that make a
transformer diagram readable: the residual stream, and the tensor shape on
every arrow. Three figures replace it.

block_opened  one block with the stream down the left and both sub-layers
              opened - attention through W_qkv, heads, RoPE and W_o; the
              feed-forward as its three matrices with one branch gating the
              other. Pre-norm, so norm sits inside the branch and the stream
              is only ever added to.
trunk_stack   the whole model as a vertical tower, bottom to top, shapes on
              every arrow, the recurrence as a loop back into the adapter.
trunk_bptt    the loop unrolled left to right with the backward pass drawn on
              it. All 24 passes at the real bptt_window of 16, so the cut
              falls after pass 8 where it actually falls - the earlier version
              drew it after pass 2 and mislabelled the elided passes.

Halting mass per pass is measured, not assumed: pass 1 carries 58%.

subject: pool: the growth docstring still described PAID, which is gone
body:
PAID and growth.max_density were removed when the generalisation gap replaced
them; the docstring kept pointing at a config key that no longer exists, which
is a good way to send someone hunting for the wrong brake.

subject: the learning rate is governed by held-out, not by a horizon
body:
A cosine schedule asserts that the run ends. For a model that reads
continually that is false, and it failed in a specific way: when the regime
changed, a count of characters already read said the model was finished when
it had just started again. That is why --lr-reset had to exist. This replaces
the schedule with the thing the reset was doing by hand.

config.yaml training now has exactly two knobs, lr and trunk_lr_mult.
lr_horizon, lr_warmup and lr_floor are gone, and a config still carrying them
fails at startup rather than being silently ignored. lr_origin is gone from
the manifest; --lr-reset survives as a manual override that restores full
plasticity.

Two rules, pointing opposite ways, which is the point - a cosine can only go
down:

  PLATEAU  a least-squares slope over a growing window, tested against its own
           standard error. It steps the rate down by 0.7, never below 0.05x.
  REGIME   held-out jumped several standard errors and was still there at the
           next evaluation - the rate steps back up by 2x, capped at 1x.

Both thresholds come from the measured scatter, so there is nothing to tune.

The window has to grow, and the reason is measured. Over 228 real evaluations
held-out fell 1.5471 -> 1.2192: 0.00144 per evaluation against a median
standard error of 0.1026, so the improvement is seventy times smaller than the
noise on one reading. The first version compared half-window means over 20
evaluations and called that healthy stretch a plateau nine times, driving the
rate to the floor - caught by replaying the real log in the test. Half-means
need ~120 evaluations to reach significance; a fitted slope needs ~60, because
it uses the ordering as well as the values. Nothing faster is a better rule,
only a guess.

tests/test_plasticity.py replays the real log and asserts zero step-downs,
asserts a flat run IS throttled, that a confirmed regime change raises the
rate while a single bad evaluation does not, and that the floor holds.

subject: measure what a newborn expert actually computes
body:
Growth has a 10% survival rate - 201 of 224 born experts pruned - and the
reason is measurable rather than a matter of fairness. On real hidden states
captured from the running model:

  two existing experts, output cosine   median +0.042
  a newborn against its parent          +0.980

The pool has specialised into near-orthogonal functions, and a newborn is a
duplicate of the busiest member. It cannot earn a gate because raising it only
double-counts a contribution the parent already makes.

The seeding noise is the direct cause. add_experts adds 0.02*randn while
expert weights have std 0.023, so the noise was never small - and because it
is ABSOLUTE, a parent with larger weights than average gets proportionally
less of it. The busiest expert, which is the one always cloned, is exactly
that parent: weight cosine to its child is 0.928.

tools/birth_probe.py measures redundancy, novelty and output scale for any
birth scheme against the population benchmark.

subject: a newborn expert is recombined from the pool, not cloned from one member
body:
Six birth schemes were born into the same pool at the same step and trained
together on the same text, so nothing separates them but the scheme. Mean gate
after 1,825 steps against a prune bar of 0.005:

    clone + 0.02 noise (the old default)   0.00095   0 of 4 cleared
    clone + 2x its own std                 0.00195   0 of 4
    crossover with one other expert        0.00128   0 of 4
    fresh random, rescaled                 0.00121   0 of 4
    recombination from 16 experts          0.02410   4 of 4
    ...the same, rescaled                  0.02792   3 of 4

The old default declined from its birth gate, which explains the 201 of 224
experts pruned in the live run. Measured on real states its output sits at
0.98 cosine to its parent where two established experts sit at 0.04, so
raising its gate only double-counted what the pool already had. The router
agreed: the failing schemes drew 14k-69k selections, the recombined ones 2.7M
to 3.9M.

A random expert failed for the OPPOSITE reason - perfectly novel, and
computing nothing worth routing to. Novelty is not the property; novelty built
from TRAINED parts is. Rescaling the output made no reliable difference and is
not adopted: the gate is itself a learned scale, so a quiet expert that is
worth hearing gets amplified anyway. The unrescaled scheme was 4 of 4 and the
rescaled one 3 of 4.

A hidden unit is (w1[u], w3[u], w2[:, u]) and units are interchangeable, so
whole units are taken from different experts - each unit's learned function
stays intact while the composition is one nothing in the pool computes. The
expert the caller asked to split stays among the sources. recombine=0 restores
the old clone.

Also here: add_experts grows a `make` seam so a scheme can be supplied from
outside; --grow-every 0 no longer divides by zero; and the per-checkpoint
history is written on a dry read too, so an experiment that does not want its
weights kept can still record what happened.

subject: plumb read_only through load_recur, and keep the trimmed config comment
prune: never empty the pool, and index with a long tensor
body:
torch.tensor([]) is float32, so a prune that kept nothing crashed on the first
index rather than doing anything useful. Reachable when every expert is old,
silent and flat and none happens to be resident - unlikely in a healthy run,
certain in a collapsed one, and the crash hid the real problem, which is that
a pool of zero experts cannot route at all. The best-gated expert now survives
whatever the thresholds say.

subject: one definition of a dead gate, stable expert ids, and moments that survive
body:
THE DEADLOCK. saturation() called an expert idle below idle_gate_frac of the
median gate; prune deleted only below an absolute 0.005. Measured on the live
model: 44 of 175 experts sat in the gap - counted as idle capacity so the USED
condition failed and growth was blocked at 0.2514 against a ceiling of 0.25,
and none of them below 0.005 so pruning could never clear it. The pool could
neither grow nor shrink. saturation()'s own docstring had already worked out
that 0.005 was too low and the fix was never propagated.

Both now read PagedPool.dead_gate(). prune.min_gate is gone from config; what
counts as dead is growth.idle_gate_frac of the median, and anything counted
idle is by construction eligible to be deleted. AutoGrow._earning reads the
same line. A relative bar also cannot empty a pool: a uniform collapse leaves
nothing below its own median, which is a safety property the tests pin down.

STABLE IDS. An expert's file is named by a uid it keeps for life. Pruning used
to renumber - one deletion could rename every other file, and every record
written by position, expert_history.jsonl included, silently stopped meaning
what it said. Nothing is renamed now; the directory simply has holes, and a
new expert takes the next id rather than a dead one. A directory written
before ids existed has files named by position, which is exactly what
uid = arange gives, so it loads unchanged.

MOMENTS. Growing or pruning builds a new gate tensor and new routers, and the
optimiser dropped their Adam state - so every 400 steps the machinery that
decides WHICH expert to use restarted its moment estimates from nothing.
_carry slices the moments on a prune and pads them on a growth.

The birth-gate guard now compares against the relative line rather than a
number that no longer exists.

subject: plasticity: drop a field that was always zero, report what it is thinking
body:
since_action was written into every manifest and never incremented - the
plateau rule was rewritten to use len(hist) and the old counter was left
behind. It read 0 forever, which is exactly what a broken controller would
also look like.

state() now carries n, t and needs: how many evaluations have been gathered
since it last acted, how many standard errors of downward slope they show, and
how many it would need before declaring a plateau. A manifest can be read
without re-deriving any of it.

subject: the zoomed graph is a trailing window, and the full one is log-log
body:
plots.since was set to 40 when the run had read 60M characters. At 189M that
window covered the whole history and the zoom had quietly stopped zooming -
the same failure as an absolute prune bar, a number that means something at
one scale and nothing at another. It is plots.last now: how much the graph
covers, counted back from wherever reading has got to.

The full history gets a log character axis. It spans decades, and a power law
is a straight line on log-log, so the fitted trend becomes a ruler and a
departure from it is visible rather than inferred. The zoomed graph stays
linear: inside a trailing window the axis covers a factor of one and a bit,
where a log scale says nothing. The loss axis was already log.

--plot-since still works as an alias.

subject: a new expert gets 4800 steps, not 1600
body:
The bar it has to clear moved nine times further when a dead gate became 0.15
of the median instead of an absolute 0.005, and its deadline did not move at
all. Measured: a recombined expert reached 0.024 by 1,825 steps and was still
rising at ~0.0018 per 100, so it needs roughly 3,200-4,000 to reach the bar.
The eight on trial in the live run sat at 0.0011 to 0.0323 against a bar of
0.0499 - they were being killed mid-climb.

The oscillation this produced is not itself a problem: measured over the 32
checkpoints since the big prune, the FLOOR of the oscillation rises 131 -> 136
at +0.21 experts per window, so newborns are being adopted, only slowly.

Widening the window also widens the one KEPT judges over, which was reading a
sample of 4 experts and made the growth brake very noisy.

subject: save the experts under the names they actually have
body:
Stable ids broke saving, and the run would not start:

    size mismatch for pool.gate: copying a param with shape [137] from
    checkpoint, the shape in current model is [128]

_save_paged built each expert's filename from its POSITION, which was the
same as its name until pruning stopped renumbering. After that it skipped
every position whose file had a different name - 9 of 137 - and wrote
n_experts as that file count while saving 137 router rows. Worse, of the 128
it did record, 73 were paired with a file and a gate belonging to whichever
expert happened to share their number.
