The filename now comes from the uid, the entry records that uid, and
n_experts is the pool's own count rather than a file tally: the router
tensors were just written with one row per expert and loading sizes itself
from that number, so a count that disagrees is a shape error rather than a
warning. A pool whose files are genuinely missing now says so instead.

No weights were lost - 137 files, 137 telemetry rows and 137 router rows all
agreed; only the count was wrong, and it has been repaired in place
(manifest.json.bak keeps the broken one).

tools/repair_pool.py predates ids and assumes file number == router row.
Under uids it already misreported 9 live experts as missing and 9 files as
undescribed, and with --apply it would have dropped live experts and paired
the survivors with the wrong rows. It refuses on such a directory now, and
names the three things that must agree. Where it does renumber, it resets the
identity map to match.

tests/test_save_roundtrip.py prunes, grows, saves and reloads, and holds the
invariant: n_experts == len(uid) == router rows == files, with each entry
carrying its own gate.

subject: three efficiency ideas tested; one works and costs too much, two are dead
body:
TRAINING SHALLOWER: 1.93x faster, and it takes the model's depth with it.
train_steps_mean 12.8 -> 5 raised throughput from 668 to 1,300 char/s and cut
peak VRAM from 7,058 to 5,722 MiB. Held-out wobbled (1.218 -> 1.287 -> 1.233)
and returned inside the measurement noise, so 45 minutes cannot say whether
quality suffers. What it can say is that the depth CAPABILITY collapses:

    domain      mean before  after      max before  after
    stories            2.66   2.36              14      8
    code               2.84   2.49               8      6
    chess              5.75   3.47              13      7
    reasoning          2.72   2.54              15      7
    wikipedia          5.17   3.51              14     11

Every ceiling fell. The mechanism is the forced lam=1 on the last SAMPLED
pass: it teaches the model that its deepest option is six, so it stops asking
for more. The hardest domains lost most - chess -40%, wikipedia -32% - which
are exactly the ones that were spending depth productively.

So the 6.3% of halting mass beyond pass 3 was not waste. The mean understated
it because the distribution is heavy-tailed: most characters need one pass,
the few that need fourteen are the ones that matter, and removing the
opportunity removed the capability. Not adopted.

GRAD CHECKPOINTING OFF: does not fit. 7,792 MiB peak and an OOM inside the
pool's bmm even at train_steps_mean 5, and still OOM with bptt_window 3 at
6,770 MiB. The 1.3 GB depth frees is not the ~2 GB this needs. Kept as
--no-pool-checkpoint because the measurement is worth being able to repeat.

MORE EVAL CHUNKS: the premise was wrong. Stderr does not fall with chunk
count - 0.0496 at 8, 0.0511 at 32, 0.0962 at 128 - because
FolderEvaluator pools windows ACROSS domains, so it measures how much chess
differs from wikipedia rather than how precisely the mean is known. Computed
within domain and pooled, the real figure is 0.0178 against a reported 0.0398:
overstated 2.2x, and the plots' shaded band with it.

Also recorded: depth has been RISING with training - stories 2.03 -> 2.66,
chess 4.86 -> 5.74, reasoning 1.51 -> 2.72 since the earlier measurement - and
runs/shape.mp4 is recaptured on wikipedia, the domain that spends most.

subject: measure what the gradient clip is actually clipping
body:
Three questions, 200 real training steps against the live weights, read-only.

The pool carries 2.4% of the squared gradient norm. The trunk carries the rest
- median 2.373 against the pool's 0.365 - because every character passes
through the trunk while an expert only gets gradient when it is routed, and
then scaled by its gate. So a global clip_grad_norm_ over all 606M parameters
is, in practice, a clip on the 8.1M trunk.

That matters because the clip is not neutral for the trunk. trunk_lr_mult was
measured at 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1 with 0.1 clearly best, so the trunk does better
with smaller steps - and the clip at 1.0 is currently supplying extra damping,
firing on 99.5% of steps at a median truncation of 0.42x. Raising it to 3.0
would fire on 23.5% instead, which restores the clip as an outlier detector
but also loosens exactly the thing that prefers to be tight.

Counterfactual Adam step, clip 1.0 against 3.0, from the current moments:
cosine 0.9488, magnitude 1.165x. Modest, and not the no-op scale-invariance
suggests, because the truncation factor varies from 0.1x to 1.0x rather than
being constant.

Caveat: the probe draws random windows, so each step starts from a cold
context and its gradients run larger than the reader's - median 2.40 here
against 1.53 reported by the live run.

subject: probe: how long a trunk gradient stays useful, and whether domains agree
body:
AdEMAMix's premise is that old gradients remain informative for far longer
than beta1=0.9 assumes, and beta3=0.9999 is the paper's number for the paper's
setting. Whether it is right here is measurable: the autocorrelation of the
trunk gradient against lag says how far back an average can usefully reach,
and the cross-domain cosine says whether a slow average accumulates a shared
direction or cancels a fight.

Measured on the trunk alone because it carries 97.6% of the gradient norm, and
because the thing a slow EMA would reconstruct - a gradient balanced across
subjects - is exactly what this reader cannot compute directly: one KV cache
is 1.74 GB at a 32,768 window, so seven simultaneous lanes will not fit on the
card.

subject: a slow gradient average for the trunk, and a meter for how much is signal
body:
MEASURED FIRST. tools/grad_memory.py asks whether AdEMAMix's premise holds
here rather than assuming it. The trunk gradient never decorrelates - cosine
against lag settles on a floor near 0.11-0.15 out to lag 1024, which is
524,288 characters - so beta3 = 0.999 is what the data supports and the
paper's 0.9999 is extrapolation past anything measured.

Subjects agree weakly and positively: cross-domain cosine averages +0.070,
against +0.25 to +0.38 for consecutive steps within one subject. Two clusters,
nearly orthogonal to each other at +0.029: language (stories, reasoning,
wikipedia, chat; mean +0.158) and symbolic (chess, arithmetic; +0.109), with
code between. So a step is mostly domain-specific, which is why the trunk has
to crawl at trunk_lr_mult 0.1.

THEN TESTED, three arms from an identical start, twenty minutes each:

    adamw              1.2206
    ademamix alpha 5   1.4922   +0.272
    ademamix alpha 1   1.2343   +0.014

alpha 5 - the paper's setting - is a large, real degradation. The reason is
that alpha multiplies the trunk's effective step, and this trunk was measured
to need small ones: trunk_lr_mult went 0.3, 0.2, 0.1 with 0.1 clearly best, so
alpha 5 undoes that choice. At alpha 1 it is indistinguishable from AdamW,
which is the most twenty minutes can say - improvement is 0.0014 per
evaluation against 0.018 of noise.

Default stays adamw. --trunk-opt ademamix is available with alpha and beta3
exposed.

GradSNR reports how much of the trunk gradient is signal, every eight steps,
and acts on nothing. It reads the same in both arms - 0.198 falling to 0.012 -
because it measures the data, not the optimiser. The fall is the finding: as
its window grows past one subject visit the average collapses, so beyond a
single visit only about one per cent of the gradient energy survives.

subject: the rate controller answers the latest evidence, and says what it is thinking
body:
WHAT THE NOISE ACTUALLY IS. Evaluated five times with the model frozen, the
held-out score repeats to a standard deviation of 0.0010 - the evaluator reads
the same files in the same order and is effectively deterministic. The
checkpoint-to-checkpoint scatter is about 0.040, forty times larger. So it was
never measurement noise: the model itself moves 0.04 nats every four minutes
while improving 0.0014 per evaluation. More eval chunks would have bought
nothing, which is why raising them did nothing when it was tried.

THE RULE IS NOW SYMMETRIC, AND IT NUDGES. Every 8 evaluations, on a window
that grows to 64 and then slides:

    t > 2.0   improvement is provable        -> rate x1.05, capped at 1
    t < 0.5   no evidence either way         -> rate x0.95, floored at 0.05
    between   hold

The old rule acted only at 120 evaluations and only downward, so in twenty
hours of running it never moved once and there was nothing to watch. Measured
on a flat series at the real scatter, the new one starts easing at 16
evaluations and reaches x0.28 over 256. Replayed against the actual log of
this run, which is improving, it eases nothing and holds at x1.000.

AND IT IS VISIBLE. samples.txt now carries "evidence t +N.NN over M rate xS",
and the learning-rate panel plots t on a second axis with the two thresholds
marked - so the rate is readable even while it is flat, because the number
that decides it is on the graph.

subject: the rate controller was waiting on a modulo, and could not say it was worse
body:
Found by reading the graph on the live run: evidence t sat at -2.74 - held-out
provably rising - with the rate still at x1.000 and no event recorded.

The check was scheduled as (n - MINWIN) % STRIDE == 0, so it fired only at
window lengths 16, 24, 32, 40. The window is restored from a checkpoint at
whatever length it had, which was 33, so n went 34, 35, 36 and the next check
was not due until 40 - four evaluations, forty minutes, of visibly negative
evidence and no response. It is now measured from the last check rather than
from the window length, so a restart cannot delay it and an older checkpoint
without the field checks immediately.

Second, t < 0.5 lumped "no evidence either way" together with "provably going
the wrong way". Those are different facts and now get different answers:
below -2.0 is named deteriorating and eases 0.90 rather than 0.95.

Replaying the actual log of this run, which has been rising from 1.19 to 1.29
over the last five million characters, the controller now ends at x0.886
instead of x1.000.

subject: the rate eases continuously, on a fit with no window at all
body:
The staircase had two causes and the smaller one was the schedule. The larger
was the window itself: a hard window of N steps whenever its oldest reading
drops out the back, which is a jump in the SIGNAL that then becomes a jump in
the rate. Measured on this run's log, t on a window of 8 read +4.90 while t on
a window of 64 read -4.38 - the same data, opposite conclusions, and every
window boundary a discontinuity.

The evidence is now an exponentially weighted least-squares fit of held-out
against evaluation index, kept as running sums with LAM 0.97 - an effective
memory of about 33 evaluations, and nothing ever falls off an edge. The rate
is nudged at EVERY evaluation by exp(NUDGE * tanh((t - T_MID) / T_W)), which
is about x0.992 where there is no evidence and x1.007 where improvement is
provable, continuous everywhere between. Compounded over eight evaluations
that is x0.935 and x1.056 - what the stepped rule did in one jump, so the
speed is unchanged and only the shape differs.

Replayed against the real log: 601 evaluations, the rate moving at every one
of them once off the ceiling, 1.000 down through 0.99185, 0.98306, 0.97428,
0.96556 ... to 0.915 as t crossed from +1.37 to -1.01. It sits at the ceiling
while improvement is provable, which is the only flat stretch left and the
correct one.

Also: t is capped at 50. A perfectly straight series drives the residual to
zero and the statistic to infinity - a test found it at -1,198,839 - and tanh
saturates long before 50, so the cap changes no decision.

subject: the rate controller was measuring patience, not progress
body:
t = slope/se(slope) grows as evidence accumulates whether or not the model
is still improving: se shrinks as sqrt(sxx), sxx converges to 35,926 for
LAM=0.97, so a full window turns any downward drift at all into a large t.
Measured on the real log, a slope of -0.0024 nats/evaluation - 0.06 nats
across the whole window, 0.59 of the standard error of ONE evaluation, ie.
nothing - scored t=+22 and bought the largest increase available. Replayed
over 635 checkpoints the old rule sat pinned at the ceiling for 308 of them.
It was not controlling the rate.

The deciding number is now an effect size, e = -slope/sigma: improvement per
evaluation in units of the residual scatter, which does not grow with the
evidence. EFFECT scales it so the 75th percentile of e over the real log
lands on T_MID, keeping the design's intent that decay is the default and an
increase has to be earned. The significance test is kept as a cap, not as the
signal. A second fit at LAM_FAST=0.85 caps it again by ITS effect size - not
its t, which is mechanically small for a short window and vetoed everything.

Replayed on the real log: over the last 16 checkpoints, where held-out is
flat at -0.00003 nats/evaluation, the old rule raised the rate 5.7% and the
new one lowers it 10.5%. A run improving at the real rate still keeps its
rate (x0.992). A decline that stops is noticed in 14 evaluations instead of
never.

Also: restarts perturbed the model because `keys` is a non-persistent buffer.
It was zero on resume, and route() skips the whole key term when the keys sum
to zero - half the routing mass, and the half that can speak for an expert
that is NOT resident. The router alone speaks only for the ~32 on the card,
so the other ~190 were ranked by gate alone, content-blind. Rebuilt at load
now, exactly, from w1; 10 s for 224 experts. gate_seen is persisted too, so
`flat` measures the change since the last prune rather than since zero.

subject: seeding the fast fit from the slow one made it not fast
body:
A checkpoint written before the fast fit existed has no F. Seeding it from S
looked kinder than starting empty; it is not. The copy carries the slow fit's
n_eff - measured on the live checkpoint, 56.5 against the 12.3 that LAM_FAST
is meant to give - so for the ~20 evaluations it takes to decay, the "fast"
reading is just the slow one again. On the live checkpoint 45*e_fast came out
at +1.69 against the slow fit's +1.57, ie. ABOVE it, so min() never took it
and the cap that exists to notice a stall early did nothing.

Empty is correct and costs nothing. MIN_EFF gates this cap alone, not the
controller: the slow fit keeps steering throughout, and the fast cap starts
working after 12 evaluations instead of misreporting for 20.

subject: coming down and going up are not the same question
body:
The down half of the nudge was useless. tanh is saturated by |arg| = 2, so
with T_W = 0.75 every verdict below about -0.3 produced the IDENTICAL
x0.99104: measured on the live run, -1.5, -4.0 and -12.0 all eased by exactly
0.9% while held-out rose 0.139 nats over nine evaluations and every one of the
eight domains got worse. The controller could see the fall perfectly well and
had one speed to answer it with.

A rate that is too high SHOWS you - held-out turns and keeps turning - so
deterioration is direct evidence of overshoot and deserves a response sized to
it. A rate that is merely working says nothing about whether a higher one
would work better, so upward stays a slow probe at NUDGE.

NUDGE_DOWN = 0.025 with T_W_DOWN = 6.0 spreads the response over the range the
verdict actually reaches: 2.7x the old step at -12, 2.3x at -5.7, and slightly
GENTLER than the old one just below neutral, where a flat step was too blunt.
Both constants were swept against every test in the suite plus the real 647
checkpoint log; this pair is the only one that never reaches the floor, keeps
a healthy slow run above x0.99, still eases a flat run to x0.14 over 256
evaluations, and still answers a stall in 14.

subject: prune for atrophy, not for a low gate
body:
The rule needed three conditions: past min_age, gate below the dead line, and
`flat` - the gate had not risen since the last check. `flat` was a trap. An
expert that is not resident does not train, so its gate CANNOT rise, so the
test was automatically true for exactly the experts being starved of the card,
and the low gate had the same cause. An expert failed two of the three tests
through neglect alone, and the third was only a clock.

Measured on the run's own expert_history.jsonl, over a collapse from 235
experts to 192 while held-out lost 0.13 nats: of the 68 deleted, 57 had been
admitted to the card within 8,600 steps of their deletion, a QUARTER had been
routed to in the very interval they were killed in, and their median age at
death was 5,076 steps against a min_age of 4,800 - 70% died within 1,200 steps
of the moment their protection expired. They were not failing; they were being
judged on a gate that neglect had frozen. A newborn gets ~48 admissions across
its trial against an incumbent's 2,184: 116 steps of actual residency out of
4,800, 2.4% of the window it is nominally given.

USE IT OR LOSE IT. An expert is deleted only when its gate is below the dead
line AND it has not been admitted once in `survival` steps, and never at all
inside its first `survival` steps. Being chosen is the one thing neglect
cannot fake. Replayed over the same collapse, 62 of the 68 survive and the 6
that were never observed being chosen still go: 235 -> 254 rather than
235 -> 192.

`last_seen` counts segments and survival is in steps, so the window is
converted with the pool's own cumulative ratio - self-calibrating, nothing
stored. prune.survival is in config.yaml; prune.min_age stays, now meaning
only the ROUTING trial (pool.trial), and prune.min_delta is gone.

The cost is deliberate: an expert with a healthy gate that is never chosen
again is immortal, because not chosen means not trained and an untrained gate
does not fall. That is bounded by disk, not by correctness.

subject: one number for the trial, and the dead line belongs under prune
body:
TWO NUMBERS WHERE THERE SHOULD HAVE BEEN ONE. `survival` set how long an
expert lives before it may be judged; `min_age` separately set the ROUTING
trial - the window in which a newborn competes on how well its key fits rather
than on its gate. But that waiver is the mechanism that gets a newborn CHOSEN,
and being chosen is now the only thing that keeps it alive. Split them at 4800
and 8600 and there is a 3,800-step window where the expert is handicapped but
still on the clock, and it is then judged on exactly the stretch when it was
least likely to be picked. `survival` now drives both. The moment it is judged
is the moment its fair turn ends.

growth.idle_gate_frac -> prune.dead_gate_frac. It decides what "dead" means,
so it belongs with the rule that kills for it. Still ONE number, read by the
pruner and the growth brake alike - that invariant is the whole reason the
pool could once neither grow nor shrink - and the old key is still honoured as
a fallback.

Also: the staleness window is TRAILING, and the comments now say so. An expert
that worked for 200,000 steps and has since gone quiet dies too; age earns
nothing permanent. Two tests added for it.

test_growth_trial's waiver check was flaky about 1 run in 5, and had been
before any of this: a recombined expert draws its hidden units at random, so
on an unlucky draw its key entered no top-k and both readings came back
bit-identical. Seeded before the pool is built; 10 of 10 runs now identical.

subject: the read path saved Adam's moments and never read them back
body:
optim.npz is written at every checkpoint. cmd_read built a fresh optimiser,
attached it to the pool, saved it faithfully - and never loaded it. On the one
path this project actually runs, every restart discarded 108.9 million moment
values, 99.9% of them non-zero, and Adam re-estimated its second moments from a
single gradient. The first steps after a restart are then large and badly
scaled, in a direction inferred from one batch, and it decays over a few
hundred steps. That is the held-out jump after every restart that then settles,
on a model whose whole premise is that it never stops training.

The tell was in the file: Adam's step counter read t = 2,381 at training step
458,000. It counts optimiser steps since the last RESTART, not since the run
began.

Restoring the pool's slot-indexed w1/w2/w3 moments is safe - swap_to overwrites
a slot's moments from the expert's own file the moment it is paged in, and
zeroes them if the file has none. pool.gate is per-expert and full width so it
restores exactly, and a pool that changed size is caught by the shape guard.

Measured in the new test: after a restart the first step now lands 5.7e-05 from
the step an uninterrupted run would have taken, against 1.2e-03 for a fresh
optimiser - 21x closer.

Also pool.now, the clock the expert trial is read against, was set only inside
the loop. For the first forward of a session it was still 0, making `now - born`
hugely negative for every expert grown in an earlier session, so all of them
passed `< trial` at once and the whole pool got the newborn's waiver - routing
on key fit with the gate ignored. One batch, but it is the first batch after
every restart. Set from the restored step before the loop.

subject: the disk ceiling was measured in fp32 moments that have always been bf16
body:
growth.max_disk_gb is enforced against PagedPool.disk_bytes(), which assumed
twelve bytes a parameter - "one fp32 weight and Adam's two fp32 moments". The
moments are bf16, and have been for as long as expert files have existed, so
an expert is EIGHT bytes a parameter: 25.2 MB, not 37.75. The estimate ran
1.52x over.

Measured on the live run: growth was refused at 261 experts because
(261 + 4) x 37.75 MB came to 10.003 GB against a 10.0 GB ceiling, while the
directory on disk held 6.48 GB and the drive had 43 GB free. The pool stopped
a third short of the budget it was given, then oscillated on the boundary -
losing one expert and regrowing four - because 260 + 4 fits and 261 + 4 does
not. Every other growth gate was wide open: 1 of 261 experts idle against a
limit of 0.25, VRAM at 0.89 of 0.95.

With 8 bytes a parameter the same 10 GB budget holds 397 experts instead of
264, and means what it says.

The config comment was independently wrong in the other direction: it said
"~40 MB" and "20 GB is about 800 experts", which cannot both be true. 800 was
right, for 25 MB.

Test added where the real write path already lives, comparing disk_bytes()
against expert files written by Tiers._to_disk. It needs a realistic d_ff to
mean anything: at DM 8 / DF 16 an expert is 384 parameters and nine zip
members of npz header dwarf the data, which is why the first version of this
test read 0.59x.

subject: bias the neutral point downward: getting quieter is not getting better
body:
T_MID 1.25 -> 1.6. One number, still a single continuous tanh - no dead zone,
no discontinuity, and the rate still moves at nearly every evaluation.

TWO REASONS, and the second is the one that matters.

The costs are asymmetric. This run's one overshoot cost +0.24 nats and about
20M characters to repair; undershooting only costs time. A neutral point set at
the middle of the evidence treats those as equal.

And the statistic itself has drifted. `e` is slope over RESIDUAL SCATTER, and
that scatter is the model's own checkpoint-to-checkpoint wobble, not the
evaluation's error. Measured over the run: it fell from 0.058 to 0.0135 across
40M characters as the pool stopped churning, while the logged evaluation error
barely moved, 0.107 -> 0.098. So progress only 2.3x faster than an earlier
stretch scored 5.7x higher, and the controller answered a quieter run with more
learning rate. That is the wrong reading, and it is what put the rate back on
course for 2.31e-04 - the level it was at when the last collapse began.

1.6 is the largest shift that never reaches the floor over the last 200 real
checkpoints; 1.9 hits it 72 times. At 1.6 the run's current rate decays about
6% over 60 evaluations while twice that rate still gains 32%, five times it
still gains 49%, and the response to deterioration is unchanged at -67%.

A deadband was tried first and rejected: it holds the rate exactly still
between two thresholds, which breaks the "moves at every evaluation" property
and makes the law harder to reason about for no gain a shifted midpoint does
not give.

subject: sample every corpus, not four of seven
body:
The sample set was code, arithmetic, chat and chess against seven training
corpora. stories, reasoning and wikipedia were never generated from - and
stories is the one worth watching. Measured at 271M characters it reads 1.24
bits per character against wikipedia's 2.29 and chat's 1.82, so it is where
readable output appears first. Judging the model on the chat prompt, as we have
been, understates it.

Each new prompt is in its corpus's own format, read out of data/val rather than
guessed: reasoning opens the answer with <think>, wikipedia is raw MediaWiki
markup with [[links]] and ==headings==, stories are plain simple-vocabulary
narrative with no markers at all. A prompt in the wrong shape puts the model off
distribution before it writes a character.

chat_hermes gets its own prompt too. It shares chat's markers but its answers
need working out, and it is reported separately in the held-out breakdown.

Test added for coverage and for shape. Its first version also tried to catch
prompts lifted from the held-out set and flagged stories, chat and chess - all
by matching shared CONVENTION, not content: "Once upon a time, there was a"
appears in 20 of 20 story files and "1. e4 e5" is the commonest opening in
chess. It was penalising prompts for being correctly formatted, which is what
the shape test demands. Narrowed to whole prompts of 55+ characters, where a
verbatim hit really would mean the sample measures recall.

Cost: eight prompts instead of four, two variants each at 140 characters, once
per --sample-every. Bounded and small.

subject: gradients reach the whole window, not the last 512 characters
body:
The reader consumed `chunk` characters at a time against a DETACHED key-value
cache. Attention reached back over everything read so far; the gradient stopped
at the chunk boundary. The model could attend over 32,768 characters and be
corrected by 512 of them - 1.6% of what it was looking at. For a model whose
claim is that it learns from what it reads, that is the claim being false: the
rest of the window was context it could never be taught by.

Each step now re-forwards the whole window ending at the cursor and
backpropagates through all of it. The cache is gone; detaching it was exactly
what severed the credit assignment. `model.context` 32,768 -> 16,384, because
a window that is fully differentiated has to fit in VRAM as activations rather
than as a cache.

The loss spans the whole window. Scoring only the new chunk was implemented
first and removed: it needs a "score from here" index threaded through the
model's forward, which is a subtlety that hides in a signature. Scoring
everything also re-learns the last window at every step, which for a model that
never stops training is rehearsal. The cost is known and accepted: a character
contributes to about R/S consecutive updates, so those updates are correlated
and the newest chunk is a small share of each. The reported loss changes
MEANING as well as level - a mean over 16,384 positions instead of 512 - so
numbers from before this commit are not comparable to numbers after it.

The price is arithmetic: with reach R and a step every S characters every
character is forwarded R/S times. At 16,384 and 512 that is 32, and reading is
about 24x slower. Bought deliberately.

data.min_visit_chunks -> data.passage, in characters, 65,536. The old one was
in chunks and then rounded up to whole context windows, so the number in the
config was never the number in effect: 16 silently became 64.

subject: serving reads one stream, at the same granularity training does
body:
The model read a finished exchange once, as a unit. Now it reads everything it
is given and everything it writes as a single continuous stream and steps every
`chunk` characters - the same mechanism minagi/stream.py uses on a corpus, with
the interleaving between subjects removed because a conversation is one
subject. The cursor only moves forward; nothing is read twice at the same
position; what a step sees is the last `context` characters and the gradient
reaches all of them.

The point is that there is no second mechanism. The thing that learns from a
book and the thing that learns from you are now one code path at one
granularity, so there is no regime the model was never trained in, and no turn
structure hiding inside the learning rule. A message boundary is not a boundary
the model sees: two half-chunks in separate turns step exactly as one whole
chunk does, and there is a test for precisely that.

THE COST WAS MEASURED BEFORE THIS AND ARGUES AGAINST IT. Held-out, +/-0.06:
54 steps at the whole window every chunk cost +0.6507, against +0.1018 for one
step per finished exchange, with a control of +0.0197 for real documents of the
same size. This commit is the first row and the previous design was the third.
That measurement was taken when a "window" was a short chat turn re-read many
times, and streaming continuously is a different regime - the cursor advances
and text leaves the window - so whether it still applies is unknown. It is
recorded in the module docstring rather than deleted, because a number that
argued against a design should not disappear once the design is chosen.

learn() is kept as a thin wrapper returning the last step, so callers that
want one record still work.

subject: the dispatch had no capacity, only a comment saying it did
body:
"capacity-based batched dispatch (Switch-Transformer style)" was half
implemented. Every expert is padded to a slot buffer so the pool runs as three
batched matmuls, and the hidden tensor is [n_experts, cap, d_ff] - but cap was
`counts.max()`, whatever the busiest expert happened to receive. Switch bounds
that with a capacity factor and drops the overflow, and the bound is the entire
reason the arrangement is affordable. Without it the buffer scales with the
IMBALANCE rather than with the work.

Measured on the failure: a 4,096-character window, top_k 8, 32 experts present,
32,768 assignments. Balanced that is 1,024 an expert and a 0.13 GB hidden
tensor. One expert held 44%, cap became 14,417, and the same arithmetic asked
for 1.89 GB - fourteen times the memory - and the run died inside the held-out
evaluation before taking a step.

Nothing about the imbalance was new. What was new was the whole window being
forwarded at once, which multiplied assignments by eight and turned a wasteful
allocation into an impossible one. So the window change did not cause this; it
made a standing defect reachable.

capacity_factor 1.5 bounds the buffer to 1.5x fair share and drops what
overflows: 1.89 GB -> 0.20 GB on the same routing, and the buffer now stays
within 1.5x of the assignments actually made at 512, 4,096 and 16,384-character
windows alike. Balanced routing is never clipped. A dropped assignment costs a
token one of its top_k experts, not the token, and the load-balancing term is
what keeps it rare - if it stops being rare that is the router collapsing, and
worth seeing rather than paying for.

Taken from config.yaml at load rather than from the checkpoint: it is a
property of the card the model is running on, not of the model.

subject: measuring is not learning, and the dispatch buffer is not the residual stream
body:
TWO THINGS, both consequences of forwarding the whole window, and neither is
the window being wrong.

THE EVALUATION WAS PAYING FOR GRADIENT REACH IT NEVER USES. FolderEvaluator
drives the same FileReader the training loop does, so it started re-forwarding
a 16,384-character window for every one of its 7 domains x 60 chunks. Under
no_grad there is no gradient to reach anywhere: a cached chunk sees exactly the
same attention context and returns the identical loss. Measured, the difference
is 66 MINUTES against about two. It runs at every --sample-every, so at 10
minutes the run would have spent 87% of its life evaluating and the first
sample would never have arrived. step(learn=False) now takes the cached path.

THE SLOT BUFFER RAN IN fp32. The residual stream stays fp32 by design; the
dispatch does not have to, and autocast does not help because the weights are
cast TO the buffer's dtype a line later, so the matmul runs at whatever the
buffer is. At a 16,384 window the hidden tensor is 1.61 GB in fp32 and 0.81 in
bf16, and 1.61 is what would not fit. The capacity bound from the previous
commit was working exactly - n*cap came to 196,600 against a predicted 196,608
- it was the element size that was wrong.

subject: --context is a ceiling that binds on resume, not only on a fresh model
body:
ctx_now was clamped against cfg.block alone, and BOTH cfg.block and
context_now come out of the checkpoint. So lowering model.context in
config.yaml changed nothing on a resumed run - the window stayed at whatever
the manifest had grown to.

Found the hard way. Two runs, configured at 16,384 and then 8,192, both read
32,768 from the manifest and died with byte-identical out-of-memory errors:
same 1.50 GiB request, same 352.81 MiB free. Byte-identical is what a setting
that is silently ignored looks like from the outside, and it cost two restarts
to notice that the number in the config had never once been the number in
effect.

The arithmetic confirms both earlier fixes were working. At the window actually
in use, 32,768, the capacity bound gives cap 12,288 and the hidden tensor is
1.61 GB in bf16 - exactly the 1.50 GiB requested. The bound was right and the
dtype was right; the window was three times what the config asked for.

The window is the one setting that must be lowerable from outside, because it
decides whether the model fits on this card, and the card is not a property of
the checkpoint. At 8,192 the dispatch buffer is 0.40 GB against 1.61.

A higher --context still cannot inflate a smaller saved window: the window
grows by training, on measured gain, not by configuration.

subject: the memory was there, it was just not contiguous
body:
The 8,192 window forwards fine and dies in the backward asking for 384 MiB,
with 394 MiB free and 861 MiB reserved by PyTorch but unallocated. Nothing is
too big; the allocator is holding its free blocks in fixed segments and a run
that alternates between a few large short-lived tensors cannot get a
contiguous piece back. A checkpointed expert dispatch is exactly that pattern:
three batched matmuls, thrown away in the forward and recomputed in the
backward, twenty-four times a step.

PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True, set in the program rather
than left to the shell, because it is a property of how this model allocates
and not of how someone happened to launch it. It has to be set before torch is
imported: the allocator reads it once at CUDA init and ignores it afterwards,
which is why the same line sits above `import torch` in both entry points.

serve.py gets it too - generating a long sequence and then learning from it
strands memory the same way.

subject: a tool to measure where the VRAM goes, instead of arguing about it
body:
Reading the code accounts for about 2.9 GB of the 6.36 GB an 8,192-character
window allocates: 1.54 GB of activations at the sampled depth of 13.75 passes,
1.21 GB of resident pool weights and fp32 Adam moments, 0.1 GB of trunk. The
other 3.5 GB is unaccounted for, and guessing at it has already cost several
restarts.

vram_probe reports weights, what the forward RETAINS for the backward, and both
peaks, against what the arithmetic predicts - and --sweep doubles the window
until it fails, so the ceiling is measured rather than estimated.

It also prints the thing that turned up while writing it: bptt_window is 16 and
the sampled recurrence depth is 13.75, so the depth truncation never fires.
Every sampled pass keeps its activations. The dataclass default is 4.

subject: the window kept growing past the ceiling, which looked exactly like a leak
body:
--context was clamped at startup and nowhere else. The growth path clamped to
cfg.block, which comes out of the checkpoint at 32,768, so the window came down
to 4,096 on load and then immediately started walking back up a character at a
time. Measured over one session: context 4,151 -> 4,492 while VRAM went
7,271 -> 7,790 MB, monotonic, until it died in the backward.

That is 85% of the increase. An 8.2% larger window on 5.4 GB of activations is
+440 MB against +519 MB observed. It was reported as a memory leak and it looks
like one from the outside, which is the point: a ceiling that binds once and
then stops binding is worse than no ceiling, because it hides the growth it is
supposed to prevent.

ctx_max = min(cfg.block, args.context), computed once and used at every site
that previously read cfg.block: the startup clamp, the growth condition, the
growth step, the printed ceiling and the final record. cfg.block is how far the
rotary tables were built; --context is how far this card can afford; the window
must respect both, always, not only at load.

subject: model.context -> model.context_end, because it is a ceiling and should say so
body:
It pairs with context_start now, and the pair reads as what it is: where a
fresh model's window begins, and the furthest it may ever reach. "context" on
its own was ambiguous with the window the model currently has, which is
context_now, and the two were confused often enough to cost several restarts.

The flag is --context-end, with --context kept as an alias so an existing
command line still works. The old config key is still read as a fallback
everywhere the new one is, so a directory or config written before this loads
unchanged.

Also verified rather than assumed, since this is the third time this ceiling
has been wrong: ctx_now is assigned in exactly three places in cmd_read - the
initial read from the manifest, the startup clamp, and the growth step - and
the last two both clamp to ctx_max. There is no path that can take the window
past it.

subject: every cadence is configured in characters, not in chunks or steps
body:
A step is --chunk characters, so anything counted in steps silently changes
meaning the moment the chunk changes. growth.every: 400 was 204,800 characters
at chunk 512 and would have been 1.6 million at chunk 4,096 without a line of
the config moving. Characters are what the model reads; steps are an
implementation detail of how often we stop to update, and the config should not
be written in one of them.

  model.context_grow_every  8    -> context_grow_every_chars  4,096
  model.context_every       128  -> context_every_chars      65,536
  pool.segment_chunks       16   -> segment_chars             8,192
  growth.every              400  -> every_chars             204,800
  prune.survival            6000 -> survival_chars        3,072,000

Every value is the old one times 512, so the cadences are unchanged at the
current chunk and become correct at any other.

The conversion happens once, in cmd_read, where the chunk is known, and the
step-counted comparisons read the converted values. The old keys are still
honoured as fallbacks - multiplied by 512 - so a config written before this
loads with the behaviour it had. --segment-chars keeps --segment-chunks as an
alias.

pool.dwell is deliberately left alone: it counts SEGMENTS, the pool's own clock
for how long a newly admitted expert holds its slot, and segments are not
chunks and do not convert to characters.

subject: dwell, held-out size and sample size in characters too
body:
pool.dwell counted SEGMENTS - one per working-set decision, which is one per
chunk - so at chunk 2,048 the same 4 would have meant 8,192 characters instead
of 2,048, and a working set that holds four times as long is a different pool.
dwell_chars: 2048, divided by the chunk where it is applied.

--eval-chunks and --sample-eval-chunks were chunk counts by name and by
behaviour: 60 chunks is 30,720 characters at chunk 512 and 122,880 at 2,048, so
the same command line would have quadrupled how long every evaluation takes
without saying so. Both are now --eval-chars and --sample-eval-chars, with the
old spellings kept as aliases.

That is the last of them. Everything the run is paced by is now written in
characters and converted to steps or segments once, where the chunk is known:

  context_grow_every_chars   4,096      context_every_chars   65,536
  segment_chars              8,192      dwell_chars            2,048
  every_chars              204,800      survival_chars     3,072,000
  passage                   32,768      eval_chars           122,880

subject: an alias that keeps the name and changes the unit is worse than no alias
body:
--eval-chunks 60 meant sixty chunks. After the previous commit it would have
meant sixty CHARACTERS - one chunk of held-out per domain instead of sixty -
and the command line would not have changed. That is precisely the failure the
character conversion exists to remove, reintroduced by the aliases meant to
soften it.

--eval-chunks, --segment-chunks and --sample-eval-chunks are gone: argparse
refuses them. --dwell needed claiming explicitly, because it is a strict prefix
of --dwell-chars and argparse matches unambiguous prefixes - it would have been
accepted silently. It now exits with the conversion, and does so before
anything loads, or a busy card hides the message behind an out-of-memory.

--context keeps its alias: its unit did not change, only its name.

Tested against the parser rather than the source, by running each retired
spelling and requiring a non-zero exit.

subject: the character-to-step conversion has to come before everything that reads it
body:
`pool.trial = survival_steps` sits four hundred lines above the block that
produced survival_steps, so the first run after the units change died with
UnboundLocalError before reading a character. Python cannot see that until the
line executes, and the line executes after a minute of loading 373 experts and
running the held-out evaluation - so it cost a full startup to find.

The conversion now sits at the top of cmd_read, immediately after the retired
spellings are rejected and before anything else exists. A value that later
lines depend on belongs before all of them, not beside the first place it
happens to be needed.

This is the second ordering bug of exactly this shape - pool.now was the first,
also set beside its use in the loop and read before it on the first forward -
so it gets a test rather than a fix. test_units walks cmd_read and requires
every derived value to be assigned before it is read. Verified by moving the
block back and confirming the test fails: "survival_steps defined line 1097,
first read line 1074".

subject: self-knowledge is its own lane, and now contains the model's own source
body:
It sat in data/train/chat/self-knowledge, so the reader - which picks a LANE at
random and then a file inside it - reached it 1/7 x 1/57 of the time: 0.25% of
reading. Measured after 284M characters, the model had read about 720k of its
33M self-description, 0.02 of a pass. It had effectively never read the material
that says what it is, which is why "what are you" comes back as word salad about
bridges and blacks.

Moved to data/train/self-knowledge. Eight lanes now, so it is 12.5% of reading -
a fiftyfold increase from one mv.

The builder also writes the model's own code and documentation, 0.86M characters
across 70 files, framed as the model's rather than as anonymous Python: unframed
source would teach it to write code, which the code lane already does, instead
of to know its own. This is the only part of the corpus that changes when the
model changes, and generating it is the point - the description this tool
replaced still claimed 74 experts and a top-16 router long after both were false.

The tool now prints how often the lane will be re-read, because a lane's share
does not depend on its size: a SMALL self-knowledge lane is read more times, not
fewer, and --target is the only thing deciding whether the model learns this or
recites it. It also warns before --apply replaces 33M with 5.9M, which the
default target would have done silently.

subject: a prompt for the self-knowledge lane, caught by the coverage test
body:
Promoting self-knowledge to a lane left it without a sample prompt, and
test_sample_coverage failed on exactly that: "every corpus in data/train has a
sample prompt - missing: ['self-knowledge']". That test was added when four of
seven corpora had no prompt and the one worth watching was among them; it has
now paid for itself.

The prompt asks how the model chooses its experts, in the <user>/<bot> shape
the self-knowledge corpus is written in. It is the sample to watch now that the
lane went from 0.25% of reading to 12.5%.

subject: optional telegram notice on a new best held-out
body:
One file, one call site, and nothing to undo. minagi/notify.py posts to the
Telegram Bot API with urllib - no dependency, no cost, no account beyond
Telegram - and train.py calls it in five lines guarded by try/except.

REMOVING IT IS `rm minagi/notify.py` plus those five lines. Verified by
deleting the file and checking train.py still parses, imports and runs: the
import is inside the loop and inside a try, so the run does not notice it is
gone. That matters because the plan is to delete it before publication.

INERT UNLESS CONFIGURED. It reads MINAGI_TELEGRAM_TOKEN and
MINAGI_TELEGRAM_CHAT from the environment and does nothing whatsoever unless
BOTH are set - no network call, no error, no log line. A machine that has never
been configured behaves exactly as it did before the file existed. No
credential is in the repository or in config.yaml, and there is a test that
looks for one.

IT CANNOT STOP A RUN. Every failure - no network, bad token, rate limit,
Telegram down - is swallowed and counted, and the timeout is five seconds
because this is called from the training loop and a hung socket would stall
reading. A notifier that can crash training is worse than no notifier.

WHAT LEAVES THE MACHINE is one line of numbers: the loss, the characters read,
the expert count. No generated text, no corpus, no paths. Telegram is a third
party and a message sent there is out of your hands, so the content is kept to
what you would put in a commit message.

cmd_read did not track a best at all - the "best" in the log is computed
post-hoc by plot_progress - so it now carries best_val, seeded from the
checkpoint it resumed.

subject: read .env, and say which step actually failed
body:
A token in .env did nothing, because Python does not read .env - nothing does
unless a program goes looking, and this one was not. It now reads .env from the
project root, with the environment still winning over the file, and strips
quotes because people write them and a quoted token fails with a 404 that says
nothing about quotes.

.env was NOT gitignored. It is now, along with .env.*. Checked that it had
never been committed - it had not - but it was one `git add -A` away, and every
commit in this session has used `git add -A`.

`python3 -m minagi.notify` now does the setup and names the failure instead of
leaving it to a grep over getUpdates. The step people skip is messaging the bot
first: getUpdates returns an EMPTY list until the bot has heard from you, which
from the outside looks exactly like a bad token. It now says so, and prints the
bot's username so there is something to search for in Telegram.

Verified on the real token: it is valid, and the empty update list was the
whole problem.

subject: the vram probe was measuring an fp32 forward
body:
build_paged does not set the compute dtype; train.py does it from config at
startup, and every other tool in tools/ calls set_compute_dtype itself. This
one did not, so it measured a forward the run never performs: 2.94 GB
retained instead of 1.65, and a 6.06 GB backward peak instead of 3.75.

Takes --precision, defaults to whatever the checkpoint's config says, and
prints the dtype it settled on so this cannot go unnoticed again.

subject: RMSNorm was keeping an fp32 copy of every activation it normalised
body:
The reciprocal-sqrt needs fp32 and that part is unchanged, but upcasting x to
get it left a full fp32 copy of the activation in the graph for the whole
step. The norm runs three times per recurrent pass, so at depth 14 that is 42
copies of a [T, 512] tensor - the single largest holder of activation memory,
ahead of attention.

Accumulating the mean in fp32 while squaring in the input dtype buys the same
rsqrt without the copy. Two details decide whether it works at all, and both
are now covered by a test that was checked against each regression:

  x * x, not x.pow(2) - autocast keeps pow on its fp32 list, so written with
  pow() this moves the copy from MulBackward to PowBackward and measures as
  saving exactly nothing. That is what it did on the first attempt.

  self.weight.to(x.dtype) - bf16 * fp32 promotes the result back to fp32 and
  hands the saving straight back, silently, one layer later.

Measured on the live pool, 4,096 window, depth pinned at 14:

  activations retained   2,204 MB -> 1,852 MB
  backward peak          4,300 MB -> 3,982 MB

Cost is one bf16 rounding on the scale multiply: +0.000164 nats over six
windows of real training text, 0.005%, against a held-out interval of +/-0.098.

Worst-case window on this card, depth 24 with ballast for the optimiser state,
goes from 5,120 to 6,144.

subject: best_val read the manifest four hundred lines before it was loaded
body:
Third ordering bug of this shape in cmd_read, after pool.now and
survival_steps. The notifier's starting point was placed with the other
derived values at the top of the function, but unlike them it reads `man`,
which build_paged returns - so it raised UnboundLocalError on the first line
that touched it, before any model loading, every time.

The test that exists to catch exactly this missed it, because it checked a
hand-written list of eight names and `man` was not one of them. A whitelist
can only catch the bugs someone already thought of. It now walks every local
in cmd_read - 102 of them - and flags any first read that precedes the first
assignment, skipping loads inside nested defs since those run later and
textual order says nothing about them.

Verified by reintroducing the bug: the general form fails with the line
numbers, the old form passed.

subject: a read could start inside the window and end past the rotary tables
body:
Both readers opened a fresh window on `seen >= context` and then forwarded the
next chunk at `pos_offset = seen`. That test covers the characters already
read, not the ones about to be read, so the last chunk of every pass ran from
`seen` to `seen + chunk` - past the ceiling the rotary tables were built to.

Invisible while the chunk divides the context: at 32,768 and 512 the reset
lands exactly on the ceiling and both spellings agree, and so they do at
1,024, 2,048 and 4,096. chunk 1536 is the first value used here that is not a
power of two. 32,768 / 1,536 is 21.33, the last reset falls at 32,256, and the
next read ends at 33,792.

The predicate now covers the read about to happen, at all three sites. A
window whose chunk does not divide it ends short of the ceiling by up to one
chunk, which is the correct reading of "a reader never reads past its own
context".

The test is parameterised over chunks that divide the context and chunks that
do not, since only the second kind can fail, and it reads the offset the
forward is actually given - `seen` observed from outside shows the value
before the reset and made the first version of the last two checks pass on a
reader that never reset at all.

subject: the vram probe left out the gradients, and recommended a window that died
body:
It zeroed the grads before reading the peak and built the model read_only, so
it measured a step that holds neither a gradient nor an optimiser moment. The
run holds both: 0.44 GB of fp32 gradient for 109 M parameters, and 0.47 GB of
Adam state. On that basis the probe said a 5,120 window peaked at 6.61 GB and
would fit; the run reached 7.69 GB and died at context 5,116.

The probe now keeps the grads, stands the moments up as ballast, and reports
the gradient figure in its own column so it cannot quietly go missing again.

Even corrected it reads 0.64 GB below the run, calibrated against that one
hard point, so the ceiling is set from the measurement plus that correction
rather than from the probe alone:

  window   probe   real (est)   margin to the observed wall
   4,096   6.02G      6.66G     1.27G
   4,352   6.28G      6.92G     1.01G
   4,608   6.53G      7.17G     0.76G
   5,120   7.05G      7.69G     0.24G   <- died here

context_end goes to 4,352. The 4,096 that ran before the RMSNorm change sat
at 0.70 GB of margin and did occasionally crash, so this is both a wider
window and a wider margin than the configuration it replaces.

subject: the rate controller was raising where raising measurably hurt
body:
T_MID 1.6 -> 2.2, NUDGE 0.009 -> 0.005.

Over 240 evaluations of the live run, splitting WITHIN bands of t so that
regression to the mean cannot account for it:

  t >= 1.0, rate above its median   -0.0241 nats over the next 6 evaluations
  t >= 1.0, rate below              +0.0039
                                    -3.8 sigma, and -3.3 / -2.2 at horizons
                                    of 4 and 8 evaluations
  t <  1.0, the same split          -0.4 sigma

The control is the finding. Mean reversion would show in both halves and does
not: the penalty appears only in the regime where the controller RAISES. The
time confound runs against it, since a high rate means early in the run and
the early run improved faster. An undetrended first pass read -4.6 sigma and
was mostly mean reversion; the within-band number is the honest one.

t reached +2.44 at most over the last 100 evaluations, so this moves raising
from 34% of evaluations to 10% at 55% of the speed rather than disabling it.

An earlier note in the file said 1.9 reaches the floor 72 times. That replayed
the whole run including the stretch when the pool was still churning. Over the
last 200 checkpoints the rate settles at x0.066 against x0.116, minimum x0.065
against a floor of 0.05, and never reaches it.

The test's bar was an absolute scale, and this is the third time T_MID moved
it. It now compares an improving run against a flat one - 4.86x apart - so it
records the property rather than the constants, and it was checked against a
controller that cannot see a slope at all, where the ratio falls to 1.00.

subject: measure how much of the 9.9 GB of experts is actually distinct
body:
Two experts can be the same function and look orthogonal in weight space,
because a SwiGLU expert is unchanged if you permute its 2,048 hidden units.
So this measures three things that answer different questions: raw weight
cosine (a LINEAGE test, since a child is born as a copy in the parent's
ordering), cosine between w1'w1 (permutation-free, so it asks what part of the
input space the expert answers to at all), and cosine between router rows.

The Gram comparison has to be centred and that is not a detail. w1'w1 is
positive semi-definite, so every expert's Gram sits in the same orthant and
they share a large common component - the average expert. Uncentred, the
median pair reads +0.78 and the pool scores 2 effective experts out of 394,
which is an artefact of the statistic and not a property of the pool. Centred,
the median pair is -0.007 and 33 come out effective.

Runs on CPU, never imports torch, and reads each expert once - it is meant to
run while training owns the card.

subject: a long story sample, to see whether it holds a thread or just a sentence
body:
Every prompt in the log is a few hundred characters, which asks whether the
model writes plausible sentences. None of them ask whether it can hold a
thread across the window it is trained at, and that is the question the
context work of the last weeks was for.

stories-long hands it 3,000 characters before it writes anything and then asks
for 1,000. Adapted only: the raw reading of a thousand characters is a loop,
the short prompts already report that, and every generated character is a
forward pass through all 24 rows.

The pretext is a fixed slice of data/val/stories. Held out, so this measures
continuation rather than recall - prompting with training text would show the
difference nowhere in the output - and fixed, so two entries a week apart are
comparable.

It is NOT copied into the log. 3,000 characters every ten minutes is hundreds
of KB a day of the same text and it would bury the generations; the entry
carries the length, a sha1 and the last 240 characters, and the passage itself
is written once beside the log as pretext-stories-long-<sha1>.txt. Measured on
the test: a 725-byte entry for a 3,000-character pretext.

pretext + generated is trimmed at startup if it does not fit model.context_end,
because past that the model is being asked to read beyond its rotary tables and
what comes back says nothing about long context. sample.long_new_chars 0 turns
it off.

SAMPLE_PROMPTS entries may now carry a third element, options, and two-element
entries keep working unchanged.

subject: teach the coverage test about three-element sample entries
body:
It unpacked two-tuples in three places and broke the moment stories-long
carried options. It now reads the optional third element, arms the long prompt
the way a run does so the checks see what a run sees, and skips an entry whose
text is None - which is the state stories-long is in before arming, and which
the sampling loop handles by asking for nothing.

The verbatim check needed an exemption rather than a fix. stories-long IS a
verbatim slice of data/val/stories and that is the point: held out, never
trained on, so continuing it measures continuation and not recall. It is
exempt by name with the reason written down, and test_long_sample.py checks
the half that actually matters - that the passage is absent from
data/TRAIN/stories.

subject: remove the long story sample
body:
It was there to answer one question - whether a story holds a thread over a
long generation or only over a sentence - and it answered it: the thread does
not hold. Adapted looped on "He didn't know how to say, but he didn't know
how", and stories is the one lane where adapted repeats MORE than raw, 16%
against 11%. Nothing further was going to come of keeping it.

Reverts both commits whole, since they existed only for this: the prompt entry
and its pretext machinery, the two --long-* flags and their config, the side
file the pretext was written to, tests/test_long_sample.py, and the
three-element entry handling in the coverage test - stories-long was the only
entry that ever carried options, so SAMPLE_PROMPTS is nine plain pairs again.

Also drops the per-round want_experts calls it added. Those advance the pool's
segment clock and stamp last_seen, which is what prune reads, so a sample
prompt could keep an expert that no reading ever asked for.

subject: the usage graph was still calling a segment 512 characters
body:
chunk is 1,536 now and the graph's x axis is in segments, so the caption told
the reader to multiply by the wrong number - 800,000 segments reads as 410M
characters when it is three times that. Says what a segment IS instead of how
wide it happens to be this week, so it cannot go stale again.

subject: prune stops reading the gate, because the gate was pointed the wrong way
body:
The keep rule was `young or alive or seen`, where `alive` spared anything
whose |gate| cleared dead_gate(). Scored against what each expert actually
went on to do over the following 11M characters - 44 full passes of all eight
lanes, so a lane specialist gets 44 chances - and asked to pick the ones that
would do nothing:

    rule                    top 25   top 50  top 100  top 150
    not admitted recently     100%     100%     100%      94%
    lowest |gate|               8%      16%      28%      39%
    base rate                  63%      63%      63%      63%

Lowest-gate is not merely uninformative, it is ANTI-predictive: the smallest
gates belong to the busiest experts. Twelve sit in the bottom gate quartile
having been admitted within 646 segments, one carrying 2.5e7 routing hits at a
gate of 0.0099. They act as a sink - chosen constantly, contributing little per
token - and the gate test read that as death while sparing a high-gate expert
nothing had wanted in 700,000 segments.

Combining the two was worse than either: gate as a factor in the ranking pulled
a 100% rule down to 84%. So the term is gone rather than rebalanced, and
`min_gate` with it. A traffic-rate test was measured too and ties with
staleness exactly - same top 100, 100 of 100 - because an expert can only take
traffic while resident, which is what last_seen tracks. Staleness is already
there, so it wins on being free.

The collapse guard kept the best-gated expert when everything qualified; it now
keeps the most recently wanted one, for the same reason.

dead_gate() stays, and the growth brake still reads it. That is a different
question - how much of the pool contributes nothing right now, which decides
whether to GROW, not what to delete.

The tests marked their victims with a low gate, which now selects nothing, so
six fixtures pick theirs by staleness instead. Two assertions were the old
contract stated outright - "an expert with a healthy gate is never deleted for
going quiet", and "idle and prunable are the SAME line" - and are inverted to
state the new one.

NOT SAFE TO RUN AS CONFIGURED. At prune.survival_chars 3,072,000 this deletes
313 of 382 experts in one pass. The config change is deliberately not in this
commit.

subject: dead means unaddressed, for the brake as well as the pruner
body:
Removes dead_gate_frac, idle_frac_max, dead_gate() and AutoGrow's min_gate.
There is one definition of dead now - how long since anything asked for this
expert, as a share of prune.survival_chars - and two thresholds on it:
dying_at stops growth, the window itself deletes.

    dying() -> 0.0 the moment something asks for it
               1.0 when it has gone exactly `survival` unasked
    a newborn inside its trial reads 0: it has not failed to be chosen,
    it has not finished being offered

THE GATE TEST WAS BACKWARDS, not merely imprecise. Asked which experts would
take no traffic over the next 11M characters - 44 passes of all eight lanes -
lowest-gate picked them at 8% against a 63% base rate; longest-unaddressed
picked them at 100%. The smallest gates belong to the busiest experts: a sink,
chosen constantly and contributing little per token, reads as dead on a gate
test while a high-gate expert nothing has wanted in 700,000 segments reads as
alive.

It also needed a valley that no longer exists. The 0.15 was calibrated on a
bimodal pool - 127 of 157 around 0.42, 27 below 0.05, nothing between - so its
exact value did not matter. After the pool fell to 56 the gates run smoothly
from 0.0033 to 1.71 with no valley anywhere and all 56 are in use. No fraction
answered the question correctly: 0.15 called 34% of a fully-employed pool idle
and blocked growth outright. The new rule reads 0 of 56 dying on that same
pool, and 0 to prune.

The brake's self-limiting mechanism changes with it, and the growth-trial test
now says so. It used to be immediate - an expert was born below the gate line,
so every addition counted as idle at once. A newborn is now exempt for its
whole trial, so the brake engages one trial later: measured on the stub, 4
batches instead of 1. Growth still self-limits, it just gets a fair number of
tries first.

The birth_gate startup guard goes too. It existed because an expert born above
the dead line could never be pruned for failing to earn a gate; neither rule
reads the gate now, so the birth gate is only a starting scale.

minagi/pool.py's old non-paged Pool class keeps its own gate-based prune. It
is not on the live path and is left alone.

subject: cap the experts in flight, and say "dying" where the graphs said "dead gate"
body:
max_in_flight: 16. Neither usage brake can see an expert inside its trial - a
newborn reads dying 0 by design, and keep_ratio judges only experts whose
trial has ENDED, returning 1.0 when there is nothing to judge. So for one
whole trial after growth starts, nothing on the usage side can refuse.
Simulated against the real AutoGrow at a 500M trial and a 204,800 decision
interval: 2,441 decisions of blindness, 340 experts added across 85 of them,
with the disk ceiling as the only thing that ever said no. That is five hours
of reading to refill the disk.

Capping it also makes keep_ratio_min bind for the first time: cohort two
cannot arrive until cohort one has finished its trial and been judged. The
ceiling that means something is `resident` - an expert can only prove itself
while it is on the card - so 16 is half of 32.

dying_at moves from growth to prune, directly under survival_chars. It is a
SHARE of that number and means nothing without it.

The graphs said "% of experts at a dead gate", computed as |gate| < 0.01. They
now say what share has gone dying_at of the way to being deleted unaddressed,
read from the same staleness prune acts on. On the real log that reads 52%
before the pool collapsed and 0% after - which is the thing the gate metric
was hiding. Older rows carry no last_seen, so `since` stands in; it differs
only for an expert that stayed resident without being re-admitted, making it a
slight over-estimate. last_seen is now written to the history for future rows.

Also removes the inherited-dead-gate purge in cmd_train. It cleared experts
under |gate| 0.01 so they would not hold the brake forever; the brake does not
read gates any more, and the mechanism had become lethal - it set born and
last_seen to -1e9 to strip every protection and called prune, which under
"dead means unaddressed" matches EVERY expert. The pool would have come back
holding the one the collapse guard spares. --keep-dead goes with it.

subject: every restart replayed the same text from the beginning
body:
Each subject lane picks a random file and a random offset from a generator
seeded `shuffle_seed + lane_index`. Both halves are fixed and the file list is
sorted, so the generator was rebuilt IDENTICALLY at every start. Every session
read the same files at the same offsets in the same order, from the front.

Measured over 43 real sessions: the median read 3.2M characters, the longest
66M, and read_chars reported 500M. The UNIQUE text is about the length of the
longest session - every short session was re-reading the opening of the same
sequence. The counter over-reports by roughly seven and a half times.

This is the restart spike. At the last one, across the seam:

    train      0.6746 -> 0.4456
    held-out   0.9247 -> 1.1054
    gap        +0.250 -> +0.660
    lr, rate, expert count: unchanged

Train falling that hard while held-out rises is not lost state, which is what
it was mistaken for three times. It is the model being handed text it has
already memorised and pushed to overfit it further. The learning rate being
identical on both sides of the seam is what ruled out everything else.

Mixing the read count into the seed means a restart continues into text the
model has not seen. Nothing new is persisted - the count is already in the
manifest - and a run stays reproducible from any given checkpoint. Measured on
the fix: consecutive sessions now share 0.0% of their visits, against 100%.

test_units section 5 pinned growth.every_chars to its migrated value and that
value has since been deliberately retuned, so it now checks the units are
intact rather than the number. Pinning a tuning knob forever turns a units
test into a nuisance; the other three are untouched.

subject: one pool graph, drawn with every sample, instead of three drawn by hand
body:
expert_history.py, expert_state.py and expert_usage.py are gone, and so are
the three PNGs. They had to be run by hand, so they were stale whenever
anyone looked at them - the last set was two days old while the pool had
collapsed and regrown in between.

tools/plot_experts.py replaces all three with one figure, appended to the
same hook that redraws training_progress and training_recent, so it is
rebuilt with every sample entry. Six panels:

  who is doing the work   routing share over the last survival_chars,
                          coloured by gate, with the 99% line marked
  how close to deletion   staleness as a share of the window, with the
                          dying_at and delete thresholds drawn on it
  concentration           cumulative share against rank
  gate against usage      the two plotted directly, so the relationship is
                          visible rather than asserted
  the pool over the run   size and dying share, from the history log
  are newcomers earning   share against birth order, trial state coloured

Usage over a window needs experts matched across time, and pruning renumbers
them, so uid now goes into the history row alongside last_seen. Until those
rows accumulate the panel falls back to lifetime usage and says so on the
axis rather than quietly showing a different quantity.

The units test pinned growth.every_chars to its migrated value, then to a
multiple of 512 when that value was retuned. Both were wrong: a character
count has no reason to be a multiple of the old chunk. It now checks the
thing that actually matters - that the number is a character count and not a
step count left in a field whose name says characters.

subject: ...and the graph that replaces them
body:
tools/plot_experts.py, appended to the hook that redraws training_progress
and training_recent, so the pool figure is rebuilt with every sample entry
instead of whenever someone remembers to run a script.

Six panels: who is doing the work (routing share over the last
survival_chars, coloured by gate, with the 99% line marked); how close each
expert is to deletion, with dying_at and the delete threshold drawn on it;
concentration as cumulative share against rank; gate against usage plotted
directly so the relationship is visible rather than asserted; the pool's size
and dying share over the run; and whether newcomers are earning, as share
against birth order with trial state coloured.

Usage over a window needs experts matched across time and pruning renumbers
them, so uid now goes into the history row beside last_seen. Until those rows
accumulate the panel falls back to lifetime usage and says so on the axis,
rather than quietly showing a different quantity under the same label.

The units test pinned growth.every_chars to its migrated value, then to a
multiple of 512 once that value was retuned. Both were wrong - a character
count has no reason to be a multiple of the old chunk. It now checks what
actually matters: that the number is a character count and not a step count
left behind in a field whose name says characters.

subject: the model's self-knowledge now includes its own source and every .md
body:
SKIP is what stops it eating itself. `data` holds the corpus INCLUDING this
lane's own output, so walking it would fold the training data into the
training data and grow without bound; `runs` is logs and images, `weights*`
is the model, `.git` is history.

Also hardens _Lane.open against a file that is no longer there. A corpus can
change under a run that lasts days, and this lane in particular is
REGENERATED - rmtree then rewrite - while the path list was taken at startup.
as_stream opens with no guard and _Lane.open did not catch it, so a
regeneration would have ended the run within minutes, self-knowledge being
one visit in eight. A vanished file is now a reason to pick another one.

subject: the gate-against-usage points were invisible on white
body:
YlOrRd put almost every point on its palest yellow. Nearly nothing is ever
dying, so nearly every point sits at 0, and 0 is the lightest end of that map
- the panel was drawing a scatter the reader could not see.

The colour now runs from the palette's blue through grey-blue and amber to
red, so the common case (nothing wants it yet, nowhere near the line) is
visible and the rare case still reads as alarm. Points get a thin dark edge so
they stay legible where they overlap, and the panel gets a colourbar, since
the mapping was only stated in prose before.

Fixing it exposed a second problem next door: with the bars now reaching the
thresholds, the "counts as dying" label sat underneath them and read as "ts as
dying". The bars are sorted descending, so both threshold labels move to the
right-hand side where there is nothing to hide them.

subject: a sample re-picked its experts from one character, every 64 characters
body:
The generation loop re-asks the pool what it wants every 64 characters, and
the intent is right - what the text wants after a hundred characters of chess
is not what the prompt alone asked for. But it asked with `cur`, and `cur =
nxt` sits at the bottom of the same loop, so from the second step onward `cur`
is the single token just chosen. The whole working set was being re-picked
from one character's embedding.

That is worse than not re-selecting at all. It is a re-roll on whichever
character happens to land on the boundary, and it can evict experts the prompt
had chosen correctly - then do it again 64 characters later. Verified by
spying on what the call receives: the lengths were 12, then 1, 1, 1.

It now asks with `ids + got`, the text so far, which the decoder was already
building for the repetition guard. The same lengths are now 12, 76, 140, 204.

The trailing `[-cfg.block:]` is a safety net that cannot actually fire:
generation is bounded by the same block, because the rotary tables are built
to it and the forward refuses to read past them. The test asserts that rather
than exercising it, since a case where it binds is a case where the forward
would already have raised - which is how the first version of that test
failed.

The initial per-prompt selection was always correct and is untouched: it gets
the full prompt, with dwell and margin zeroed so a change of subject is free
to release the incumbents.

subject: report what the capacity bound throws away
body:
The batched dispatch pads every expert to a fixed slot buffer, so an expert
wanted by more tokens than its cap loses the excess: the assignment is
discarded, the token goes without that expert's contribution, and the expert
takes no gradient from it. The bound is what makes the arrangement affordable
- without it the buffer grows with the worst imbalance rather than with the
work, measured at 1.89 GB against 0.13 GB of real arithmetic - and the
dispatch comment says an overflow is "worth seeing rather than paying for".

Nothing ever looked. `self.dropped` was incremented from the day the bound
was added and read by no code anywhere, so the one trade capacity_factor
makes had no number against it: whether clipping costs anything, whether a
larger factor would buy anything, whether the concentration in the usage
graph is partly this bound starving the tail.

A raw count would not have answered those either. A cumulative figure over a
week of reading says nothing about now and nothing about scale, so there is a
`routed` denominator beside it, and RecurCoder.pool_dropped() returns the
share over the interval since it was last read, clearing as it goes. The
progress line prints it only when it is non-zero, which keeps the common case
quiet.

The test's own first version consumed the counters before asking the progress
line to report them, and read zero - which is the reset working exactly as
intended, and the reason the helper that does a forward is now separate from
the one that reads.

subject: clear the run-specific special cases out of the graphs
body:
Three things in the plotting existed only because of one particular run's
history, and would have gone on quietly re-anchoring a fresh one:

  the regime-change detector  found the largest jump in held-out and measured
                              everything after it - the best score, the fitted
                              power law - from there. It was added because a
                              collapse took held-out from 1.19 to 2.44 in one
                              evaluation and a fit spanning that averaged two
                              models. On a clean run there is no such jump, so
                              it would anchor on whatever the noisiest day was.
  the "wrong experts" mark    an annotation naming a specific fixed bug, drawn
                              wherever held-out fell by more than a nat.
  plots.last                  40M, chosen when the run had read 60M. Now 100M,
                              which is what the window is wanted at.

Also removes the fallback in plot_experts that only engaged once the history
spanned a full window. Before that it showed LIFETIME usage under the same
axis label and then switched in one step, so the panel changed completely
overnight and looked broken. It now windows against the oldest row it has and
says the span it actually got, so it shows the same kind of thing on the first
day as on the thirtieth.

tools/export_history.py turns samples.txt into JSONL and CSV, one row per
evaluation with every number the log carries - so a visualisation built later
does not have to re-parse prose whose format has changed twice. 1,319
evaluations, 30 columns, 8 domains, 44 sessions, 34M to 611M characters.

Its first version reported zero domains, because the per-domain line FOLLOWS
held-out and was being attached to a record already appended. Its second
matched loosely and invented fifty domains out of the generated samples -
"add 6", "travels 60". The domain line is nothing but name/value pairs, so
that is now what it requires.

subject: the model's self-description had drifted from the model
body:
Seven answers described mechanisms that no longer exist, and one of them was
the one that matters most. Asked how far learning reaches it said "the
gradient stops at the chunk boundary... the learning signal does not run back
through it" - which is the arrangement that was deliberately replaced by
re-forwarding the whole window. Asked when an expert dies it gave the rule
from three versions ago: old enough, gate below a bar, AND the gate has
stopped moving. Asked about growth it quoted a parameters-per-character
density cap that was retired.

Rewritten against what the code does now: death is staleness and the gate
plays no part in it, growth asks four questions with the train/held-out gap
as the one that matters, the gradient reaches the whole window and what that
costs, and the learning rate follows evidence rather than a schedule.

_self_facts was reading weights/manifest.json while the run has written to
weights_rows/ for months, so EVERY man.get() fell through to a hardcoded
default and the model was being told it had 74 experts and a top-16 router -
exactly the drift the file's own header warns about. It now tries the
configured directory, then any weights* that has a manifest.

Six more facts read the manifest or a hardcoded default and never the config,
so without a manifest they reported a top-16 router, a depth of 6 and a dwell
of 4. They fall back to config now. MINAGI_FACTS_WEIGHTS=config forces the
config as the only source, which is the honest description of a run that has
not checkpointed yet.

prune.min_gate and prune.min_age are gone from the config, so the facts that
