read them are gone too; survival_chars, dying_at and max_in_flight take their
place.

body:

It now writes thirty synthetic progress blocks to a temporary log and points

runs/dashboard.png is both, nine panels in three rows:

subject: the near-deletion panel was blank for the first day of a run
body:
dying() reads 0 for anything inside its first survival window, which is what
the RULE does - prune never touches those, so their distance to the line is
not a live number. As a graph it is the wrong default: for the whole first
window of a run EVERY expert is young, so the panel drew nothing at all for
about a day while the staleness accumulated underneath it.

Measured 13,524 steps into the fresh run, with every bar masked to zero:
median staleness 0.0002 of the window, p90 0.2475, and the stalest expert had
already gone 41.5M characters unasked out of a 100M window. About a fifth of
the pool was a quarter of the way to the line and the panel said nothing.

dying() takes mask_young now, the dashboard passes False, and protected
experts are drawn in the trial colour - so the distribution is visible while
it is still obvious which of it prune may act on. The count in the title
separates the two: "0 dying, 97 still protected" rather than an empty frame.

subject: an expert cannot have been ignored for longer than it has existed
body:
The blue bar that kept appearing above the "deleted" line in the near-deletion
panel was a newborn, every time.

`last_seen` answers two different questions with one field. As the exploration
key it wants a new expert at the FRONT of the queue, so it is initialised to 0
- "wanted at segment zero", the oldest possible claim. As the staleness key it
is read as "how long since anything asked for it", and there the same 0 means
the opposite: ignored for the whole run.

So every expert was born already scored as maximally stale. On the live pool
that is segments/window = 1.143, above the 1.0 line prune deletes on, from the
instant it existed. The bar appeared at each birth and vanished the moment the
expert was first admitted and `last_seen` updated - which is why it came and
went, and why it was gone by the time it was looked for.

No expert was lost to it: `young` protects a newborn through exactly the period
the inflated figure covers, and the growth brake reads the masked value. This
was the panel telling the truth about a number that was wrong.

Fixed in the reader, not the initialiser - exploration still wants the 0. Both
copies of dying() now clamp idle to the expert's own age. An expert that really
has been idle a long time, like the one at 1.14 explained last week, still
scores above the line; it is old enough for the clamp not to bind.

subject: measure the forgetting claim instead of asserting it
body:
The project claims continual learning without catastrophic forgetting, and
until now the evidence for it was that the run improves on eight domains at
once. That is suggestive and it is not a measurement: the training loop
revisits every subject about every 262K characters, so the regime never asks
the model to hold anything across a real gap.

Three instruments.

forgetting_probe.py trains the REAL checkpoint on one subject and scores every
held-out domain as the exposure lengthens. Two things make it trustworthy.
The evaluator reads the same files from position zero every call, so the same
characters are scored every time and a difference is the model moving rather
than a different sample of text - there is no sampling noise to average away.
And the pool may not grow during a probe, or "did not forget" would be
confused with "bought new capacity".

It also carries its own control. With --rotate it reads EVERY subject, which
makes forgetting impossible by construction, so whatever that run degrades is
damage and not forgetting. That control is what caught the first version of
this being wrong: at the run's nominal 3e-4 with a cold AdamW, the interleaved
arm degraded domains it was actively reading, by +0.13 nats. A cold Adam has
no second-moment estimate, so its opening updates are near full step size in
every direction at once. More than half of what the massed arm had called
forgetting was the probe damaging the weights. Hence --warmup, a much lower
rate, and the rule that the control must be flat before the massed arms mean
anything.

cl_control.py is the architectural control - routed pool against a dense model
of matched parameter count, same seed, same stream, strictly sequential
curriculum. Matching the budget needs care: setting cfg.d_ff widened the two
prelude blocks as well as the recurrent one and made the "matched" dense model
134% too big, which would have handed it the comparison.

plot_cl.py draws it. Highlight-plus-context rather than eight competing
series, and the arms use a palette checked with the validator rather than by
eye - red/yellow/aqua/blue, worst adjacent CVD dE 9.1, every line directly
labelled because three of those sit under 3:1 on the light surface.

Nothing here writes to a real weights directory. The pool marks a paged-in
expert dirty whether or not anything touched it, so each arm gets a pristine
copy and the caller is expected to hand it one.

subject: the trunk learning rate is what prevents forgetting, not the expert pool
body:
Reading 524K characters of chess and nothing else, on the real 136-expert
checkpoint, at the model's own rate, with the optimiser moments restored:

    frozen working set, trunk LR = expert LR    +2.5871   42.88% retained
    swapping,           trunk LR = expert LR    +2.2300   50.68% retained
    swapping,           trunk at 0.1x           +0.0067   99.84% retained

The 0.1 multiplier is worth a 333x reduction and 86.2% of the distance between
collapse and stability. Expert swapping is worth 13.8%. The configured model
does not merely survive half a million characters of one subject - it ends up
better at chess and no worse at anything, the largest regression anywhere being
chat at +0.014.

The frozen arm is what makes this conclusive. 93 of 136 experts took no
gradient at all - 68% of the parameters preserved exactly - and the model still
collapsed, with arithmetic ending at 5.7498 against a chance level of 5.5797.
Past chance: not merely worse, confidently wrong. So preserving most of the
weights is real and is not sufficient, and README.md's account - the experts
"should not be the reason the model forgets" - is true about the experts and
silent about where the forgetting actually is.

It is in the trunk. 8.27M parameters, 1.9% of the model, the only part every
character passes through. The drift measurement shows it directly: 1.70% of
its own norm under the mitigation, 7.88% without.

AdEMAMix makes things worse, 118x, and mechanically rather than
mysteriously. alpha 5.0 means the update is m1 + 5*m2, so the effective step
grows by up to 1+alpha once the slow average fills - it hands back most of a
10x cut. It is at odds with the one mitigation that works.

METHOD.md is the longer half of this commit and the more useful one. Seven
faults in the instrument were found, every one by a control rather than by
reading the code: a cold optimiser (the probe reproducing train.py's own
restart spike), too high a rate, the wrong AdEMAMix warmup, the wrong optimiser
entirely, lanes rewinding to position zero on every visit, AdamW's state names
fed to AdEMAMix, and a drift metric confounded by slot reuse. The first
version of this measurement produced a clean, confident, wrong answer - more
than half of what it called forgetting was the probe damaging the weights. The
interleaved control is what caught it: it reads every subject, so anything it
degrades cannot be forgetting.

Earlier passes are kept under v1_lr3e-4/, v1_cold/ and invalid/. They are not
results; they are the evidence for why the settings are what they are.

Nothing here wrote to a real weights directory. Every arm ran against a
single-use copy - the pool marks a paged-in expert dirty whether or not
anything touched it.

subject: drop AdEMAMix from the results
body:
It bought nothing and cost a third tensor. Measured on the arm that otherwise
scores +0.0067, adding the slow average took forgetting to +0.7899 - 118x
worse - and the drift says why: the trunk travelled 7.88% from its starting
weights against 1.70% under plain AdamW. alpha 5.0 makes the update m1 + 5*m2,
so the effective step grows by up to 1+alpha once the slow average fills, which
hands back most of a 10x cut. It works against the one mitigation that works.

Three things beyond the measurement argue the same way. It was never switched
on - trunk_opt is unset, the default is adamw, and optim.npz has no m2 - so
every result this project has ever produced came from AdamW anyway. Its slow
average cannot be restored from a checkpoint, because no checkpoint has ever
carried one, so enabling it means re-accumulating from zero at every restart
and being strictly worse than AdamW during the warmup, on a model whose whole
premise is that it never stops training. And it reaches only the trunk: across
the experts m2 is 1.74 GB and 50% more bytes through every page-in.

With the optimiser axis gone the figure stops being a 2x2 and becomes what the
experiment actually is - one variable, the trunk rate, plus the architectural
control. The right panel is now progress retained against chance, which is the
number that answers whether "catastrophic" is the right word: 42.88% frozen,
50.68% unmitigated, 99.84% as configured.

The frozen arm is that control, and a stricter one than a dense comparison
would have been: the same checkpoint, the same weights, the same training
history, with one property switched off. A matched dense model would have been
freshly initialised at a fraction of the scale, matched to within a percent of
parameter count and nothing else.

Measurements kept under runs/cl/rejected/ - the decision should stay
falsifiable even though the arm is out of the figures.

subject: comments describe the mechanism, not how it was found
body:
Every docstring and comment in minagi/ and config.yaml now says what the code
does today. The archaeology is gone: the six birth schemes, the 68 experts
deleted during a pool collapse, the t-statistic that measured how long it had
been watching, the 22.5 loads per chunk, "this used to be a gate test".

Three of them were not merely stale but wrong:

  pool.py        opened with "forgetting is held off by replay". It is held
                 off by the trunk learning rate, and there is no replay.
  optim.py       read as an argument for AdEMAMix. It is implemented, never
                 switched on, and measured 118x worse on the same arm.
  paged.py       saturation() said idle is a gate question in the docstring
                 and a staleness question three lines below it.

Also corrected: store.py named the expert files .npy when they are .npz and
carry Adam moments; config.yaml referenced prune.min_gate, which no longer
exists, and had the segment_chars and capacity_factor comments interleaved
with a trailing note that contradicted the value.

No code changed. Verified by comparing the AST of every file against HEAD with
docstrings stripped - all nineteen are identical - and no config value moved.

subject: a readme that matches the model on disk
body:
The parameter table was describing a different model: 19.1M against 458M,
67 experts of 98,304 against 143 of 3.15M, six distinct blocks against three,
top-16 against top-8. The layout listed nine modules of the nineteen that
exist, and the "not yet true" section listed three things that have since
become true - paging during training, learning while serving, and a pool that
is not capped by residency.

Restructured to follow the shape of the Anagnorisis readme: motivation, one
section per mechanism, a worked CLI, benchmarks, installation, layout, and
what is claimed but not measured.

Three figures added under assets/, each beside the claim it supports rather
than in a gallery:

  mitigations.png   forgetting under three configurations, with the control
                    arm that makes the other three readable
  probe_massed.png  the same probe per subject, and how much of the pool a
                    massed read actually touches
  scaling.png       held-out loss against every model with a published BPB

subject: the scaling section says what the curve says
body:
Drops the two-regime narrative. Refitting over the whole run past the warmup
gives a single clean power law - L ~ D^-0.221, R^2 0.94 across 485 points and
more than a decade of data - so there is nothing to explain away.

The section now states where the model is (1.2735 BPB on its own eight-subject
mixture at 236.8M characters), what the data gap to the published models
actually is, and what the fitted trend implies: 1.00 BPB at 0.91B bytes,
0.93 at 1.26B, 0.80 at 2.50B. Weeks of reading, all of it inside one pass of
the corpus.

Benchmark tables refreshed to 236.8M characters and 143 experts.

subject: log how far the model gets before an impossible move
body:
Chess is the one sampled prompt whose output can be checked, so it now is -
on the text already generated, which makes it free. 338 microseconds per
reading, twice per checkpoint, against a ten-minute sample interval.

    [adapted]  repeated 8-grams 0%   11 legal moves, then Be7

The number is legal moves before the first impossible one. If p is the chance
a single move is legal, a run of n estimates it as n/(1+n), and a game where
the model plays m moves finishes cleanly with p**m - so a 40-move game needs
p > 0.983. Replaying the 520 chess samples already in the log puts the model
at p = 0.906 and a mean of 9.65 moves, which is not a game yet.

It is the optimistic number: the model plays both sides here and can steer
toward lines it knows. tools/chess_legality.py measures the honest version on
held-out positions, at the cost of a forward pass each.

python-chess is imported inside the function and every failure path returns
None, so a missing package or a malformed prompt cannot take down a run that
has been reading for a week.

export_history.py picks it up as chess_legal_raw and chess_legal_adapted.

subject: the chess benchmark was prompting outside the training distribution
body:
`<g>` is a single marker token and the corpus format is `<g>ELO RESULT 1. e4`.
ModelPlayer built `<g ELO RESULT>` instead, which tokenises as twelve raw
bytes the model has never seen - so every game it has ever played started from
a prompt that does not occur in the data. Any chess number recorded before
this was measuring that, not the model.

Two more, while the instruments are open:

  benchmarks/code.py   load_any takes read_only, so a benchmark run against a
                       live weights directory cannot write expert files back
                       underneath the run that owns them.
  tests/                the prune tests still passed min_gate=, which the
                       staleness pruner does not take.

subject: the model at 242.8M characters
body:
146 experts, 467.7M parameters, 4.13 GB on disk, step 118,563.
Held-out 0.8887 nats = 1.282 bits per byte on the eight-subject mixture,
against 1.805 at 60M and 1.135 at 150M.

The manifest is the only part of weights/ that is tracked, so this is the

subject: remove what nothing calls, and one import that was missing
body:
corpus.py used json.load with no `import json`, so Corpus.__init__ raised
NameError on construction - which train.py batch and five experiments do.

Four symbols were defined and called from nowhere in the repository:

  model.MiniAGI       the plain transformer, ~80 lines. Nothing constructs it:

subject: show the model choosing its own depth
body:
runs/shape.mp4 regenerated from the current weights - step 119,626, 146
experts - and assets/shape.gif is a 15-second window of it for the readme,
820px, 2.9 MB, looping.

The clip is the one thing in the project that shows the architecture rather
than describing it: each row is one application of the recurrent block, the
eight tiles in it are the experts that row ran, and the grey rows below the
halt line are computation declined. Mean depth over the clip is 8.0 of 24.

The depth turns out to be legible. Measured over 400 characters of the same
text: whitespace 7.00 rows, the first letter of a word 7.65, a letter inside
a word 8.90, punctuation 10.12. Punctuation is the most expensive thing the
model reads, which is where a sentence commits to its structure.

The first draft of that paragraph said a character inside a word was the
cheapest. It is the second most expensive; the numbers above replaced the
guess.

subject: show the model writing, not just reading
body:
tools/animate_generate.py is the companion to animate_shape.py. That one
teacher-forces held-out text and shows what reading costs; this one primes the
model with a passage and lets it continue, so every character on screen is the
model's own.

Two things differ from reading and both are on screen. A paged model loads
with an empty card, so the prompt has to choose the working set before
anything is generated, and it is re-chosen every --reselect characters. And
greedy argmax on this model repeats itself, so decoding uses the adaptation
trace - the same reading the sample log labels [adapted]. Nothing is sampled;
the output is the same text twice.

Primed with 2,500 characters of held-out stories, trimmed back to the last
finished sentence - cutting at an arbitrary byte leaves the model halfway
through a word and the first thing it writes is the rest of that word.

    They worked together and saw their favorite shore. One day, they
    wanted to play with their favorite shore. They wanted to play with it,

Grammatical, on-topic, repeats itself. Depth runs 6-16 with a mean of 9.9
against 8.0 for reading the same subject.

runs/generate.mp4 is the full 140 characters; assets/generate.gif is the
first 90 at 820px, 2.0 MB, looping.

subject: no unnecessary comments
arithmetic in the notation the rest of the corpus uses
body:
Answers were written least-significant-digit first, so 7944019 + 364996
read as 5109038. That is the standard small-model trick and it does help
decoding, but this model also reads wikipedia, chat, reasoning and code,
where every number runs forwards - it was being taught two conventions
for the same thing. The scratchpad now carries the right-to-left
structure that reversal used to provide.

The scratchpads themselves asserted their results rather than deriving
them. mul stated a bare total, mod stated a bare remainder, sub stated
"borrow-chain" and the answer. A note that states the answer teaches the
model to emit a plausible number and copy it, which is what the corpus
was doing. Every step is now derivable from the ones before it, and
round switched to half-up so the rule its own trace states is the rule
it follows.

Dropped the BPE path. The model is byte-level, a digit is already its
own token, and the space-separation that SEP existed for was pure
overhead - along with --char, --tokenizer and sp(). --char was in any
case unusable: the script put corpora/ on sys.path instead of the repo
root, so minagi.tokenizer never imported.

Verified by re-deriving answers from the operands as printed: 500,000
lines, 0 wrong; 624,501 arithmetic claims inside scratchpads, 0 false.
Output is byte-identical to the previous --char path.

expand_corpus grows --only, which empties a lane before rebuilding it -
shard counts change, and a shorter rebuild would otherwise leave the
tail of the old corpus behind, mixing two formats in one subject.

subject: catch the callers up with the arithmetic format
body:
The previous commit removed sp(), SEP and rev() but left four call sites
reaching for them. serve.py's /api/math built its prompt with
math_data.sp(), which is now an AttributeError - the endpoint raised on
every request - and then ran the reply through unrev(), which would have
reversed an answer that is already forwards. It now writes the operands
plainly and reads the answer after the scratchpad, with enough budget to
clear a full <think> trace.

unrev() had no other caller, so it goes. The three remaining
`math_data.SEP = ...` assignments in benchmarks, corpora/chat.py and
train.py were no-ops writing an attribute nothing reads.

benchmarks.evaluate() was never affected: it compares against the
generator's own output rather than recomputing the expected spelling.

subject: make the public subset a repo that can stand on its own
body:
Publishing assets, corpora, minagi, weights, config.yaml, README.md,
serve.py and train.py leaves three things that do not work, and each was
load-bearing rather than cosmetic.

serve.py imported load_any from benchmarks.code at module scope, so it
would not start at all. load_any is eighteen lines that hand off to
minagi.recur.load_recur - it is how anything loads this model, not a
benchmark concern - so it moves to minagi/recur.py and benchmarks/code.py
re-exports it. The three endpoints that genuinely want the benchmarks
package now answer 503 rather than raising a 500 that reads like the
model broke.

Nothing could create a model or feed one: init_weights.py is the only
bootstrap, and expand_corpus.py is the only bridge from what corpora
writes (.bin) to what `train.py read` consumes (.bin is in ingest's
SKIP_EXT). Both assumed they sat in tools/ and computed the repo root by
counting two directories up, which lands outside the checkout once they
sit at the top level - silently, by resolving data paths against the
parent. They now find the root by looking for minagi/.

There was also no way to obtain the corpus. fetch_data.sh builds all
eight lanes in one command, skipping any already present so an
interrupted run resumes, and judging each lane by what it wrote rather
than by its exit code - the streaming reader aborts in
PyGILState_Release during interpreter shutdown, after every file is
written. fetch_corpus.py grows --config and --streaming for that, since
wikipedia is tens of gigabytes and only the text is wanted, and its
cache cleanup now removes ~/.cache/huggingface/datasets rather than the
whole directory, which also holds models it did not download.

publish.sh is the filter. It copies tracked files only, so an untracked
.env or stray .bin cannot escape by accident; it drops minagi/notify.py
and the five lines in train.py that call it; and it neither commits nor
pushes.

Verified by publishing into an empty repo and using nothing else:
init_weights, corpora arithmetic, expand_corpus, then train.py read -
loss 3.09 to 2.10 over 0.33M characters, one expert born, weights saved.

subject: the published repo needs nothing from the workshop
body:
Four changes, so that what ships is the model and the things that make it
work, with no scripts borrowed back out of tools/.

Building a corpus lives in corpora/ entirely. expand_corpus, fetch_corpus
and fetch_reasoning move there as expand, fetch and reasoning, and a new
build.py drives all eight lanes behind one command:

    python3 -m corpora all

Lanes already on disk are skipped, so an interrupted build resumes by
being run again, and a lane that fails is named at the end rather than
stopping the rest. Each runs in its own process: fetch.py ends with
os._exit once its files are written, because the streaming reader leaves
a thread alive that CPython aborts on, and in-process that took the whole
build down after the first lane. --limit also scales the held-out hold,
since a trial of 40 records against a fixed hold of 400 put every record
in val and none in training.

Creating a model lives in minagi/create.py, and `train.py read` calls it
when pointed at a weights directory that is not there. A directory that
does not exist yet is a model that has not been made yet, not an error -
config.yaml already says everything about its shape, so there is nothing
to ask. tools/init_weights.py stays as a thin command line for building
one with settings other than the file's.

The README no longer names anything that does not ship: no tools/,
benchmarks/ or experiments/, and the quickstart lost its "create a model"
step because there is no longer one to take. publish.sh checks this
rather than trusting it, comparing against the directories the source
actually withholds - matching any "word/" had been flagging halves of
URLs.

publish.sh itself moves to the root, where it can be called directly, and
its rescue list is gone.

Verified from an empty directory with nothing but the published tree:
corpora all --only wikipedia arithmetic downloaded and generated both,
then train.py read created the weights directory itself and trained.

subject: ship the run's history, not just its summary
body:
runs/samples.txt goes into the repository and into the published one. It
is 543 entries covering the whole run so far: what the model was at each
point - step, characters, experts, context, held-out loss per subject -
and then the same nine prompts continued, so any one of them can be
followed from `the the the the the` to most of an argument. Anyone can
check the loss curves against the thing they are curves of.

The ignore rule had to become runs/* with a negation under it. git does
not descend into an excluded directory, so !runs/samples.txt beneath a
bare runs/ would never have matched, and the file would have stayed
invisible while looking tracked in the diff.

publish.sh now asks the DESTINATION whether it ignores anything just
published. mini-AGI/.gitignore carries a bare runs/, which would have
swallowed samples.txt silently - copied every time, committable never.

The README gains a section saying to read the file rather than trust the
tables, with the raw-versus-adapted repeat rates that show greedy
decoding still collapsing where the adapted path does not, and a note
that trained weights are not published yet - the run is on its first
pass, and they go up when it has read the whole corpus, a couple of
weeks out. A filled-in Hugging Face template sits commented out beneath
it, download commands and all, ready to uncomment.

Two claims in that section were wrong when first written and are fixed
against the file: there are nine prompts rather than eight, and code does
not "read cleanly" - it is 82% repeated 8-grams raw, 8% adapted.

subject: remove AdEMAMix
body:
It was never the default and it was measured as worse: against the
mitigated arm the slow average took forgetting from +0.0067 to +0.7899
nats. With alpha = 5 the effective step grows by up to 1 + alpha once the
slow moment fills in, which hands back most of the 10x cut in trunk
learning rate - and that cut is the one mitigation that does work. Every
result this project has produced came from plain AdamW.

Gone from minagi/optim.py, which is now the gradient signal meter and a
paragraph on why the optimiser is not there; from train.py, along with
--trunk-opt, --beta3, --ademamix-alpha and --ademamix-warmup, which
leaves one unconditional AdamW; from the probe that produced the finding,
where the arm can no longer be selected; and from its test, which keeps
the GradSNR half. config.yaml never set any of it.

Also, two things this turned up:

TRAINING COULD NOT START FROM A FRESH CLONE. The auto-create added two
commits ago tested whether the weights DIRECTORY existed, and the
repository shipped weights/manifest.json - so the directory was always
there, creation was always skipped, and the first run of every new reader
died on a missing core.npz. It now tests for core.npz, and refuses rather
than wipes if the directory holds something other than a manifest.

The manifest is no longer published at all, so weights/ joins runs/ and
data/ as a directory the program writes rather than one the repo carries.

445 lines to 155. Every key and every value is unchanged - the run that

subject: serve.py: a chat window, and it learns from the conversation
body:
Replaces the old panel of tabs - model picker, benchmark buttons,
arithmetic checker, introspection - with one thing: a conversation.
Streams a character at a time, which at this size is most of the
information, and reports what each reply cost.

Two bugs came out of writing it, both inherited from the old file.

IT WAS RUNNING ON THE TRUNK ALONE. A paged model loads with an empty
card - every slot -1, every expert weight zero - so generating without
calling choose_for first uses 8M parameters of 468M. Not a degraded
model, a different and much smaller one, and it reads as fluent-shaped
nonsense: "What are you?" answered ": str==-1, xyo. #: str=-1, xyo."
With the prompt choosing the working set, and the reply re-choosing it
every 64 characters as generate() does, the same question answers "One
card with eight gigabytes. The pool is larger than that and is one
swap."

POSITIONS WALKED OFF THE END OF THE ROTARY TABLES. pos_offset was a
running count clamped to block, but the tables cover 0..block-1, so a
conversation long enough to fill the window asked for position `block`
and the model refused. The offset is read off the trimmed cache now,
which cannot drift from what the positions have to agree with.

Learning is on by default and CHANGES THE WEIGHTS ON DISK: the finished
exchange joins one continuous stream through minagi/live.py, a step every
training.chunk characters, the same path stream.py takes through a
corpus. Only the new turn is fed - the prompt already carries the
history, and re-feeding it would read the earliest turns once per
exchange. The weights open writable for it, since read_only marks
nothing dirty and what was learned would never leave VRAM. --no-learn
serves read-only.

Verified end to end: an exchange took 2 steps, wrote core.npz and
routers.npz, left the manifest intact at vocab 265, and the directory
reloaded afterwards.

subject: serve.py: show how far the stream is from its next step
body:
Learning was on and working, and looked broken. A step needs
training.chunk characters - 2048, tuned for reading a corpus - and an
exchange carries about ninety, so the first twenty-odd turns take no
step at all. No step means no backward, no Adam moments, and VRAM
sitting at the inference figure, which is indistinguishable from
learning never having been wired up.

The reply now always reports where the stream has got to, stepped or
not: `learning: 184/256 characters to the next step`, and the step count
and loss when one fires. --learn-chunk sets the granularity for a
session without touching what the corpus reader uses.

Measured against a copy of the trained weights, one step per 256
characters:

  turn 1   0 steps, 184/256 pending   1408 MiB
  turn 2   1 step,  loss 0.9868       2126 MiB
  turn 3   0 steps, 154/256 pending   2126 MiB
  turn 4   1 step,  loss 0.5842       2698 MiB

The card moves when the step fires and not before. core.npz changed, the
manifest survived at vocab 265, and the directory reloaded.

subject: serve.py: open the conversation with a passage of the corpus
body:
--prime-chars, 1024 by default. It buys two separate things.

The router gets something to choose from. choose_for on "hi" has two
characters to work with, and a paged model that picks its working set
badly answers out of the wrong quarter of itself. Measured against the
trained weights, the prime changes 6 of the 32 resident experts for
"hi", 2 for "what are you", 1 for "how deep do you think" - largest
where the user typed least, which is where it was wanted. Whether those
six are BETTER is not demonstrated; a three-question comparison of the
replies was inconclusive either way.

And the learning stream starts 865 characters along instead of at zero,
so the first optimiser step is about nine exchanges away rather than
twenty-two. That part is certain rather than inferred.

Taken from the self-knowledge lane, the `self-` files rather than
`auto-src-`: the first are short question-and-answer turns, the second
are whole source files quoted back, and priming with one of those biases
the router toward code and opens the conversation by dumping a module.

CUT WHERE THE MARKERS BALANCE, not at the last closing tag. That corpus
documents its own format, so a file contains a code block reading
"<bot>   </bot>" as prose - real marker tokens, not spellings. Trimming
to the last </bot> landed inside it and produced a prime with an
unclosed turn, handing the model an open <bot> to answer inside before
the conversation had started.

subject: serve.py: show the prime in the page
body:
The prime is prepended to every prompt server-side and never appears in
a reply, so the model was answering partly from context the person
talking to it could not see. /api/prime returns it and the page opens
with a collapsed disclosure above the conversation: how many characters,
how many turns, and the text itself.

Also fixes the input box, which opened at its 180px maximum when empty.
grow() set height to 'auto' before measuring, and 'auto' does not shrink
a textarea inside a flex row - scrollHeight then reported the height it
already had, so the box could only ever grow. Zero before measuring.

subject: one setting for how often writing re-chooses its experts
body:
Reading and writing used different values and only one of them was in
the settings. pool.segment_chars, 2048, is how much text one working-set
decision covers while reading a corpus. Generation re-chose every 64
characters - thirty-two times denser, and written as a literal in three
places that had nothing tying them together: serve.py, RecurCoder.generate
and tools/animate_generate.py.

The difference is right. A reader stays on one subject for a whole
passage; a reply changes subject with the prompt and drifts as it
develops. Being invisible and triplicated was not.

pool.reselect_chars now sits next to pool.segment_chars with a line
saying which is which. generate() takes None to mean "whatever the file
says", so its six callers keep the value they had.

subject: serve.py: show the two mechanisms working
body:
Both of the things the model does to itself were invisible. A reply that
taught it nothing looked exactly like one that did, and which quarter of
the pool answered a question could not be seen at all.

A strip above the conversation now carries both, always, not only after a
reply:

  long-term memory    characters until the next optimiser step, as a bar.
                      It flares and says how many updates when one fires,
                      and whether they reached disk. This is the answer to
                      "why did it not remember that" - usually because the
                      exchange was ninety characters and a step needs two
                      thousand.

  working set         characters until the next re-check, and a flare when
                      experts actually move. Only when they move:
                      choose_by_demand refuses to swap unless a candidate
                      beats a resident by `margin`, so most re-checks
                      change nothing and animating those would report an
                      event that did not happen.

Under them, the experts on the card, by uid. A slot number says where an
expert sits; the uid says which expert it is, and that is what survives
pruning. Newly arrived ones highlight for a moment.

/api/state serves both counters so they are right between replies, and
the stream now emits swap events as they happen rather than at the end.

Two fixes it turned up. The card is EMPTY at load - every slot -1 - so
the page showed no experts until the first question; the prime now
chooses a working set at startup, which does not change any reply
because generation re-chooses from the prompt anyway, but makes the
display true. And grow() ran before the flex row had a resolved width,
so the placeholder wrapped, scrollHeight read tall, and the input opened
at its 180px maximum every time.

Verified against a copy of the trained weights: counters tick per
character, "2 weight updates, saved to disk" with the bar resetting to
209/256, and swap events at characters 64 and 128 moving 2 and 1 experts.

subject: scaling graph, regenerated, and a tool that can do it again
body:
Updated to 308M characters, 648 evaluations:

  alpha   0.221 -> 0.238   (R2 0.940 -> 0.953, 485 -> 626 points)
  BPB     1.282 -> 1.226
  pool    143 -> 165 experts

The exponent steepened while the fit got tighter, which is the opposite
of what a curve bending toward a floor would do.

The point now carries what the model IS: 527M parameters over 165
experts, and ~344M dense-equivalent per byte. The second number is the
one this chart should be read against - the others on it are dense, and
what a byte costs here is the trunk plus top-8 of the 32 experts
resident, not the whole pool. Read from the manifest each time it is
drawn, since the pool grows while the run reads.

runs/scaling/SCALING.md is brought along: architecture table, the fit,
the per-domain slopes, the data-versus-parameters comparison and the
extrapolation targets. Leaving half of it at 0.221 beside a figure
saying 0.238 would have been worse than not touching it.

subject: remove the fixed-window batch trainer
body:
cmd_train and its `batch` subcommand go, 356 lines: independent windows
drawn at random, several per step, one autograd graph over each whole
window. Nothing has used it since reading replaced it, and it cost about
three times as much at an eighth of the reach - 6857 MB at 4k characters
against 3090 MB at 32k - because the retained graph was bounded by the
window rather than by the chunk.

tools/train_batch.sh goes with it. It called `train.py batch` with a
data_char mix and described itself as "the current mini-AGI training
run", which it has not been for a long time.

`stream` stays. It is batch 1 behind a cache, the same mechanism `read`
uses over a packed corpus rather than a directory - not the batched
regime, despite the name adjacency.

minagi/corpus.py moves to experiments/. Fixed random windows are how the
continual-learning arms were measured, and an experiment that changes
how it reads halfway through is not a comparison - but with the batch
trainer gone its only callers are those five experiments, and the
published repo was carrying it for nobody.

Also two stale lines in the README that I left behind earlier: it still
listed schedule.py, moved to experiments/ in "lean the published surface", and still
described optim.py as holding optimisers after AdEMAMix went in "remove AdEMAMix".

Verified: 33/34 tests, every entry point, all six experiments import,
and a published tree trains to the same loss as before - 3.7634 to
2.8115 on the same fixture.

subject: README: current benchmarks, current parameter count
body:
At 318.1M characters and 169 experts:

  held-out   0.8827 -> 0.8336 nats   1.2735 -> 1.2026 BPB
  train      0.7355 -> 0.6809 nats
  total      467.7M -> 540.1M parameters
  on card    101M   -> 109M of it

Per-subject losses, the data-scaling prose, the extrapolation targets and
the comparison multiples all move with them. MambaByte read 94x more
data than this model has, not 127x.

THE PROJECTION BAND MEANT THE WRONG THING. It was the trailing 140M
against the whole run, on the assumption the recent trend was the
steeper of the two. That stopped being true: the last 100M now fits
0.214 against 0.239 for the whole run, so the band collapsed to a line
and the figure went on claiming "if the recent, steeper trend holds".

It now spans the exponent across every fitting window - 20M onward
through 200M onward, plus the trailing 100M and 140M - which is 0.21 to
0.32. That is the honest quantity, and unlike a single window it cannot
quietly collapse. The y-axis drops to 0.40 so the optimistic edge is not
clipped, since clipping would hide exactly the part of the uncertainty
worth seeing.

subject: stream: make the two pools answer the same calls
body:
Reported from outside: `stream` trains fine and then raises TypeError at
its first prune. Confirmed, and it was worse than reported - fixing the
prune only moved the failure to the next call.

`read` replaces the pool with a PagedPool; `stream` keeps the SharedPool
a fresh model is born with. One AutoGrow and one loop drive whichever is
there, and two calls existed on only one of them:

  prune(step, survival=...)                  SharedPool called it min_age
  add_experts(..., birth_gate=...)           SharedPool had no such thing

Both now bind on both. `survival` means on SharedPool what `min_age`
always did, and `min_age` still works. `birth_gate` defaults to 0.0
there, which is what that pool has always used, so nothing changes for a
caller that does not pass it.

THE TESTS DIFFER AND SHOULD. SharedPool prunes on the gate because every
expert trains on every step and the load-balancing loss flattens usage
until it cannot separate live from dead. PagedPool prunes on residency
because an expert off the card does not train, so its gate cannot move
and a gate test would condemn exactly the ones being starved. Same
question, different evidence. Only the parameter name had diverged.

tests/test_pool_api.py binds every call the loop makes against both
pools. Reverting either fix fails it, which is what was missing: nothing
exercised these calls against the SharedPool, so no revision ran clean.

Verified on the reporter's own invocation, unchanged: 40 steps, loss
5.59 -> 4.78, val 4.2745, grew to 72 experts, weights written, exit 0.

Two more things this turned up. test_router_width counted every .npz in
weights/experts, including the e00013.npz.tmp.npz an interrupted save
leaves behind - so stopping a run made it fail. PagedPool builds expert
paths by index and never globs, so the file is litter rather than a
fault; the test now ignores it. And `stream`'s help said "the way it
runs", which is what sent the reporter there first.

subject: corpora: chat and code were still on the removed BPE path
body:
Reported from outside: `python -m corpora chat` dies on a tokenizer at
data/tokenizer.json, which does not exist. Confirmed, and it is my bug -
arithmetic.py lost --char and --tokenizer in "arithmetic in the notation the rest of the corpus uses" and the other two
generators did not, so they still fell through to a BPE that nothing
fits any more.

chat.py was broken twice over. Its --out defaulted to data_chat while
`corpora expand` reads data_chat_char, so even a run that got past the
tokenizer wrote where nothing would look for it.

`corpora all` passes no flags, so its chat and code lanes have been
broken since the day build.py was written. I tested that command on
wikipedia and arithmetic and never on these two.

Both are byte-only now, like the other two. The BPE machinery in code.py
goes with it - _fit_bpe, _load_fitted, --vocab, --tokenizer-sample-mb -
and corpora/ no longer imports `tokenizers` at all, so the README stops
telling people to install it.

`char` was already dead in chat.py's text path: it threaded down to
render_math_turn, whose only use of it was the math_data.SEP line removed
in "catch the callers up with the arithmetic format". Dropping the parameter changes no output.

tests/test_corpora_contract.py checks what actually drifted - that every
generator's --out default is the directory expand reads, and that none of
them still carry --char or --tokenizer. Reverting either fix fails it. It
inspects the parsers rather than building anything, so it costs seconds.

Verified by generating both: chat 295,278 train tokens, code 429,268,464,
both meta.json reading vocab 265 tokenizer byte.

subject: scaling graph on PG19 alone, and the means to measure it
body:
The figure carried GPT-2, GPT-3, Gopher and Chinchilla beside this model
and said in a footnote that the vertical positions were not comparable.
A caveat under a picture does not stop anyone reading the picture. Those
are Pile-CC numbers and they are gone - tables, marks, annotations,
legend rows, and the 4-bytes-per-token conversion that existed only for
them. What is left is the four byte-level models with a published PG19
bits-per-byte, which is one quantity on one held-out set.

`corpora pg19` takes the test split and only the test split. The Hugging
Face repo is a loading script rather than data and it carries the split's
file list, so the 100 test books come straight from the bucket - 41.3 MB
against 11.74 GB for the whole thing. One book per file with nothing
inserted between them: the corpus fetcher writes <|endoftext|> between
records, and those are real token ids that would be scored as text.

`tools/eval_pg19.py` scores consecutive windows and pools by byte, and
writes runs/scaling/pg19.json so the figure reads a measurement rather
than a number typed into it. --fraction samples every nth window rather
than a prefix; the first version took prefixes and read 2.55 BPB off
Gutenberg title pages and licence headers, which is not prose.

The figure now carries the measured PG19 point and, dotted, the fitted
exponent anchored at it. That line is a hypothesis: it assumes PG19
improves at the same rate as this model's own held-out, which nobody has
checked, and PG19 is out of distribution so it may well be optimistic. A
second PG19 point replaces the assumption with a fit. The legend says
"assumed, not fitted" rather than leaving that to be inferred.

The x-axis stops a little past MambaByte at 30B now instead of 3e13,
which was two thirds of the figure holding nothing once the subword
models left.

subject: scaling: drop the changelog from the figure, keep the MambaByte label inside
body:
The note under the plot said which models used to be on it. A figure states
what it shows now; the footnote is down to what is true of this one, and the
docstring carries the rule instead - a model belongs here only if it has a
published PG19 bits-per-byte.

The MambaByte label was placed in data coordinates past the right limit and
overprinted the other panel's tick labels. Right-aligned in axes fraction.

subject: scaling: the PG19 point is the whole test split, 2.4496 BPB
body:
100 books, 41,289,001 bytes, context 4,096, 88 minutes. The tenth-split
estimate it replaces read 2.4599, so sampling every nth window was
representative and the stride can be trusted for a quicker number later.

The label no longer says which part of the split it covers. The whole split
is what a PG19 number means; only a partial one has to say so.

subject: a boundary chooses its experts from its own text, not the last subject's
body:
demand() scores the states the call sites routed on while reading, which is
right in the middle of a passage and meaningless at the start of one. The
first chunk of a new passage, and a prompt, have no previous chunk of their
own, so the buffer still held the LAST subject's states and the choice was
made for text the model had stopped reading. The prompt was not an input at
all: the same buffer with two different prompts returned byte-identical
working sets, and one prompt after seven different passages returned seven
different ones.

peek_experts reads the text first and scores on its own states. It reads
from a FIXED starting set, because the peek routes through the pool at every
step and its states otherwise depend on whatever was resident when it began
- which is the previous subject again. Peeking from wherever the last
passage left off still gave 4.8 distinct working sets over those seven
passages, and re-reading up to three times gave 3.3. From the canonical set
it gives 1.0, and one answer per arithmetic prompt instead of two.

The pool specialises more for it: mean pairwise overlap across the nine
sample prompts 29.1/32 -> 23.4, experts wanted by every prompt 26 -> 15,
distinct experts reached 37 -> 62 of 176.

Held-out over 240 chunks is unchanged, 0.8064 -> 0.8061 nats against a
0.0174 stderr, which is the expected result: the peek runs on the first
chunk of each file and most chunks are not first. Costs one forward and two
swaps per passage, no disk reads - the canonical set is the top of the gate
and is always in the RAM cache.

Training peeks only at j == 0, the chunk that opens a passage; every chunk
after it keeps want_experts. Sampling peeks per prompt and puts the
observation buffer back, so a sampling round no longer decides what the next
training chunk reads with.

subject: merge: expert selection at a boundary comes from the text itself
serve: re-choose the working set from the reply, not from one character
body:
The generation loop re-asks the pool every `pool.reselect_chars` and asked
with `cur`. `cur = nxt` at the bottom of the loop, so from the second step
onward it is the single token just chosen: the working set was being
re-picked from one character's embedding, which is a re-roll on whichever
character landed on the boundary rather than adaptation to the reply. `out`
is the prompt plus everything produced and is already built for the decoder.

train.py's sampler was fixed this way and guarded; serve.py was not, and
kept the shape of the bug. It has been harmless rather than correct -
demand() ignores the tensor it is handed whenever it holds states of its
own, which during a reply it always does, so the single token was never
scored. Harmless by accident is still worth closing.

The guard now covers both loops.

subject: peek: score the whole chunk, not a literal that came from elsewhere
body:
`window` was 512. A chunk is training.chunk, which config.yaml sets to
2,048 - the 512 was train.py's fallback for when that key is missing, and
the key is never missing. So a passage boundary scored the last quarter of
the chunk it was choosing for and discarded the rest, and the docstring
asserted the two matched.

It defaults to the setting now, so the peek reads what reading reads. The
forward is under no_grad and reading carries the same 2,048 characters with
gradients every chunk, so the evidence was being given up for nothing.

Serving still passes its own bound: a transcript is however long the
conversation has got, and that is what the tail slice is for.

This refines the boundary fix rather than correcting it - the choice already
came from the passage's own text and was already invariant to what preceded
it, and those measurements were taken at 512.

subject: publish: the figures and the numbers are generated, not typed
body:
Three things in the README were facts about the run, maintained by hand:
the benchmark tables, the scaling paragraph, and the chart. A stale number
is worse than no number - it looks maintained, so nobody re-checks it. The
scaling prose had drifted furthest, still describing GPT-3, Pile-CC and
three held-out sets months after the chart became PG19 alone.

publish.sh now redraws assets/scaling.png and runs tools/refresh_readme.py
before it copies, so what ships is current by construction. Both run before
the uncommitted-changes check, so anything they rewrite is either committed
or reported rather than published behind this repo's back.

subject: replication: ship the continual-learning probe, both runs, and the weights
body:
The README's central claim is a measurement, and a measurement nobody can
repeat is an assertion. The probe that produced it was in tools/, which does
not ship, and its results were under runs/, which is gitignored - so the one
number the design rests on could not be checked by anyone outside.

replication/ carries the probe, the summary, the figure, and both sets of
results: the 147M-character checkpoint the README's table was measured on,
and a re-run at 428M. The mitigated arm holds, +0.0067 -> +0.0030, while both
unmitigated arms got worse with training rather than better - a model with
more to lose loses more of it.

The re-run also found the probe's own learning rate had gone stale. 3e-4 was
near the run's operating rate at 147M and is above it at 428M, so the control
- in which forgetting is impossible by construction - fails its own check
there, and the two unmitigated columns are upper bounds rather than
measurements. At the rate the model actually trains under the floor returns:
the control moves -0.0021 on the lanes it reads, the mitigated arm -0.0007 on
the seven it does not. That caveat is in the README rather than left for a
reader to discover.

The figure names checkpoints by what they had read rather than by "then" and
"now", which said nothing a reader could check.

subject: continual learning: measure it on a domain the model has never read
body:
The probe read chess. The model had already read 96M characters of chess and
sat at 0.496 nats on it, its best domain by a wide margin - so a massed read
could not teach it anything, and "nothing was forgotten" was measuring the
absence of an event rather than the presence of a mechanism. At 2.3e-4 the
mitigated arm moved chess by -0.0009 over half a million characters. There
was nothing there.

PG19 replaces it: 19th-century novels, never read, 1.67 nats against the
model's 0.77 average. A million consecutive characters of it, at the rate the
plasticity controller actually settled on. Four arms:

  interleaved, PG19 as a 9th lane   pg19 -0.3124   the other 8 -0.0065
  massed, trunk at 0.1x             pg19 -0.4216   the other 8 +0.1297
  massed, trunk = expert LR         pg19 -0.3106   the other 8 +1.2628
  massed, working set frozen        pg19 -0.2909   the other 8 +1.2663

Three things the chess probe could not show. The mitigation is not a
trade-off: it learns the new domain FASTER than either unmitigated arm while
forgetting ten times less. Freezing the working set is worst on both axes, so
the pool is not what prevents forgetting. And interleaving - what the run
actually does - absorbs a ninth domain while the eight it already knew come
out slightly ahead.

The section says plainly that the massed arm is a worst case: a million
characters is 32 passages back to back, where the run would have interleaved
224 passages of the other seven between them.

Also here: --read-root, so a new domain can be read from outside data/train
rather than becoming a ninth training lane by accident; the trunk's share of
the squared gradient norm re-measured at 98%; and the control's verdict no
longer calls an improvement contamination, which it did on the absolute
value.

subject: continual learning: show the interleaved read, and the exchange rate
body:
Two things the section stated but did not show.

The exchange rate is now a column: nats gained on the new domain per nat lost
across the eight. 0.23 and 0.25 for the unmitigated arms, 3.25 for the one
the run uses, and no trade at all when the domain is interleaved. That is the
number the comparison is actually about, and it was left for the reader to
divide.

The interleaved figure is now in the section rather than only on disk - and
it was drawing the wrong thing. fig_probe accented the MEAN of the read
lanes, which was right when one lane was read and wrong the moment several
were: PG19's -0.31 averaged against seven subjects that barely moved and the
figure showed -0.046, burying the result it exists to show. It accents the
probe's own domain in both arms now, so the eight are the flat band at zero
and PG19 is the line leaving it.

Also fixed: the minimum gap between right-edge labels was a fraction of the
labels' own spread, so eight subjects sitting within 0.02 of zero on an axis
0.8 tall printed on top of one another. It scales to the axis now.

subject: README: audit every number, and label the projection so it cannot be misread
body:
The projection table said "bytes needed | days" where the bytes were
CUMULATIVE and the days counted from here, so "0.49B | ~1 day" read as
reading half a billion characters in a day - against seven days already spent

separates total from further, says how far the model has already got and how

Five other claims were wrong or stale:

  routing      "each of the 26 applications picks its own top-8" - two of
               those 26 are prelude blocks with ordinary MLPs; 24 route
  paging       described the working set as always scored on the previous
               chunk, which stopped being true when boundaries began reading
               their own text from a fixed starting set
  parameters   169 experts and 540.1M total; it is 175 and 559.0M
  compute      "about 2.4 GFLOPs per byte, a dense 400M transformer" against
               the 344M the scaling figure computes from the manifest - the
               figure is right, and the README now states what activates and
               why it is 344M rather than 559M
  the clip     "where the model is at 243M characters" for a recording made
               200M characters ago; it is where the model WAS

subject: pool: key_floor to config, and up to 0.25
body:
Selection scales an expert's fit by gate/max_gate, floored at key_floor.
While an expert is inside its trial the scaling is waived; once the trial
ends it competes on that floor. At 0.1, against originals sitting near 0.68,
that is a 7x handicap - and it is self-sealing, because the gate it is judged
on only moves when it is chosen. The docstring beside it already said so.

The effect is visible in the run. The pool grew from 129 experts to 175 since
250M characters while the number carrying 99% of routing stayed at ~70, and
experts with no routing at all in a 30M-character window went from 2 to 45.
By birth cohort, at 486M characters:

  original (born 0)     47 experts,  3 idle, mean gate 0.340, 62.1% of routing
  grown, oldest third   41 experts, 26 idle, mean gate 0.067
  grown, middle third   41 experts, 16 idle, mean gate 0.033
  grown, newest third   43 experts,  0 idle, mean gate 0.025

The newest cohort is fully employed because it is still inside its trial, and
each older cohort is further out of use - which is the handicap landing, not
wear. An original gets 4.4x the routing of a grown expert.

0.25 takes the handicap under 3x. Not A/B'd: the effect wants days of reading
to show, and that time is better spent reading.

It lives in config.yaml now rather than as a constant, and build_paged applies
it beside pool.capacity_factor - both are properties of how the pool is
scheduled rather than of the checkpoint, so serving and the probes schedule it
the way the run does.

subject: README: cite Block-Recurrent Transformers
body:
Carrying a recurrent state across blocks is the shape any continuity beyond
the attention window has to take here, and it is the prior art for the
chunk-to-chunk latent carry now being considered.

subject: README: project the full corpus pass, not just the BPB targets
body:
The table said how long to reach 1.10, 1.00, 0.93 and 0.80 BPB and stopped
there, so the one milestone the run is actually walking toward - reading the

The last row is that pass. Its BPB is read OFF the trend rather than chosen,

The closing sentence followed from the old rows and said "days to weeks",

subject: dashboard: the routing window is 100M, and was showing the whole run
body:
window_use took the LAST row at or before the target, meaning last in file
order. The log is append-only and its character counter is not monotonic
across it: a run resumed from an earlier checkpoint rewinds it, and a run
pointed at another weights directory restarts it from zero while still
writing here, because --history defaults to runs/expert_history.jsonl
whatever --weights-dir says.

Either of those puts a low-character row late in the file, and the window
then reached back to it. The panel said "routing share over the last 100M
characters" and was drawing 508M - the whole run - while every other panel
on the dashboard honoured --last.

It picks the latest row by character count now, which is what was meant.
Against the same log that produced 508M, it gives 100M.

The two windows still come from different places - the panels from --last,
this one from prune.survival_chars - and agree at 100M only because both
happen to be 100M. Worth tying together if either ever moves.

subject: dashboard: every panel on the same window
body:
The routing panels windowed on prune.survival_chars while the curves
windowed on --last. Those are unrelated numbers - one is how long an expert
may go unasked-for before it counts as atrophied, the other is how much of
the run the dashboard is drawing - and they agreed only because both
happened to be 100M. A dashboard drawn with --last 20 put a 20M curve beside

`Who does the work`, `Are the newcomers earning their place` and `How

--last now. Rendered at 20M and 100M: 65 carry 99% against 82, which is the
panel tracking the flag instead of ignoring it.

`Near deletion` stays on the survival window, because staleness as a share
of that window is the pruning rule rather than a view of the data - and its
subtitle now says so, since it is the one panel on a different clock.

body:
Four lines of caveat under one panel, most of it explaining that the panel

subject: pool: give idle experts an audition
body:
Nothing in demand() ever favours an expert because it has been idle. Fit is
scaled by what it has earned, `margin` makes incumbency sticky on top of
that, and a non-resident expert's router row never trains - so one that
falls off the card cannot argue its way back. It ages out and is pruned,
having failed by never being asked rather than by being asked and adding
nothing. Measured over a 100M window: 78 of 168 experts carry 99% of
routing, the top gate quartile takes 64%, and corr(gate, share) is +0.75.

pool.audition_slots reserves slots of the working set each boundary for
whichever expert has gone longest without a turn.

TWO THINGS MAKE IT SAFE, and both are the whole design.

An audition is a hearing, not a reprieve: swap_to leaves last_seen alone for
auditioned experts. last_seen is the clock prune deletes on, so resetting it
would make the pool immortal - every dead expert auditioned, freshly seen,
never removed. It keeps ageing; only a normal admission, meaning demand
actually asked for it, stops that.

And auditions cycle on their own clock. Picking by last_seen cannot, exactly
because the audition leaves last_seen untouched: the stalest expert would
stay stalest and be picked every boundary forever. last_try is that clock.

Boundaries are exempt. An audition depends on what was read before, which is
the dependence a passage boundary and a prompt are meant to be free of, so
peek_experts suppresses them - fifteen of every sixteen chunks still get one.

Default 1. At 0 the code path is inert and the model is bit-identical.

subject: pool: audition_slots off - the reprieve leaked
body:
swap_to resets last_seen for every id in the plan, and that includes experts
that were already resident and stayed. An audition puts an expert on the
card; `margin` then keeps it there; the next chunk counts it as an ordinary
resident and resets the clock. One chunk of protection, then immortality.

Measured on the live run after a day: the stalest expert in the pool had
gone 355 segments of a 48,828-segment survival window - 0.7% of a distance
it has to cover in full to be deleted - and nothing was dying at all, where
12 had been before.

The guard test could not see it: it checks a single swap, and the leak is in
the swap after.

What it exposes is that last_seen means "was in the working set" while prune
reads it as "anything asked for it". Those were the same thing only while
residency had to be earned, and an audition makes residency free. Fixing the
audition alone cannot close it, because the reset arrives through the
ordinary incumbency path.

The mechanism stays in the tree at 0, where it is inert.

subject: pool: audition the expert the text wants but the discount buries
body:
Two changes, and the second is why the first is usable at all.

SELECTION. An audition now goes to the non-resident expert with the highest
UNDISCOUNTED fit among those sitting on key_floor - the ones this text is
asking for whose only problem is that they have earned nothing. demand()
already computes that similarity and then multiplies it by `earned`, which
is right for choosing a working set and useless for choosing who to hear:
that is exactly a question about the experts the discount is burying. The
old rule picked the stalest, which says nothing about whether the expert is
any use on the text in front of it.

LIFETIME. An audition lasts one chunk. Whoever was auditioned last time
gives the slot back and has to win it through the ordinary path. Without
that they become incumbents, `margin` keeps them, and the next swap_to
counts them as an ordinary resident and resets the prune clock - which is
how the first version made the pool immortal while passing a test that only
looked at one swap. The clock is measured over many boundaries now.

It self-terminates: an expert that earns gate stops being suppressed, stops
being audition-eligible, and competes normally - and that admission resets
its clock legitimately. One that earns nothing keeps ageing and is pruned.

last_try is kept: it no longer picks, but it records that a hearing was
given, which is worth having when reading the telemetry.

subject: runs: a resume drops what the abandoned branch wrote
body:
The history log is append-only and its character counter is not monotonic
across a restart: reading on from a checkpoint leaves rows describing a model
that no longer exists, sitting after the point being resumed from.

Every reader has had to cope with that, and none of them did. The dashboard
drew a seam at the join. window_use took the last row at or before its
target, meaning last in FILE order, and reached back to an abandoned row -
the panel said it was showing 100M and showed 508M. Both were found by
noticing something looked odd, not by anything checking.

cmd_read drops those rows at startup, once, at the point it knows where it
is resuming. A row AT the resume point is the checkpoint's own and stays;
a run starting from zero has no checkpoint and truncates nothing; an
unparseable line is kept, because a reader can skip what this must not
delete.

This is the third time these logs have needed cleaning by hand after an
abandoned experiment.

subject: pool: one selection rule - the router admits what each text asks for
body:
The working set is gone: demand scores, expert keys, margin, dwell, the
cold-start sweep, auditions, the canonical peek and the re-choice every 64
characters while writing. One rule replaces all of it, and it is the router's.

While a text has room on the card, every character at every pass ranks the
whole pool with the router and asks for its top 8, each request carrying the
probability the router gave it. The text admits experts in order of requested
probability until the card's 32 slots are full, and every character then
routes among the admitted - one whose request was not admitted takes its best
admitted expert. A text is a forward that starts at position 0: a training
window, a held-out cache window, a prompt with its reply. In training the
first pass of a window already asks for 121-136 experts, so the window's set
is fixed there and holds through the backward pass and the optimiser step.

An expert already on the card keeps its slot; a newcomer takes the slot of one
the text did not admit, an empty one first, then the one admitted longest ago.
The rows that admit are the rows that route, so admission is learned by the
language-model gradient itself.

Measured on one snapshot (step 295,101), 15 minutes of the real reader each:
held-out 0.7170 -> 0.7036 zero-shot and 0.7111 -> 0.7011 after 15 minutes,
reading 1,695 -> 1,802 characters a second, loads 6.39 -> 2.43 a step, VRAM
unchanged. Admission resets per text rather than per forward: per forward, a
sampling round took 856 s against 183 s, reloading 18.6 experts a character.

A newborn's router row is its parents' rows averaged by how many units each
gave, so it starts out scoring characters the way they do. Checkpoints written
before load unchanged; their segment-router rows are skipped.
test_audition and test_demand_prefers_earned tested mechanisms that no longer
exist.

subject: docs: the one selection rule, wherever the old one was described
body:
README's paging section is rewritten around admission, including how the
gradient trains the router. The routers row of the parameter table drops to
0.09M with the segment router gone, and the replication arms are dated: they
were measured when the experts on the card were re-chosen before every chunk.
ARCHITECTURE's storage section, the talk script's paging paragraphs and the
continual-learning write-ups follow. docs/adaptation.md keeps its analysis
and says what replaced the machinery section 5 was built on.

every 64 characters; 15 answers now describe admission, and chat.py no longer
