until tools/rebuild_self_knowledge.py --apply is run.

subject: README: re-record the reading and writing clips at step 296,153
body:
Both clips dated from step 119,626 and the working-set rule. Recorded again
from a copy of the weights at 605.8M characters - on the CPU, because the run
had the card - and cut as before: the first 15 seconds, 820px, looping.

The reading clip was captioned as held-out text but read data/train. It now
reads held-out stories, and its first 2,048 characters start the text and
admit its experts; nothing loads while the clip plays. The writing tool fed
the prompt's last character twice. It now feeds the prompt once, as
RecurrentLM.generate does, and its on-screen text no longer falls behind the
character being written after an end-of-text marker.

Reading and writing now cost about the same depth - 11.4 and 11.0 rows a
character - so the README no longer says writing costs more. The prompt
admits all 32 experts before the reply begins, and no reply character admits
another. The reply closes the cherry tree story after three sentences and
starts one that contradicts itself; the caption says so.

subject: pool: every forward admits its own experts, and an untrained one is not written back
body:
Admission used to last a whole text, so a reply lived on the experts its
prompt admitted: any prompt of a few dozen characters asks for more than 32 at
its first pass, and nothing could be loaded after it until the context window
filled. The 32 is a training limit - everything a training forward used must
stay on the card through its backward and the optimiser step - and a forward
with no backward after it needs its experts only while it runs. So now every
forward admits afresh: a training window as before, each held-out chunk, the
prompt, and every character of a reply, which can follow its topic wherever
it goes. A forward from position 0 still begins a text, and only that moves
the prune clock, so writing one character at a time does not age the pool.

That makes loads constant while writing, and every expert leaving the card
was copied back and marked dirty as if it had been trained, so each load
became a disk write. Now a slot remembers the slot tensors' version counters
and the optimiser steps seen when its expert arrived; while both are unchanged
the expert is exactly its copy and parking it copies nothing. flush() skips
the same experts at save.

Measured on a copy of step 297,469, on the CPU, 139 characters written after
a 2,459-symbol held-out prompt: 19.6 experts loaded per character, every
character loading some, 3.3 read from disk; 0 expert files written, against
389 with the old write-back; 0.67 s a character against 0.52 when the reply
kept the prompt's experts. Held-out was measured per forward in the A/B that
chose this rule: 0.7036, against 0.7045 per text.

The chat page keeps a running total of a reply's loads instead of one note
per character, and the reading and writing clips show what each character
loaded.

subject: docs: every forward admits its own experts; the clips re-recorded under it
body:
The README's paging section, ARCHITECTURE's storage block, the note on
docs/adaptation.md section 5 and the talk script now describe admission per
forward: a training window, a held-out chunk, a prompt, each character being
written. The README gains the third paging rule - an expert nothing trained
is not written back.

self_knowledge.yaml answers the same way, including what happens when the
model writes; two answers that were wrong before are corrected too - the
expert file is not compressed, and the RAM cache writes an expert out only
if it was trained since it was last written.

Both clips are recorded again from a copy of step 297,469 (608.5M
characters), on the CPU while the run had the card. Reading: depth 8-16 over
the clip, about 19 experts loaded per character. Writing: 10.7 rows a
character against 11.2 for reading the same stories, 19.6 experts loaded per
character with every character loading some, and the reply continues the
cherry tree story its prompt ends on - the captions quote it and say what is
wrong with it.

subject: pool: a load copies only what the card will use
body:
_rearrange moved every tensor of a fetched expert onto the card - its Adam
moments included - and then copied the weights a second time into the slot.
Now the weights are copied straight into the slot, and the moments only when
an optimiser holds state for them.

Measured on the GPU at step 298,919, 139 characters written after a
2,459-symbol held-out prompt, with every expert in RAM: 188 ms a character
once RAM is warm, against 276 before this change and 92 when a reply kept its
prompt's experts. With learning on, the moments still travel - an expert
loaded while writing can still be on the card when the next training step
updates every slot - and a character costs 308 ms. With the trainer's RAM
cache of 96, about three of the 19 loads a character come from disk: 293 ms.

subject: pool: explore while training - a bonus for experts used less than their share
body:
The router's scores are flat - a character's eighth-best expert scores 0.48
above its median one - and a newborn's row, its parents' rows averaged, sits
just under that cut: a median 0.44 logits below. Only chosen experts get the
gradient, so most of the pool never learned. Over 30 real training windows
at step 298,919, 45 of the 50 experts on trial were never admitted, and only
67 of the 170 were used at all.

Now every expert keeps `recent`, its share of the last ~1,000 training
forwards that admitted it, and a forward that trains adds
explore_bias * exp(-recent / fair share) to each router score wherever
something is chosen - what a character asks for, and the top_k it takes -
the fair share being resident / experts. The mixing weights stay the router's
own softmax over the chosen, so the gradient that reaches a chosen expert's
row is the same as if it had been chosen on its score alone. Measuring and
writing never explore. A newborn starts at no use, with the whole bonus.

Being tried must not keep an expert alive, so the prune clock - and with it
both growth brakes - now counts only what the router would have admitted
without the bonus, tracked beside the real admission at no extra cost.

explore_bias 0.35. Fifteen minutes of the real reader from step 298,919, the
same text in the same order: 128 experts reached the card against 92, 39 of
the 50 young against 22, 3.0 of each step's 32 admitted for the bonus alone;
3.67 loads a step against 2.56, 1,727 characters a second against 1,818;
held-out moved +0.0007 against +0.0013, with a standard error of 0.015.
`recent` starts at zero in a checkpoint written before it existed, so the
bonus is even at first and differentiates as the busy experts' share climbs.

subject: docs: exploration, and a prune clock that counts only the router's own choice
body:
The README's paging section explains the bonus - who gets it, what it
changes and what it leaves alone, and how the gradient then decides - and the
growth section says a newborn starts with all of it. "Dead means unaddressed"
now reads the router's own admissions, since being tried keeps nothing alive.
ARCHITECTURE and the talk script say the same in a sentence each; the
paged.py docstring went in with the code.

self_knowledge.yaml gains a question on how rarely used experts get their
chance, and the answers on choosing, growing, protecting against a bad
newborn and deleting mention the bonus; chat.py fills explore_bias from
config.yaml.

subject: train: reading and writing speeds apart, and the sample clock starts when a round ends
body:
Since every written character admits its own experts, a sample round - 9
prompts, two readings each, 140 characters - takes about 15 minutes in the
trainer, and the 10-minute sample clock started when a round began. A round
longer than the interval made the next one due at once: from 14:38 the run
read one step between rounds, and the log reported 2 char/s.

The clock now starts when a round ends, so the next round is due after
sample_every minutes of reading however long a round takes. And the log
reports two numbers: reading, the characters trained over the time spent
reading since the last round - the held-out check and the samples excluded -
and writing, the characters the samples wrote over the time spent writing
them. "reading N char/s" keeps its format, so the tools that parse it still
do; it now means the training alone.

Checked with the real reader on a tiny model, rounds three times longer than
a 1.2-second interval: the old code read 1 step between rounds and reported
12-15 char/s; this reads 10-11, at 480-1,149 char/s reading and 128-175
writing.

subject: README: project at the pace the run keeps on the wall clock
body:
The days in the projection were the characters still to read over the
reading speed in the latest header. That speed leaves out what the
reading waits for - held-out checks, rounds of samples, saves - so the
days came out short, and "which took about N days at the current rate"
was a hypothetical dressed as a fact.

The pace now comes from the sample log's own clock: each session's banner
says how much had been read when it started, each round's header how much
by then and how many minutes in, so characters over minutes is the pace
with everything included. The latest session runs the current code, so
its pace is the one used; a session shorter than three hours borrows the
ones before it. The running time is the same minutes summed over every
session, and replaces the hypothetical.

The sentence under the table is worked out from the rows: it said "the
first four" over three, and "days to weeks" whatever the pace.

Numbers now read every thousands separator, so the parse keeps working
past step 1,000,000.

Also committed, made earlier and left in the tree: the projection's last
row loses its label and the months-to-a-full-pass sentence, and publish.sh
ships the three plot tools train.py runs to draw its graphs.

subject: pool: moments travel only to a step, and every expert is stepped with its own
body:
An expert used to bring its Adam moments to the card with its weights on
every load, whenever an optimiser held state. In the trainer one always
does, so a sample round - 2,520 characters, about 20 loads a character -
copied some 50,000 sets of moments onto the card, 12 MB each, for a round
in which no step happens. On the free GPU a written character took 308 ms
with moments travelling and 188 ms without.

Now an expert arrives with its weights alone. Just before every optimiser
step (_own_moments, a step pre-hook) every expert on the card that is not
already holding its own moments gets them from its entry in RAM or on
disk. AdamW steps every slot, used or not, so that is exactly the set that
needs them. A stepped expert is parked with its moments as before; an
unstepped one still writes nothing, and an entry that is not its own keeps
the moments it had, because an entry replaces the old one whole. The
README states the rule as it now works.

It also fixes a bug that bit at every restart. The trainer's held-out check
puts experts on the card before the optimiser exists; the restore that
follows writes the slot-indexed moments from optim.npz, which belong to
whichever experts sat in the slots when it was saved. An expert kept from
the check into the first training step was stepped with that stranger's
momentum, and wrote it back as its own. The pre-hook fills every slot
again after such a restore, since the moment tensors it filled have been
replaced.

tests/test_own_moments.py keeps its own ledger of every expert's moments
and checks every slot before every step, through replies, held-out
forwards, disk round trips and a restart. Against the previous code it
fails twice: moments moved while a reply was written, and after a restart
one of two kept experts was stepped with another's moments. The rest of
the suite passes, except test_notify, which finds the local .env.

subject: live, replication: every optimiser resumes Adam's moments and knows the pool
body:
The chat server's learning mode built a fresh optimiser and never read
optim.npz. Its first step started every tensor from zero moments - the
trunk's, and every expert on the card instead of its own - and its first
save wrote that short history over the trainer's in optim.npz, step
counters included, so the next training session resumed from it. The
learner now restores the moments the way the trainer does, and the pool
puts each expert's own in place before every step.

The replication probe never attached its optimiser to the pool, so the
pool could not give an expert paged in its own moments: it was stepped
with whatever its slot held for the one before it. One line. The probe's
published results were measured without it and have not been re-run.

tests/test_live_learning.py: the learner starts from the saved trunk
moments and step count, and its first step steps every expert on the card
with its own.

subject: model: freeze and carry - a character that has halted stops being computed
body:
Halting used to choose only which pass's prediction a character keeps:
every character ran every pass up to the ceiling, 24 when writing, and
about 13 of them were computed and thrown away. The README said the rows
below the halt were computation the model declined to spend; the code
never did that, in any version in git.

With model.halt_freeze a character's state stops changing at the pass
where it halts, its experts stop running, and the characters after it
read that final state at every deeper pass. They read it through the keys
and values the recurrent block makes of it, which are the same at every
pass - one block, one final state - so they are computed once and carried.
Training does exactly the same, so what the model learns from is what it
writes with: a halted character's later loss terms are its final
prediction's, and the halting head is trained through them as before.

  recur.py   the pass loop: halted characters are frozen, only the rest
             reach the block's experts, and once all have halted the
             remaining passes only receive the carried keys and values
  model.py   Attention.kv / extend; Block passes `active` to the pool
  pool.py    PooledMLP routes only the active characters: a halted one
             asks for no experts, takes no capacity and counts in no
             statistics or balancing loss
  train.py   --halt-freeze, from model.halt_freeze. The depth settings
             from config.yaml are now applied before the first held-out
             check, which they change, instead of after it

Off by default until the A/B says whether to keep it. The carry is exact:
tests/test_halt_freeze.py reads a text one character at a time through
the cache, the way writing does, and gets the one-forward read's
predictions to 1e-7 with the same halting passes - 199 passes run for 48
characters against 288. test_dispatch_capacity reads the dispatch where
it now lives.

subject: config: halt_freeze on - the A/B says it costs little and saves a lot
body:
From the same weights (step 308,412), on the same 240 held-out chunks:

  without training, frozen against full depth
    held-out as the log reports it     -0.0003 +/-0.0001
    what each character emits          +0.0006 +/-0.0001
    writing                            4.31 -> 6.88 char/s, 19.8 -> 16.1
                                       experts loaded a character

  15 minutes of the real reader each, frozen against full
    training                           1,777 -> 2,038 char/s, 888 steps
                                       against 773
    peak VRAM                          6.87 -> 5.04 GB
    held-out as the log reports it     -0.0018 +/-0.0004
    what each character emits          +0.0011 +/-0.0004 (mixed by
                                       subject: chat_hermes +0.004,
                                       wikipedia +0.004, chat -0.002)

What each character emits is slightly worse, by about a thousandth of a
nat; the log's own held-out is slightly better; everything the run
spends time on is cheaper. The README describes halting as it now works:
a character that has stopped is finished, and training does the same.

The summary is in runs/results/halt_freeze_ab.json.

subject: pool: the text chooses - every forward is admitted by its text's vote
body:
Writing had drifted into gibberish while the held-out loss kept falling:
"trave5", "someth5", "kallowed", "kaaaaaa". Raw samples went from about 9%
words that appear nowhere in the training text to 22%. The cause was the
admission rule, not the model. Every forward admitted its own experts, and
a written character is a forward of one character, so it routed among the
experts it alone asked for - a situation training never produces: a
training window's 32 are chosen by all of its characters together, and
only the router rows of experts a window admitted are ever trained.

Now every forward's first pass adds its requests to the vote of its text,
everything read since position 0, and the forward is admitted the experts
its text has voted for most. A training window is a text of its own, so
training is unchanged. A written character routes among what its prompt and
the reply so far have asked for: the choice a window over that text would
make, cut off at the character being written. A new text starts an empty
vote; a prune renumbers the experts and starts it again.

Measured on the same held-out characters, 8 subjects x 128, each with close
to 4,096 characters of context, step 317,062:

                                          before     now
  scored as the held-out check reads      1.1229     1.0950
  scored as writing reads                 1.3490     1.1111
  writing, experts loaded a character      15.1        0.07

Writing now matches the held-out check on the same text to 0.016 - what is
left is the check's look-ahead: every character of its chunk votes,
including the ones after the character predicted. Spending more at
writing time did not help: a halting threshold of 0.97 gave 1.1191, a
48-slot card 1.1736.

The held-out check changes too, and its number will drop at the next
restart for that reason alone: a chunk that continues a file is now chosen
by the file so far, not by itself.

Docs, the chat page, the self-knowledge answer, the clip tools and the
tests say the rule as it is; test_expert_selection recomputes a text's vote
from the router and checks every forward of a prompt and its reply against
it (1 of 47 forwards agreed under the old rule). The README clips are
re-recorded under it at step 317,062: not one expert loaded after the
prompt, and the reply is spelled right.

subject: pool: a temperature of expert selection, pool.select_temperature
body:
Characters are always chosen greedily; this decides how randomly the
experts that compute them are chosen, and is meant to be where the model's
variety comes from instead of a temperature on the text.

  0     the rule as it has run: the card holds the 32 experts the text's
        first row votes for most, and each character takes its own top 8
  > 0   drawn: at each row 8 experts are drawn from the text's
        probabilities - the router's full distribution, summed over every
        character read since position 0 - in proportion to p^(1/T),
        until the card's 32 are full; each character draws its own 8
        from its own probabilities over the card the same way, weighted
        by the router's probability as a taken expert is

1 draws in proportion to the probabilities, 0.5 to their squares. Close
to 0 the draws approach each row's top 8, which is not quite 0 itself: a
drawn card fills 8 a row, so its first row has 8 experts where 0 gives
all 32. A drawn expert counts as asked for on the prune clock.

The default is 0, so nothing changes until it is set. The measurements
that led here - 15 minutes each from step 478,910, held-out on 30 chunks
per subject, own rule after training: 0.6538 at 0 with the bonus, 0.9264
at 1, 0.8329 at 0.5; training at 1 and 0.5 ran at half speed with 23-25
loads a step - are in runs/results/rule_samples.md.

tests/test_select_temperature.py: the card fills 8 a row; each row's
probabilities are every character's, summed over a prompt and its reply,
recomputed from the router; characters route only on the card; at 1 fresh
texts bring 39 of 40 experts onto it, close to 0 a row's draw is its top 8
every time; a new text starts empty; at 0 the card is admitted whole at
the first row, as before.

subject: pool: a balance term replaces the exploration bonus; use resets the prune clock
body:
Left alone the router keeps choosing the same experts: reading held-out on
its own it put 59 of its 118 on a card. The bonus spread the training work
(116 experts in 15 minutes) but not the model's own use (58 after). A term in
the loss now charges the router, in every forward that trains, for the
probability it puts on each expert over the whole pool, in proportion to that
expert's share of recent admissions - Switch's balancing term with the share
taken over ~1,000 training forwards, so a text may still want few experts.
It changes the router itself, so reading and writing choose the way training
does. pool.balance in config.yaml, 0.003; only the router's rows learn from it.

Whatever admits an expert now resets its prune clock, so prune and both usage
brakes read one clock of use, and the merit tally is gone.

15-minute arms from step 478,910 (held-out after; experts in use on held-out):
bonus 0.65 0.6541, 59 -> 58; balance 0.01 0.6793, 59 -> 114; offset per
expert at 0.001 0.7019 and at 0.0002 0.6518, 59 -> 73.

subject: readme: the parameter count is counted from the weights at every publish
body:
The README's parameter table was typed by hand and still claimed 175 experts
and 559M parameters when the pool held 150 and 480M. minagi.store now counts
the model from its files - core and router bundles element by element, every
expert the manifest names - and prints the table under `python3 -m
minagi.store`, as the README says it does. tools/refresh_readme.py, which
publish.sh runs before copying, regenerates the README's table and the VRAM
paragraph under it from the same count, between auto:params markers. The
scaling chart reads its sizes from it too, so the three cannot disagree.

The paragraph also said the 344M per byte counts 24 recurrent steps; it counts
train_steps_mean, 12.8, and now says so. And the chart it refers to is above
it, in Benchmarks.

subject: tools: every PG19 measurement is kept and drawn, and out of distribution says so in bold
body:
eval_pg19.py overwrote runs/scaling/pg19.json, so a second measurement would
have erased the first. It now also appends to pg19_history.jsonl (seeded from
the old record), and takes the characters read and the step from the weights
it scored rather than from the log's last line - a snapshot measured behind
the log would otherwise be drawn where the model was not.

plot_scaling.py draws every measurement. With two or more, the dotted
projection follows the rate PG19 itself improved at between them instead of
borrowing the exponent fitted on the model's own held-out, as the comment there
always said it would; with no improvement it projects nothing and says so.
"PG19 is out of distribution" is now bold at the point, in the legend, and as
its own line of the caption. The published-models label and the "28x more
data" arrow moved out of the projection's way.

Measured on the full test split at step 516,696 (1.057B characters, 156
experts): 2.091 BPB, from 2.450 at 376M; between them PG19 improved at
alpha 0.153, against 0.239 on the model's own mixture.

subject: readme: the architecture drawn layer by layer, redrawn from the weights at every publish
body:
Under 'How the architecture works', two figures in the transformer paper's
own style: the layer stack - embedding, the 2 prelude layers, the recurrent
layer and its readout and halting head - and the inside of one attention
layer: 8 heads of 64, rotary on q and k, the per-application cache, concat
and the output projection.

subject: readme: the architecture back to one figure
body:
Two images took too much of the page. tools/draw_layers.py writes the one
file, and publish.sh redraws it.

subject: pool: writing and held-out cast the experts once and run only the ones they use
body:
A forward with no gradient - a character being written, a held-out chunk -
no longer casts all 32 slots' weights to the compute dtype at every row:
PagedPool.inference_weights keeps the cast copy until something changes it
(keyed on the slots' version counters, the optimiser's step count and the
card's arrangement, and dropped by every load and by any forward that
trains, so training's memory is unchanged). A forward of a few characters
runs only the experts it was routed to instead of every slot.

Also free: the routing statistics stay on the device instead of making
every row wait for the GPU, and a single query attends without a mask.

Held-out loss is identical to the bit and replies are the same text; on
this CPU at the real model's size, writing went from 1.33 to 2.09 char/s.

subject: precision: bfloat16 on CPUs that multiply it in hardware
body:
Autocast now runs on the CPU too, but only for bf16 and only where the
CPU has it natively (AVX-512 BF16 on AMD Zen 4 and later and recent
Intel, or Intel AMX): there it is the GPU path's own precision at about
twice fp32's arithmetic rate and half its memory traffic. Everywhere else
the CPU path is exactly the fp32 path it was. The expert dispatch follows
the same rule (dispatch_dtype), so on such a CPU it computes in bf16 from
the copy cast once. MINAGI_CPU_BF16=1/0 overrides the detection.

Forced on this CPU, a forward agrees with fp32 to 0.004 in the logits
with the same predictions, and a training step steps fp32 weights.

subject: model: attention in blocks where no fused kernel exists, AMD's own kernels switched on and checked first
body:
Without a flash or memory-efficient kernel, scaled_dot_product_attention takes
the math path, which keeps every score matrix for the backward pass - 26 per
chunk at this depth. On an RX 6800 XT that was most of 16 GB and an
out-of-memory error two minutes into reading.

- blocked_attention computes the same causal attention a block of queries at a
  time, scores and softmax in fp32, each block recomputed in the backward
  instead of stored: training keeps q, k and v, as a fused kernel does.
- On ROCm builds TORCH_ROCM_AOTRITON_ENABLE_EXPERIMENTAL now defaults to 1.
  PyTorch 2.9's AOTriton carries fused kernels for RDNA2 behind it: 60 ms to
  17 ms for a 4096-length attention on the 6800 XT.
- A fused kernel, causal or masked, is used only after its output and
  gradients have matched the blocked path once on this device and dtype; a
  missing or wrong one falls back to blocked. MINAGI_ATTENTION=blocked|fused
  overrides the check.
- A single query always takes plain SDPA: its score matrix is one row.

subject: model: a cached chunk's attention through the lower-right causal bias
body:
A chunk read after a cache needs causal attention aligned to the bottom-right.
It was asked for with an explicit offset mask, which only the
memory-efficient kernel takes - with a mask tensor to read, and every block
computed whether or not it lies wholly in the future. causal_lower_right says
the same thing without a mask: PyTorch gives it to the flash kernel where one
exists, or to the efficient kernel's own causal variant. Where neither does,
it materialises the same mask, so the CPU's output is bit-identical (checked
in fp32 and bf16). The probe now checks this exact call.

Used by held-out scoring and a prompt's prefill. Reading forwards its whole
window with no cache and is unaffected.

subject: pool: a written character stops the host for the device a few times a row, not a dozen
body:
A character of a reply is latency-bound: at T=1 the card's arithmetic per row
is a tenth of a millisecond, and every read-back of a device value, or tensor
built from a Python list, makes the host wait for everything queued before
it. Per row there were ten or more of them. Each one below gives the same
result:

- the slots' expert index (router rows, gates, usage count) is built once per
  arrangement of the card instead of three or four times a row, and the
  admitted mask once per admitted set instead of once per forward
- admission tests "requested at all" in one vectorised pass instead of two
  torch calls per expert in the pool, and reads last_seen back once instead
  of once per candidate slot
- a few-character no-grad forward reads its expert assignments back once,
  before the counts and capacity that only the batched path needs; capacity
  that would drop an assignment still sends it the long way
- the halting loop reads the active count once a row (everyone active passes
  no mask at all) and no longer asks whether anyone newly halted before an
  unconditional where()

Counted on a real-size model writing on the CPU: 1,156 calls that would
stop the host -> 122 per character, mostly host-side tensors now; 9,756 torch
calls -> 7,583, more on the real pool, where the removed loop scaled with
the number of experts.

subject: tools: device_check, what a machine does with the model's arithmetic
body:
For the AMD question - an RX 6800 XT reading at a fifth of a 3070 Laptop's
speed - and any card after it. On the spot, with the card to itself (it
refuses a busy one):

- which fused attention kernels exist for bf16 and fp32, for the reading
  window and for a cached chunk, and what the fused, blocked and math paths
  cost there in time and memory
- matmuls at the model's own shapes in fp32, bf16 and fp16, in TFLOP/s:
  RDNA2 has no bf16 arithmetic, and whether its bf16 is slower than fp32 is
  a number, not a guess
- one real-size learning step (random weights, temporary directory) in bf16
  and in fp32, as reading speed and peak memory; --profile breaks it down
  by op

subject: model: say once when attention falls back to blocks
body:
A fused kernel that is missing, or present and refused by the check, used to
send attention to the blocked path in silence - correct, and slower than the
run expected. Now the first time it happens for a device, dtype and case, the
log says so.

The check's 5% margin is wide on purpose and was measured: attention with
every intermediate rounded to bf16, far noisier than a flash kernel, stays
within 0.47% of the fp32 reference across seeds; the wrong kernels the test
plants miss by more than 20%.

subject: publish: ship tools/device_check.py
body:
Hardware is the reader's, not ours. The diagnostic measures what a machine
does with the model's arithmetic - which attention kernels exist and pass
the check, bf16 against fp32 at the model's own shapes, one real-size
reading step - so a report that the model is slow on some card comes with
the numbers that say why. It needs only minagi/ and train.py, both public.
The AMD port is being measured with it from the public tree.

subject: serve: a chat past the window re-reads from position 0 instead of reusing the last position
body:
Keys are cached with their rotary position applied, so a cached key says
forever where it was read. When a reply filled the window, stream() trimmed
the oldest key and placed the next character at the cache's length - block-1,
every time - so the newest keys all said block-1 and attention could no
longer tell those characters' order apart. The prompt budget counts
characters and the model reads bytes, so a long chat in Cyrillic (two bytes a
letter) filled the window before the reply began, and every character of the
reply was written that way.

Now, as model.generate does: when the window is full, the newest half of the
text is re-read from position 0 - a new text, as every training window is.
tests/test_serve_window.py follows the position each cached key was read at
(it used to end ..., 62, 63, 63) and checks that a reply crossing the window
six or seven times, in English and in Cyrillic, is character for character
what model.generate writes. trim_caches has no callers left and is gone.

The same function never entered autocast either: a chat computed in fp32
apart from the expert layer, whatever --precision said. Its forwards and the
priming forward now run in the process-wide precision, as reading and the
training samples do, and --precision no longer offers fp16, which this model
overflows (RMSNorm squares a state that reaches ~10,000).

subject: model: attention casts q and k to v's dtype, which the lower-right bias needs under autocast
body:
Under autocast q and k leave apply_rope in fp32 (the rotary tables are fp32)
while v is in the compute dtype. Plain SDPA casts all three itself, being on
autocast's list. causal_lower_right, used since "model: a cached chunk's attention through the lower-right causal bias" for a chunk after a
cache, is dispatched in Python before autocast sees the call and refuses
mixed dtypes: the first held-out check of a bf16 run on the GPU raised
"Expected query, key, and value to have the same dtype". The CPU tests ran
fp32 and could not see it.

q and k are now cast to v's dtype before attention - what autocast casts them
to, so the fused paths compute what they did. The fused-kernel check is
asked about that dtype too: it had been probing fp32 on the GPU, not the
bf16 the kernel runs in.

tests/test_cpu_bf16.py now reads a chunk after a cache and writes after it
under bf16 autocast (it fails on the previous commit with the same
ValueError), and agrees with fp32 to 0.0002 nats. Checked on the 3070: a
held-out chunk after a cache and a training step run in bf16, and the check
accepts flash for both cases.

subject: precision: a GPU without bf16 arithmetic computes in fp32 when it has the memory
body:
PyTorch runs bf16 on every GPU, converting where the hardware has none, and
on an RX 6800 XT (RDNA2, gfx1030) that cost far more than it saved: bf16
matmuls at 9 TFLOP/s against fp32's 15, and a whole run 3.7x slower - 336
characters a second read against 1,242, 15.3 written against 35.2. bf16
asked for on such a GPU (RDNA1 and 2, Vega, NVIDIA before Ampere) now
computes in fp32 when the card has 14 GB: fp32 holds twice the activations,
and the 6800 XT peaked at 13.2 GB against bf16's 7.6. A smaller card keeps
bf16, slower but fitting. Ampere and later, RDNA3 and later, and the CDNA
accelerators compute bf16 in hardware and are unchanged - the 3070 among
them. MINAGI_GPU_BF16=1 or =0 overrides the detection.

The run's first lines now say what it actually computes in, and why when that
is not what config.yaml asks for. The test checks the rule on described GPUs
(an RTX 3070, RDNA2 at 16 and 12 GB, RDNA3, MI300X, a T4), never a real one.

subject: model, train, serve: start quietly on PyTorch 2.9
body:
A run on torch 2.9.1 (the ROCm build on the RX 6800 XT) opened with about
twenty warnings, none of them news:

- the fused-attention check asks PyTorch for kernels that may not exist, and
  PyTorch explains each one it skips. They are silenced inside the check; the
  one line it prints when it falls back to blocks says what matters.
- float() on a tensor that requires grad now warns. last_steps and the
  check's error ratios are read detached - the same numbers.
- PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF is deprecated in 2.9 in favour of
  PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF, which earlier versions do not read. train.py and
  serve.py set whichever this PyTorch reads, and neither when the
  environment already sets one.

subject: tools: device_check times the rest of a learning step in bf16 and fp32
body:
On the RX 6800 XT bf16 matmuls were 1.7x slower than fp32 but a learning
step 3.6x slower, and the profiler recorded no GPU times under ROCm, so
nothing said where the rest went. A new OPS section times each other kind of
work a step does - the experts' outputs added back (index_add_, which AMD
GPUs can only do in bf16 with emulated atomics), the gather and its
backward, a transposed weight-gradient bmm, the elementwise silu * b - in
both dtypes, with the ratio.

The DEVICE section also says what a run on the machine would compute in, and
the reading step's bf16 row forces bf16 where a run would now pick fp32, so
the two rows still compare the two precisions.

subject: readme: GPU support, with measured speeds on NVIDIA, AMD and a CPU
body:
NVIDIA and AMD GPUs both run the model, and a CPU does on its own. A short
section before "Running it" gives the measured reading and writing speeds at
the repository's settings (window 4,096, chunk 2,048, 32 experts on the
card): RTX 3070 Laptop 1,528 / 27.0 char/s in bf16 (medians of eleven
rounds), RX 6800 XT 1,242 / 35.2 in fp32, Ryzen 9 9900X 186 / 29.9 in bf16.
It says what each platform needs and does: the ROCm build of PyTorch, fp32 on
RDNA2 cards with the memory for it, blocked attention where no fused kernel
exists, bf16 on CPUs that have it. "Running it" no longer asks for a CUDA GPU.

subject: readme: the RX 6800 XT in bf16 too, the row an 8 GB AMD card runs
body:
An RDNA2 card under 14 GB computes in bf16, so its row belongs in the table:
336 characters a second read, 15.3 written, 7.6 GiB at peak - it fits an
8 GB card with little to spare. The text points to it and to
MINAGI_GPU_BF16=1 for choosing it on a bigger card.

The memory column now says GiB, as the tools measured it; the 3070's
5,890 MiB is 5.8 GiB, not the 5.9 GB it said.

subject: plasticity: the rate probes upward while held-out improves, and bad readings stop counting
body:
On 590.8M one broken held-out evaluation (1.126 among 0.73s, five subjects at
once) entered the slow fit and sat there for dozens of evaluations, and thirty
back-to-back rounds with nothing read between them each counted as an
evaluation of no progress. Together they cut the rate from x0.38 to x0.21.
After that the controller's own rule kept it falling - it eased down whenever
improvement was merely slow, and a lower rate learns more slowly - to x0.052
today while held-out was still improving. Replayed through the controller,
the run's own history reproduces that curve to the third decimal; without the
two bad inputs the same history keeps the rate several times higher.

Evidence:
- a jump the next evaluation does not confirm never enters the fits
- an evaluation with fewer than MIN_STEPS optimiser steps since the last one
  is not evidence (only where steps are counted)

Movement (Plasticity.move):
- up while held-out improves: nothing below one standard error, rising to
  PROBE (0.4% per evaluation) at T_MID, up to 0.9% above it, sized by the
  weakest of the last four verdicts so one good reading is not enough
- hold when held-out is flat: a plateau no longer eases the rate down
- down, as before, only when held-out measurably gets worse - the slow fit
  and the fast one both - and only on the second such verdict running; a
  back-off then pauses rises for twelve evaluations

Closed loop, in worlds calibrated to the run now (held-out 0.642, its slope
and scatter), over the next 600M characters: where the rate is irrelevant it
climbs to about x0.08 and stops (+0.003 nats against the old controller);
where progress is the rate's area it keeps climbing (x0.094, -0.0025 nats).
The old controller sits on the floor in all of them.

The tests that encoded "a flat run eases down" now say what replaced it, and
new ones cover the unconfirmed jump, the no-reading rounds, harm having to
repeat, the pause after a back-off, and the real 590.8M episode replayed
from the log (the rate now stays at x0.383; the run went to x0.21). The
README and config.yaml describe the new rule. The floor (x0.05) is unchanged.

subject: pool: each slot multiplies exactly its own characters, not a rectangle padded to the busiest
body:
The dispatch padded every slot to the busiest slot's count before its three
batched matmuls. Within a text the busiest slot takes about twice its share,
so on the real pool 36-43% of that arithmetic - forward, recompute and
backward - was padding. Each slot now multiplies just its own run of the
sorted characters: the same experts, the same capacity drops, the same
arithmetic on every real row. The per-slot counts come from the same single
read-back that sized the rectangle, so no new waits on the device.

Measured on an RTX 3070, the layer alone (one reading row, checkpointed as in
training): bf16 67.2 -> 60.4 ms and 1.08 -> 0.44 GiB, fp32 173.5 -> 150.1 ms
and 2.17 -> 0.87 GiB. A whole reading step on real weights: 1.02x in the
3070's own setup, with peak memory 3.81 -> 3.48 GiB; losses equal to bf16
rounding. Slower per FLOP than one batched matmul, so the gain is smaller
than the padding.

unbind, not W[e]: indexing the stacked parameter per slot makes a full-size
zero gradient per slot in the backward; unbind's backward is one stack.
Single-level experts only. MINAGI_DISPATCH=padded restores the rectangle.

tests/test_dispatch_exact.py: two models from one weights directory, one per
path, with capacity dropping 125 of 1,194 assignments - the same loss, the
same gradient for every parameter, the same drops, the same held-out logits.

subject: model: blocked attention with its own backward
body:
Where no fused attention kernel exists (AMD RDNA2), attention ran in query
blocks, each checkpointed: the backward re-ran a block's whole forward and
let autograd differentiate it. _BlockedAttention does what a fused kernel
does instead. The forward keeps the output and each query's softmax
normaliser; the backward rebuilds a block's probabilities from them with one
matmul and computes dV, dP, dS, dQ and dK directly - no second output matmul,
no second pass of every elementwise op over the scores. Keys before a block's
first query are visible to all of it, so only the diagonal square is masked.

On an RTX 3070, forward + backward at the reading window: fp32 37.2 -> 21.0 ms
(1.77x), bf16 36.1 -> 21.3 ms, a cached chunk 1.62-1.66x; memory unchanged.
A whole reading step on real weights with this path forced, standing in for
the RX 6800 XT: 1.690 -> 1.392 s (1.21x) together with the exact-size expert
dispatch, losses equal to rounding. The 3070 itself uses flash and does not
take this path.

Outputs and gradients match PyTorch's reference to about 1e-6 in fp32 (2.6e-4
on the 3070 is TF32 rounding; RDNA2 has no TF32). The memory test now checks
what is kept - inputs, output, one normaliser per query - and that it grows
with the lengths where the math path grows with their product.
MINAGI_BLOCKED=recompute selects the first version, which still passes.

subject: readme: GPU numbers after the reading optimizations
body:
The RX 6800 XT in fp32, measured by the AMD tester on the new code: reading
1,242 -> 1,388 char/s, writing 34.7, peak VRAM 13.2 -> 10.1 GiB. The 3070
row is now from the same kind of early snapshot (133 experts, an isolated
ten-minute run on the new code): 2,042 / 28.4 char/s, so the rows compare.
The 3070's own run reads slower - about 1,310 char/s at 355 experts - and

subject: readme: the bf16 and CPU rows re-measured on the current code
body:
The AMD tester's 8-minute runs on the optimized code: RX 6800 XT forced to
bf16 reads 301 char/s and writes 15.1, peak VRAM 7.1 GiB; Ryzen 9 9900X
reads 186 and writes 27.6. Every row is now from the current code, so the

subject: paged: read expert files straight into their arrays, not through np.load
body:
np.load takes an .npz member through zipfile: a CRC over every byte, read
in 256 KB pieces and copied twice on the way into the array - and
_from_disk then cloned what it got. On the live run with a RAM tier of 96
the CRC alone was a tenth of the main thread's time. read_npz takes each
member's offset from the zip directory and reads its bytes into an array
of its own in one call; the tensors take that memory over instead of
copying it. A member np.savez would not have written - compressed, or a
header this does not parse - still goes through np.load, and one shorter
than its own header says is refused.

On the live run's expert files: bit-exact, 33-35 ms -> 8-10 ms per expert
(page-cached). In a ten-minute run on the 3070 at a RAM tier of 96, the
main thread's time reading experts fell from 20% to 6%; reading was
1,292 and 1,578 char/s against 1,225 and 1,340 before, within one run's
noise. Peak RSS with a 200-expert tier is 12.8 GB, where the old read
was still climbing at 14.4 GB when the OOM killer stopped it.

subject: corpora: self-knowledge in several wordings, and none of the model's own samples

subject: plasticity: a long plateau eases the rate down gently; floor x0.01; restarts keep the trend, not the level
body:
Measured first: on the live run's plateau at x0.058, the same weights read
the same 3M characters at x0.02 came out ahead at every held-out check, by
0.002 to 0.005, in all eight subjects, and 0.007 on the full evaluation.
Holding the rate on a plateau was leaving that on the table, and the floor
of x0.05 forbade it.

- FLOOR 0.05 -> 0.01.
- SETTLING: once the slow fit projects less than one scatter of improvement
  across its own window (E_STALE) for 36 evaluations in a row, every further
  such evaluation takes 0.2% off the rate and blocks rises for 36
  evaluations, so the consolidation it buys is not read as a reason to raise
  it straight back. Stale is judged by SIZE: the slow fit's t rated the
  1,342-1,560M plateau +2 to +12, because a long window makes any drift
  significant. Replayed through the real log, re-levelled at its 63
  restarts: no ease anywhere before 1,342M characters, 96 on the plateau
  after it (x0.825 in all). A run improving by 0.003 per 100M characters
  gets rises, not eases.
- RESTARTS: the first evaluation after a restore re-levels both fits, keeping
  the slope and the scatter and dropping the step. capacity_factor 0 moved
  held-out by 0.006 at a restart and the fits took it for a day of
  improvement.

From the run's own controller state on a continuing plateau, the first ease
comes after about a day: the slow fit still remembers the real improvement
after the last restart.

subject: optim: a parameter with no gradient for a step counts as zero in the signal meter
body:
The run stopped 346 minutes in with "the size of tensor a (8135169) must
match the size of tensor b (8134656)" in GradSNR.observe. The 513 values
are the halting head, Linear(512, 1): a step whose sampled depth is a single
pass forces that pass to stop and never reads the head, so its gradient is
None for that step alone. Poisson(12.84) draws zero about 3 times in a
million steps; this one landed on a step the meter reads.

The meter now counts a parameter that took no part as a zero gradient,
which is what it contributed, and starts its average again if the set ever
changes shape - it reports on a run and must not be able to stop one.
Training itself was unaffected: Adam skips a parameter with no gradient.

subject: plasticity: the rate comes down when held-out stops improving, and up only for new material
body:
Raising the rate whenever held-out improved was measured to make held-out
worse: from the same weights, x0.02 beat x0.058 on the same 3M characters
at every check and in all eight subjects, and over two days the old rule
took the rate from x0.058 to x0.067 while held-out went from its best,
0.6255, to 0.6290 - improvement, a raise, held-out worse, a recovery read as
improvement, another raise. Over a few million characters held-out answers
the rate mostly through the noise the rate leaves in the weights, so
improvement says the run is learning, not that the rate is low. And this
stream is stationary: the rate that serves held-out only comes down.

Every rule is now a comparison of levels over a fixed horizon:
- a level per check: the mean of the last 8, one through each subject
- noise: the spread of the difference between two rotation means, measured
  robustly on the run itself (0.00120 now)
- harm: worse than 16 checks ago by more than 2.5 sd -> cut
- plateau: better than 36 checks ago (~30M characters) by less than 1 sd ->
  cut; with this run's noise, improving slower than ~0.004 per 100M
- a cut is x0.9, then nothing for 36 checks, so the next decision sees it
- a confirmed jump in held-out (new material) doubles the rate; nothing
  else raises it
- a restart carries the trend, not the level: the levels before it are
  shifted onto the first level after it. A +0.006 step at a restart cuts
  100/100 runs carried as a trend and 1/100 across a restart.

Gone: both least-squares fits, the t-statistic and effect-size calibration,
the probe upward, the harm-twice rule and the stale counter - fifteen
constants become nine. A state saved by the old controller has no readings,
so train.py seeds the history from the sample log, leaving out the full
evaluation each session ends on.

Replayed through the real log from x0.38 at 600M: 15 cuts, 3 while it
improved fast, 8 on the plateau after 1,342M, and cuts at 1,704M and 1,738M
where the old rule was raising. On the run's state now it would cut within
eight checks of a restart: the latest level, 0.6295, is worse than 36
checks ago.

subject: plasticity: the 19 September controller again, at most 2% a check, blind to spikes and restart steps
body:
The rate is nudged at every evaluation by the evidence of two exponentially
weighted fits: eased unless held-out is clearly improving, raised by at most
0.5% when it is, doubled by a confirmed regime change. On top of the
original:

- no single nudge moves the rate by more than 2%; the floor is x0.01
- a reading further than 5 residual sigmas from the slow fit's line is
  held back, and counts only if the next lands nearer it than the line.
  The run's spikes are single readings 0.01-0.02 above their neighbours,
  far under the old 0.25 jump bar; replayed from 500M, 22 are dropped,
  the 1.126 broken evaluation among them
- an evaluation with fewer than 32 steps read since the last is ignored
- after a restart, the step is the median distance of the first 5
  readings from the fast fit's line, and both fits are shifted by it. A
  +0.006 step leaves the rate x1.00 of the run without it (x0.60 carried
  as a trend). Measured against the slow line instead, it would erase a
  turn for the worse made just before a restart
- a state from the plateau controller has no fits; train.py rebuilds
  them from the last 256 per-round readings in the sample log, leaving
  out each session's final full evaluation

subject: plasticity: 0.16 of the 19 September gains - a plateau takes a tenth in six hours, not half
body:
On a flat run the verdict sits near -3 - min() of three noisy readings is
pessimistic by design - and at the original gains (0.005 up, 0.025 down)
that eased the rate 1.7% a check: halved in six hours of ten-minute rounds,
x0.17 in a day. Both gains are cut by the same factor, so the shape is the
original's and only its speed changes: ~0.2% a check on a flat run, 0.4% at
most down and 0.08% up. From the current state, flat held-out takes the
rate x0.060 -> x0.054 in six hours, x0.040 in a day.

The restart tests now read the verdict, which does not depend on the gains,
and the pace itself is pinned: a flat run loses 1-15% in 36 checks, and no
36 checks of the real log take more than 14%. The 19 September gains fail
both.

subject: publish: publish_weights.sh pushes the weights to Hugging Face
