ingest: a character cut by the sample no longer makes a file binary; skips are said
body:
GitHub issue #30. looks_like_text decoded the first 4,096 bytes strictly, so
a sample ending inside a multi-byte character made a text file look binary,
and collect() dropped it without a word: 1,663 files of this corpus (954
reasoning traces, 413 conversations, ...), 9% of the reporter's.

- the sample is decoded so that only a character cut by the sample itself is
  forgiven - not one broken elsewhere, and not a file that really ends
  mid-character. Against the old rule on every file here and 3,000 random
  ones: nothing it read is refused; everything newly read is a cut case
- verdicts are cached per file against size and modification time, so a file
  rewritten under the same name is checked again; the cache is versioned, so
  verdicts made by the old rule are not trusted (one full survey, ~1.5 min)
- collect() says what it skipped, how many and why, unless quiet
- why_not_text() gives the reason; looks_like_text() is unchanged in meaning

subject: readme: two references say how they were used, nothing else
body:
The dynamic-MoE paper no longer carries a remark about how long a fix
took, and AdEMAMix is described as tried and removed, which it was on 20
September, rather than as implemented and available.

subject: pool: a newborn expert learns at the full rate and comes down to the main one
body:
training.newborn_lr (off by default). An expert born under it starts at the
base lr - its weights, its gate and its router rows - however far the main
rate has come down, and how far above the main rate it is halves, in log
terms, with every newborn_half (2,500) steps of its own training; an expert
that sits idle keeps its rate. Applied after each optimiser step by scaling
the change each such expert just made, which for AdamW is exactly a step at
its own rate. Experts the pool already had stay at the main rate.

Also: --drop-quietest N deletes the N smallest gates before reading (on 16
Oct, barring 150 of 397 left held-out where it was; 200 cost 0.01);
--max-chars stops a session after N characters; each check records every
expert's rate in expert_rates.jsonl, and the dashboard draws them as thin
lines with their average as the main line.

subject: pool: a newborn's rate converges over weeks, not days
body:
newborn_half 2,500 -> 15,000 of its own steps. Measured in the A/B: a
newborn is trained in 4% of ~50,800 steps a day, so 2,500 halved its log
distance from the main rate every 1.2 days - within 10% in a week. At
15,000 it halves every ~7.4 days: 5.5x the main rate after a week, 2.4x
after two, 1.3x after four.

subject: pool: dropping the quietest leaves experts inside their trial; the newborn rule is on
body:
A newborn's gate starts at birth_gate, so it was the first thing
--drop-quietest took. It now skips any expert inside its first
prune.survival_chars, as prune() does. And training.newborn_lr is on: the
A/B's rule-on arm kept to the run's own held-out trend (0.6110 against
0.6109 expected) while reading 16% faster with 50 fewer experts.

subject: dashboard: the thick learning-rate line is the main rate, not the experts' mean
body:
Six newborns at ~25x the main rate put the mean of 303 experts at 1.5x it,
a staircase that rose with every birth while the controller was easing the
rate for everyone else. The thick line is now the main rate the controller
sets - the one every expert converges to - joined to the log's own line;
each expert keeps a thin line, newborns are labelled where they start, and
the controller's 'raises above here' moves to the left edge, clear of them.

subject: held-out: checks read blocks spread over the whole set, at one level everywhere
body:
A check read the first 30,720 characters of each subject - the opening of
one wikipedia file, about one reasoning trace of 400 - and the evaluation a
session ends on read four times as far, so each clean stop logged a point
about 0.01 below the line: the 0.5982 "best" on the dashboard.

Measuring scores a file as independent 4,096-character blocks (the cache
and the expert vote both start over), so a block read alone scores exactly
what reading from the top scores there. Checks now read 8 blocks of each
subject spread evenly over all of it, the same ones every time; each
session starts with a 30-block evaluation and reports its checks at that
level, and writes what it measured into the banner. The plots and the
README move checks logged before the change onto the new level by the
difference the first such session measures, subject by subject, and leave
out the old closing evaluations. Other tools keep reading from the top.

subject: train: --drop-quietest asks for the number back before deleting anything
body:
A flag left in a command copied from the last restart deleted another 50
experts. Now the run asks at launch, before anything loads, and goes ahead
only when the count is typed back; anything else, or no input at all, keeps
every expert and the run carries on. A drop that finds nothing it may take
says so instead of failing on an empty list.

subject: plots: held-out history as logged, with a starred line where reading changed
body:
Checks from before blocks were spread over the whole set keep the numbers
they were logged with - nothing is moved onto the new level. The dashboard,
the whole-run graph and the scaling chart draw a dashed line with an
asterisk where the change was made, and a footnote under the figure says
what it means: those checks were measured slightly wrong, reading only the
first 30,720 characters of each subject, which put the overall loss a
little higher than it should have been and the subjects at different
values. The README says the same, with the 0.011 measured at the change.
The old closing evaluations stay out.

subject: plots: the scaling chart goes without the starred line
body:
It breaks the curve's continuity on a chart that is already full. The
dashboard and the whole-run graph keep the line and the footnote, and the
README now says it is the progress graph that marks the change.

subject: plots: earlier checks drawn at the level measured at the change, unmarked
body:
Back to moving the checks logged before held-out was spread onto the level
the first spread session start measured, subject by subject, on every graph
and in the README - so the curves run on without a step. No line, asterisk
or footnote on the graphs. The sample log keeps them as they were measured,
and the README says they read high and were adjusted.

subject: publish: held-out measured on the weights being published, for the README
body:
publish.sh now runs tools/measure_heldout.py before refreshing the README:
the evaluation a run's sessions start and end with - the same 30 blocks of
each subject, spread over all of it - on weights/ as it is, about two
minutes on the card. The README's "where the model is" table is built from
it, and says so; if it was taken on other weights, or could not be taken
because a run is training, the table carries the latest check as before.
--all reads every block of the held-out set instead.

On a tiny model it reproduces the run's own numbers to the last digit: the
start of a session read 3.7008 +/-0.0246 and the end 3.5879 +/-0.0246, and
so did the tool on the same weights.

subject: publish: the README's held-out is measured on the model as it is now
body:
publish.sh publishes the code and the run's progress; weights are
published separately and only now and then. The measurement was always
taken on weights/ as it stands, and the README, the tool and the comments
now say that, rather than calling them the weights being published.

subject: publish: refuse while a run is training, and stop if held-out can't be measured
body:
The README's held-out has to be measured on the model as it is, which needs
the GPU and weights that are not changing on disk. publish.sh now checks
for a training run first (tools/measure_heldout.py --check: a python
process running train.py from this repository, or naming its weights) and
refuses to start while one is going, saying why. It measures before
regenerating anything, and stops if the measurement fails rather than
publishing the latest check in its place. A dry run only notes the run.

subject: publish: reuse a held-out measurement of the same weights instead of retaking it
body:
A run stopped cleanly ends its session with the same evaluation publish.sh
would take, on the weights it leaves behind. tools/measure_heldout.py now
takes that from the last entry of the sample log when it is on exactly the
weights in weights/ (same step, pool and characters read), and likewise
reuses a measurement it took itself earlier - only touching the card when
neither exists. --all is satisfied only by a reading of every block. The
README now says the held-out was measured on the model as it stands.

subject: readme: enwik9 against published models, re-measured at every publish
body:
A table in Benchmarks sets this model beside the published enwik9 results
for models of about its size - Llama-3.2-1B (Tsai, Jan 2026) and Chinchilla
1B (Delétang et al., Sep 2023) - each linked to its paper, best first, the
best score in bold, with a note on how this model was scored: the way
Chinchilla 1B was, enwik9 in pieces of 2,048 bytes with no memory between
them, on a 50 MB slice of enwik9 it never trained on.

tools/measure_enwik9.py takes that measurement on weights/ as it is and
reuses it while the weights are unchanged; publish.sh runs it after
held-out and stops if it fails, and tools/refresh_readme.py rebuilds the
table from it. The first table is from this afternoon's measurement on the
stopped run: 1.32 bits per byte.

subject: readme: say how the enwik9 scores are calculated, with each paper's own figure
body:
The papers print a compression rate, not bits per byte, so the scores could
not be found by looking for them. The notes under the table now say what
bits per byte is, that it is the published rate times 8, and give for each
row the table, row and column of the figure as printed with the
arithmetic - 0.085 x 8 = 0.68, 11.3% x 8 = 0.90 - and how mini-AGI's own
score is measured. They are generated with the table, so every publish
keeps them.

subject: readme: GPT-2 XL in the enwik9 table, measured here the way mini-AGI is
body:
No paper scores GPT-2 XL on enwik9, so tools/measure_enwik9_gpt2.py
measures it on the pieces tools/measure_enwik9.py reads: 2,000 pieces of
2,048 bytes from the held-out slice, each cut back to whole UTF-8
characters, started from <|endoftext|>, at full precision. GPT-2 XL
(1.56B) reads 1.073 +/- 0.005 bits per byte; mini-AGI on the same pieces,
at 345 experts, 1.328 +/- 0.006. The row says it was measured for the
page, and a note says how.

subject: readme: the enwik9 table dates each model by when it came out
body:
Where a score was measured says nothing about how far behind or ahead a
model is; when the model came out does. The table gains a published
column - Llama-3.2-1B Sep 2024, Chinchilla 1B Mar 2022 (its paper; the
weights were never released), GPT-2 XL Feb 2019 (its paper; the weights
followed in Nov 2019), mini-AGI the day its weights were measured - and
the rows measured here no longer carry a date of their own.
tools/measure_enwik9_gpt2.py names whichever GPT-2 it measured.

subject: readme: the enwik9 rows measured here just say "measured"
readme: the enwik9 table says what each model was trained on and what it cost
body:
Two columns: how much text each model learned from, and roughly what that
training cost when it came out - Llama-3.2-1B from its model card (9T
tokens, 370k H100-hours at ~$2.5), GPT-2 XL from WebText and Karpathy's
~$43k, mini-AGI from what it has read and its hours on one RTX 3070 Laptop
at ~$0.10, recomputed at every publish; Chinchilla 1B's were never
published, and the table says so. The cheapest training is in bold beside
the best score, the score column carries a ↓, and the notes are folded
into a <details> block under the table.

subject: readme: GPT-2 Large in the enwik9 table, and every cost estimated
body:
GPT-2 Large, measured on the same 2,000 pieces: 1.119 +/- 0.005 bits per
byte. Where nobody published what training cost, the table now gives a
best-effort estimate marked "(est.)", priced when the model came out:
Chinchilla 1B from its own paper's compute-optimal recipe for 1B
parameters (20.2B tokens, 1.21e20 FLOPs, Table 3) on TPU v4 at $3.22 a
chip-hour, ~$1k; GPT-2 Large as Karpathy's GPT-2 XL figure scaled by
parameter count, ~$21k. mini-AGI's hours are priced at the cheapest RTX
3070 rental tracked in 2026, $0.04 an hour, not $0.10: ~$24.

subject: readme: GPT-2 Medium in the enwik9 table; Chinchilla 1B's cost as a range
body:
GPT-2 Medium, measured on the same 2,000 pieces: 1.174 +/- 0.005 bits per
byte, its cost Karpathy's GPT-2 XL figure scaled by parameter count,
~$10k. Chinchilla 1B's single ~$1k assumed it read the compute-optimal
20B tokens, which nobody has published; it is now the range between that
and as much as Chinchilla 70B read, 1.4T tokens: ~$1k-$68k on TPU v4 at
2022 prices. Pythia-1B's 4,830 A100-hours for 300B tokens (Biderman et
al., Table 5) shows the low end is what 20B tokens costs.

subject: readme: GPT-2 Small in the enwik9 table; Chinchilla 1B at ~$68k; "date" column
body:
GPT-2 Small, measured on the same 2,000 pieces: 1.328 +/- 0.006 bits per
byte - level with mini-AGI's 1.328 +/- 0.006 at step 1,132,995 - its
cost Karpathy's GPT-2 XL figure scaled by parameter count, ~$3k.
Chinchilla 1B's cost is now one estimate, ~$68k: as much text as
Chinchilla 70B read, 1.4T tokens, on TPU v4 at 2022 prices, which
Pythia-1B's 4,830 A100-hours per 300B tokens puts at ~22,500 hours; the
notes say it may have read less. The "published" column is "date", and
the sentence above the table says the models go up to 1.6B parameters
rather than "about this size", as GPT-2 Small and Medium are smaller.
The GPT-2 note no longer says no paper scores them on enwik9 - only that
the GPT-2 paper reports enwik8.

subject: readme: mini-AGI's hours at Vast.ai's $0.081, the price the linked page shows
body:
The $0.04 an hour was Salad Cloud's, in its lowest priority tier, which any
better-paying job takes the card from - while the note linked Vast.ai's
page, whose price is $0.081. The hours are now priced at that: the cheapest
RTX 3070 rental no other job can interrupt, on computeprices.com on 17 Oct
2026. 610 hours come to ~$49, still the cheapest in the table; the note
says what Salad Cloud charges and why it is not the one used.

subject: scaling: enwik9 on the chart, carried on to one corpus pass
body:
mini-AGI's enwik9 score is drawn as a green square, 1.328 BPB at 2.32B
characters, with a dotted line on to one pass of the corpus, as PG19 has.
With one square there is no enwik9 rate to fit, so the line borrows the
Wikipedia held-out's rate over the last billion characters read, 0.080,
and the legend, caption and README say it is assumed; with two squares
it becomes enwik9's own rate, as PG19's did. The whole run's rate is not
used: it carries the steep early part forward, and the curve has been
flattening.

tools/measure_enwik9.py now keeps every measurement in
runs/scaling/enwik9_history.jsonl, and measures older weights into the
history only (--weights), so a backup can add an earlier point without
touching the README's table. The chart reads the corpus pass from the log
(8.04B, not the 7.87B it was drawn with), and the "13x more data" arrow
moves to the bottom to make room. The README's scaling paragraph is now a
function of its own and says what the circles, diamonds and squares are.

subject: scaling: Llama-3.2-1B on the chart at its 36 TB, the side panel narrowed
body:
A published enwik9 score now goes on the scaling chart where its model's
training data is known, at that much data: Llama-3.2-1B, 0.68 bits per
byte after 9T tokens, about 36 TB - 16,000 times what mini-AGI has read.
The others in the enwik9 table are left off, because how much they read
was never published. The table keeps that as `seen`, so a model added to
it with known data is drawn without touching the chart.

The axis runs out past it, and the "which domains still have slope" panel
gives up width so the main one keeps most of its scale. The legend moves
into the empty far right, MegaByte's and MambaByte's labels sit beside
their points, the enwik9 label hangs on a leader in the gap above the
held-out curve, and the caption says which markers are PG19 and which are
enwik9. The README's scaling paragraph says which model the hollow circle
is and why the rest are not there.

subject: paging: Adam's moments stay bf16 in RAM, and cross the bus at that width
body:
An expert's moments are bf16 on disk already, but every load widened them
to fp32 in RAM, so an entry took 38 MB instead of 25 and sent twice the
moment bytes to the card. They now stay bf16 in RAM, go to the card at
that width and are widened there (_own_moments), and come back narrowed
on the card. Parking an expert also copied its weights twice - the move
off the card and a clone of it; now once.

Timed on the live weights (350 experts, 2,329M characters), 9 minutes
each from the same copy: with the same RAM as 192 fp32 entries (288 bf16
ones), the hit rate went 0.72 -> 0.87 and reading 1,468 -> 1,901 char/s
(+29%) at the 9-minute mark, 1,547 -> 1,716 at 4. Paging fell from 28.5%
of a reading step's main thread to 14.6%. Moments that were fp32 in RAM
are now rounded to bf16 at each parking rather than only at each write
to disk - the same rounding, more often; measured at ~1e-3 relative.

subject: paging: evicted experts are written on a thread of their own
body:
An expert leaves the RAM tier in the middle of a forward, while the card
waits for the experts it admitted, and its file was written right there.
It now goes to a writer thread; until the write lands it stays in
`pending`, and a fetch serves it from there, so nothing reads a file
older than the expert and one expert's writes land in the order they
were made. flush() and pruning wait for the writer first, a failed
write is raised by the next drain, and a run that ends without a flush
still lands what it evicted (atexit).

Measured on the live weights with bf16 moments and 288 RAM entries:
writing left the reading step's main thread entirely (3.4% -> 0%), and
reading speed was 1,900 char/s against 1,901 without it - inside a
9-minute run's noise. It is kept for the pool outgrowing the RAM tier:
at a hit rate of 0.72 the writes were 13.5% of a reading step.
tests/test_write_behind.py holds the ordering, the pending reads, flush,
pruning and errors.

subject: read: a weight for each subject's share of the reading (default unchanged)
body:
Reading takes the subjects in turn, a visit each, so each gets the same
share whatever its size. On the live corpus that is 1/8 of all reading
for every subject - and the 7.1 MB self-knowledge folder has been read
about 40 times over (290M characters of 2,329M), while the 2,468 MB
reasoning folder is a tenth read.

--lane-weights subject=weight,... (or data.lane_weights in config.yaml)
takes a subject down from that share: at 0.25 it is read every fourth
round, first on round one. Nothing changes unless it is set. Checked end
to end on a tiny model: with b at 0.5, subjects a, b, c got 75, 38 and
75 visits.

subject: tests: the npz reader expects the RAM tier's moments as bf16
body:
"paging: Adam's moments stay bf16 in RAM, and cross the bus at that width" keeps an expert's Adam moments in RAM at the bf16 they are stored
as; this check still compared them with the fp32 they used to be widened
to. It now compares them with the stored bf16.

subject: read: each subject's share of the reading follows where it still pays
body:
Reading took the subjects in strict turn, so each got an eighth of it
whatever it still had to teach: the 7 MB self-knowledge folder was read
about 41 times over, and arithmetic, flat on held-out for a billion
characters, got as much as chat. Now the next visit goes where the next
character is expected to lower held-out most (minagi/lanes.py), by
default and with no flag.

Each subject's held-out is fitted as a power law in what its lane has
read, over the last ~16% of the reading in log characters; a lane is
worth sum(|alpha| * L) / D over the subjects it feeds (chat feeds chat
and chat_hermes), so a lane read more is worth less and the shares
settle where the worths meet. A subject whose held-out rises claims as
much as one falling. A lane nothing measures is valued as the typical
one, discounted exp(-k/15.4) for each reading past the first. No share
below a quarter of an even one or above three times one; shares move at
most 5% a check; visits by smooth weighted round-robin. The state is
saved with the checkpoint, and a run without one is seeded from the
sample log, whose parser moves into minagi/heldout.py so the trainer can
read it without matplotlib (tools/plot_progress.parse calls it; same
3,180 rows on this run's log).

On this run's log the targets come out as chat 28.9%, wikipedia 16.7%,
reasoning 12.9%, code 12.0%, stories 11.7%, chess 11.5%, and
arithmetic and self-knowledge at the 3.1% floor - reached over about
30 checks. --lane-schedule equal restores the rotation; --lane-weights
now pins shares rather than skipping rounds. Checked end to end on a
tiny model: observed, saved, restored, and moved at checks.

subject: config: the RAM tier holds 288 experts
body:
With Adam's moments bf16 in RAM an expert is about 25 MB there, so 288
fit in about 7 GB. The live run holds 10.9 GB resident with 12 GB still
free. More of the pool in RAM is fewer reads from disk per chunk.

subject: held-out: whole blocks only, and the history moved onto that level
body:
A file seldom ends on a block boundary, and what was left after its last
whole block counted as a block of its own. A chunk weighs the same in a
subject's mean whatever its length, so three short chunks (73, 68 and 32
characters) were 21% of chat_hermes's check. It read ~1.0 against 0.74 for
the subject, with a noise of 0.025 a check against 0.002 before checks were
spread. Stories, reasoning, chess and code also had short blocks among their
30-block picks.

Every block is now whole (`per` full chunks), unless a subject has none. The
first session after this reads the old blocks once more and writes a PARTS
line in its banner. The plots, the README and the lane schedule's seed move
everything before it by that difference, subject by subject. The lane fits
are seeded again, and the notifier's best moves with them. Neither
measure_heldout nor the README reuses a measurement from before.
measure_enwik9 keeps the old block list, because the published GPT-2 rows
were scored on it and none of its picks is a part-piece.

subject: readme: the in-flight corrections move into a section of their own
body:
The Benchmarks text now says only how held-out is read today. A
collapsible "Training in-flight corrections" section holds both fixes:
the rule they share (measured both ways on the same weights, earlier
checks moved subject by subject, raw log kept), and each fix's
per-subject offsets as the log's banners recorded them. It also covers
what the second fix leaves out, and why most of its movement is which
blocks get picked rather than the short ones. The best-round and graph
captions point to the section. The old wording, "a check from before
checks were spread", stopped being true at the second fix.

subject: scaling: enwik9's own rate only from measurements far enough apart; PG19 all purple
body:
Every publish adds its enwik9 measurement to the history, and the chart
draws each one. The dotted line was fitted through them from the second
measurement on, however close the two were. The first two are 2.320B and
2.329B characters read, 0.4% apart, and their 0.6% difference put alpha
at 1.5 and the line at 0.20 BPB one corpus pass on, which is noise. A
set's own rate is now used only once its last measurement has read a
quarter more than its first. Until then the line borrows the Wikipedia
held-out's recent rate, as it did with one measurement (now 0.087,
reaching 1.18). The legend, caption and README say it is assumed and how
far apart the measurements are. PG19's rate follows the same rule; its
two measurements are 2.7x apart and keep their 0.153.

Everything PG19 is purple: this model's diamonds and the published
byte-level models, drawn hollow like the published enwik9 score, with
their names and legend entry purple too. Filled marks are this model,
hollow ones published models, and the colour is the test set. The
caption and the README say so.

subject: chat: learns at the run's own rate, and its saves keep the run's state
body:
Talking to the model continues the stream training reads, so it now
continues training's rate as well. That rate is the run's base times the
plasticity controller's factor, restored from the weights, with newborn
experts at their own multiple of it, as in training. The learner used a
flat 3e-4, about 35x the rate the run had come down to (x0.028).
--learn-lr now sets the base the controller scales; it defaults to the
run's own base, which train.py now writes into the manifest as "lr".

A chat save rebuilt the manifest with only read_chars and context_now.
That dropped the controller's state, the reading shares and the
information count, so the next training session restarted at the full
rate. A save now carries through everything the manifest held that the
store does not write itself. It also carries the stream on: step,
read_chars, read_nats and the controller's step count advance by what
was learned. Changed weights therefore no longer pass as the ones a
held-out or enwik9 measurement was taken on.

LiveLearner.for_run sets a learner up as training is, and step_on
learns from one piece alone, for text read in pieces.

subject: enwik9: a measurement that learns as it reads, on a copy of the weights
body:
tools/measure_enwik9_adapt.py reads tools/measure_enwik9.py's 2,000
pieces twice on the same weights. First frozen, then as one stream the
model learns from, the way chat now does: the run's base rate times its
controller's factor, Adam's moments as the run left them, one step per
piece. Each piece is scored before the model learns from it, so no byte
is scored by weights that have already seen it - dynamic evaluation, the
way online compressors score enwik9. Each piece is still predicted
alone, so learning is the only difference, and the paired difference is
known to +/-0.0015.

The weights are a full copy that is deleted at the end, also on failure
or SIGTERM. weights/ is checked unchanged file by file, and a scratch
directory the tool did not make is never deleted.

First result, step 1,200,798 (2,458M characters), learning at
3e-4 x0.0279: frozen 1.3091, adapting 1.2515 bits/byte, a gain of
0.058 +/-0.0015. By quarter the gain was +0.042, +0.060, +0.061 and
+0.068, still growing at the end, in 38 minutes.

subject: readme: mini-AGI with dynamic evaluation in the enwik9 table; the frozen row says so
body:
The enwik9 table gets a row for mini-AGI learning while it reads: 1.25
bits/byte against 1.31 frozen on the same weights, from
tools/measure_enwik9_adapt.py. The row is marked, and a note straight
under the table says what the mark means:
- each piece is scored before it is learned from;
- for a continual learning model this is simply how it runs, the
  learning it does in training and in every conversation, at its own
  rate;
- the frozen models would need a separate fine-tuning loop added to be
  scored this way (Krause et al., 2017), so the row is closer to online
  compressors than to the frozen rows.
The folded notes give the method and the gain by quarter.

The other row now reads "mini-AGI (frozen)", always. Frozen is not how
this model runs, and its note says the weights learn nothing from the
pieces while they are scored.

The adaptation tool keeps its frozen pass as tools/measure_enwik9.py's
measurement of the same weights, on the standard pieces and when the
weights are weights/. The two mini-AGI rows then describe one set of
weights. This run's frozen pass (step 1,200,798, 1.3091) is recorded
that way.

subject: readme: the dynamic-evaluation note says the learned weights are thrown away
body:
The note under the enwik9 table now says it in the open: the learning is
done on a copy of the weights, thrown away after the measurement. So
nothing learned from enwik9 reaches the weights the run goes on training,
or any later score. The folded notes no longer repeat it.

subject: publish: measures enwik9 learning as it reads too, and never twice
body:
publish.sh now runs tools/measure_enwik9_adapt.py before the frozen
enwik9 measurement. It takes about 45 minutes, on a copy of the weights
that is thrown away. Its frozen pass is kept as the frozen row's
measurement of the same weights, so the frozen step after it finds that
measurement and does not measure again, and the README's two mini-AGI
rows always describe one set of weights. A failure warns and leaves the
dynamic row at its older, dated measurement; it does not stop the
publish.

Like the other measurements, it does not measure the same weights twice
(--force does). A skipped run still makes sure its frozen pass is kept as
the enwik9 measurement.

subject: scaling: an enwik9 square is drawn only once it stands clear of the last
body:
Measurements a few days apart sit a hair apart on an axis that runs out
to terabytes. Drawn as they came, the enwik9 squares and their values
piled into one smudge: 1.328, 1.320 and 1.314 on top of one another.
The first square is now always drawn, and each later one only once it
stands 14 points clear of the last one drawn. On today's layout that is
about 1.32x the characters. Only the first keeps a small value beside
it, and the last drawn has the headline.

Every measurement still counts in the rate the dotted line is carried on
at. The line and its value at one corpus pass now start from the last
square drawn. The chart writes trend.json after drawing, so the README
describes what the chart shows: the drawn square, then how many were
measured since and the latest of them. Today that is 1.328 after 2.32B
characters, with 3 measured since and the latest 1.309 after 2.46B.

subject: chat: router rows learn at the pool's rate, as in training
body:
Training puts the router rows of every routing site and the depth
embedding in the pool's optimiser group. So a newborn expert's gate,
router rows and weights all move at its own rate, the main rate
stretched by its multiple. The live learner split the groups by
parameter name instead, and the router rows ("recur.*.mlp.router.weight")
went to the trunk group at a tenth of that rate, in chat and in the
enwik9 dynamic-evaluation run.

The split now lives in minagi/pool.py (split_trunk_pool). train.py's
_split_trunk_pool and the live learner both use it, so a stream that
carries training on gives every parameter the rate training gives it.
The 19 Oct dynamic-evaluation figure (1.25) was measured with the router
rows at that tenth. The next publish measures newer weights, and the
figure it records will have them right.

subject: dashboard: the domain panel's axis has numbers
body:
The panel draws held-out per subject on a log axis. That axis labelled
only powers of ten, and every subject sits between 0.37 and 0.95, so no
tick carried a number. The ticks between powers of ten (0.4, 0.5 ...
0.9) are now labelled, as in the "Is it learning" panel beside it.

subject: enwik9: --natural reads whole pages the way training reads a file
body:
The pieces mode cuts 2,048-byte pieces out of their pages and reads each
one cold. --natural reads whole enwik9 pages instead, framed as
training's Wikipedia files are: one page a file, from <page> to </page>.
Each page is read from its top the way training's reader goes through a
file - a step every training.chunk characters, on the window of the last
context_now characters - so a window never holds two pages. Pages are
spread evenly over the slice until they hold the bytes the pieces do:
1,429 pages, 3.97M characters, 2,862 steps.

Every chunk is scored three ways on the same text, weighted by its
characters:
- alone and frozen, as the pieces are;
- in its window, frozen;
- in its window while learning, before the model learns from it.
The first two differ by what the context gives, the last two by what
learning does, and both differences carry standard errors taken page by
page.

It runs on a thrown-away copy of the weights, like the pieces mode.
Results go to runs/enwik9_natural.jsonl, which nothing else reads: the
README and the pieces-mode row are untouched until it has been looked
at.

subject: readme: the dynamic-evaluation row reads whole pages; a "read as" column
body:
The enwik9 table's dynamic-evaluation row is now mini-AGI learning while
it reads the way it reads anything: whole pages in its 4,096-byte window
sliding by 2,048 (tools/measure_enwik9_adapt.py --natural), 1.19 bits
per byte. The note under the table splits the drop from the frozen row:
- read frozen in the same windows, these pages score 1.21, so
  learning's own share is 0.024;
- most of the rest is the window, which any model reading whole pages
  has (0.058);
- the rest is the pages themselves, which read cold score 1.27 against
  the pieces' 1.31.
The notes give the clean comparison on the frozen row's own pieces,
where learning is the only difference and takes 0.059 off.

A "read as" column says what each row saw of the text at a time: 2,048
tokens, about 8 KB, for Llama-3.2-1B; 2,048 bytes alone for Chinchilla
1B, GPT-2 and mini-AGI frozen; whole pages and learning for the new row.
The notes now say what the papers did: Chinchilla over all of enwik9,
mapped to ASCII, with only the top 100 token probabilities; Tsai never
saying how the text was cut. They also say what each model trained on:
GPT-2 never on Wikipedia, Chinchilla and Llama probably on these pages,
unchecked.

publish.sh runs the whole-pages measurement too, before the pieces one.
tools/measure_enwik9_gpt2.py --natural scores GPT-2 on the same whole
pages in its own window, and alone in pieces, for a look before anything
of it goes in the table.

subject: readme: the enwik9 table says which models read tokens and which bytes
body:
A "reads" column says what each row reads the text as: tokens for
Llama-3.2-1B, Chinchilla 1B and GPT-2, bytes for mini-AGI. The notes
give each tokenizer's vocabulary and why the scores still compare: bits
per byte is the bits a model needs for the text over its length in
bytes, so a token's several bytes are paid for together. What differs is
how much text a window of the same length holds - on these pages a
GPT-2 token is about 3.1 bytes - and that is what the "read as" column
is for.

subject: readme: back to the 2,048-byte pieces only, the frozen row and learning
body:
Reverts "readme: the enwik9 table says which models read tokens and which bytes", "readme: the dynamic-evaluation row reads whole pages; a "read as" column" and "enwik9: --natural reads whole pages the way training reads a file". The whole-pages measurement
(--natural, in tools/measure_enwik9_adapt.py and
tools/measure_enwik9_gpt2.py), its row and its split of context from
learning, the "read as" and "reads" columns, the longer notes, and the
whole-pages step in publish.sh are taken out. The enwik9 table is as it
was: mini-AGI frozen on the 2,000 pieces of 2,048 bytes, 1.31, and the
same pieces with learning while it reads, 1.25, under the short note.
Both are now from step 1,221,768, the latter with the router rows at the
pool's rate.

The router fix ("chat: router rows learn at the pool's rate, as in training") and the dashboard fix ("dashboard: the domain panel's axis has numbers") stay.

subject: tests: the plot hook's test draws in a folder of its own
body:
test_plot_hook gave the hook a fake 30-round log, but the hook always
drew to runs/training_progress.png and runs/dashboard.png, so every test
run drew the fake run over the real run's graphs. A running trainer
redraws them each round, which hid it. With training stopped, a publish
after the tests would have copied the fake graph into the README. To
check a missing plotter, the test also renamed the real
tools/plot_progress.py for a moment; a running trainer redrawing in that
moment would have switched its graphs off for the rest of the session.

The hook now takes an output folder and a tools folder (_PLOTS "out"
and "tools"), runs/ and the repository's tools/ unless a test says
otherwise. The test uses a temporary folder for both and checks the
graph lands there. Training draws exactly where it did.

subject: train: the window, visit and growth-gap rules become functions their tests test
body:
Four tests checked copies of rules written into the test files rather
than the code, so they would have passed whatever train.py did:
test_context_growth, test_visit_length, test_growth_gap, and the main
checks of test_router_width. One already had: test_visit_length held a
visit to whole windows and a 16-chunk floor, a rule cmd_read dropped
long ago - a visit is the configured passage in chunks, at least one
window.

The rules leave cmd_read unchanged, as module-level functions it calls:
- _window_bounds: where a session's window starts, under the rotary
  tables and --context;
- _window_gain: whether the model still gains deep in its window;
- _visit_chunks: how long a subject is read before the next;
- _may_grow: whether held-out lets the pool grow.

The tests now call them and check that cmd_read does too.
test_router_width builds a real model whose manifest carries a stale
pool_max, larger than the pool and smaller, and loads it with
build_paged. Training does exactly what it did.

subject: readme: a best-effort enwik9 row, the model read as it reads anything
body:
The enwik9 table keeps mini-AGI frozen and with dynamic evaluation, both
on the 2,000 pieces of 2,048 bytes. It gains a third row, "mini-AGI
(best effort)**": whole pages in the model's native 4,096-byte window,
sliding 2,048 characters at a time, learning as it goes - the model
exactly as it is used in training and in conversation, on a copy of the
weights thrown away afterwards. The note under the table calls it the
model's most natural score, and says it sees more of each page at once
than the 2,048-byte pieces the other mini-AGI rows, GPT-2 and Chinchilla
1B are scored on, so it is not on the same footing as them. The folded
notes say how the pages were read and what they score frozen.

The whole-pages mode of tools/measure_enwik9_adapt.py (--natural) is
back, as it was in "enwik9: --natural reads whole pages the way training reads a file", and publish.sh measures all three rows. The
best effort shown now is from step 1,221,768, 1.19; the other two from
step 1,258,101.

subject: benchmarks: the long measurements move to measure_benchmarks.sh, with PG19's best effort
body:
Measuring enwik9 three ways had made publish.sh a two-hour job.
measure_benchmarks.sh now runs every long measurement, about four hours
of the card, then redraws the scaling chart and refreshes the README:
- enwik9 frozen and with dynamic evaluation, on the 2,048-byte pieces;
- enwik9's best effort, whole pages in the native window;
- PG19 frozen over the whole test split;
- PG19's best effort: whole books in the native window, learning as it
  reads, on a copy thrown away afterwards.
It refuses while a run is training, skips weights already measured, and
reports a failed step without stopping the rest. publish.sh keeps its
held-out measurement, uses what the script last measured, and runs no
enwik9 or PG19 measurement.

The whole-pages mode reads a file with no <page> in it as one document,
so it measures PG19's books as it measures enwik9's pages: 10 whole books
spread over the split, the same 4.1 MB budget. tools/eval_pg19.py no
longer scores the whole split twice on the same weights. The README's
scaling section states PG19's best effort beside its frozen score once
it has been measured.

The enwik9 row "mini-AGI (with dynamic evaluation)*" is now
"mini-AGI (dynamic evaluation)*".

subject: readme: a PG19 table against published models, with what each one's training cost
body:
The Benchmarks section gains "PG19 against published models", between the
enwik9 table and the scaling chart. It lists the four byte-level models the
chart draws, each with the score its paper prints in its Table 2:
MambaByte-353M 0.930, MegaByte-758M+262M 1.000, Transformer-320M 1.057 and
PerceiverAR-248M 1.104. Beside them is mini-AGI read frozen over the whole
test split, plus its best effort once ./measure_benchmarks.sh has measured
one. A test holds the table's published scores to the chart's.

Each mini-AGI row is of the weights it was measured on, with their date,
their reading, their size worked out from the pool they had (size_at), and
their cost at the hours the run had trained when it first reached that
step (ran_until). The frozen row shows the 3 Oct 2026 measurement:
0.50B, 1.1 GB, ~$25, 2.091.

Training cost is a column, as in the enwik9 table. Neither paper
publishes its cost or its hardware, so the published costs are marked
estimates. Each is the 6ND compute on A100s at 40% utilisation, as the
enwik9 notes assume for Chinchilla. Compute per byte is MegaByte's 357M
parameters a byte, which Yu et al.'s three share and Wang et al. match.
The price is Lambda's on-demand A100 when the paper came out: $1.10 on
12 May 2023 and $1.29 on 3 Jan 2024, linked to the Internet Archive's
copies. That gives about $420 for each of Yu et al.'s models and $180 for
MambaByte-353M.

Under the table, one sentence says the published models were trained on
30 to 80 GB of PG19's own books and mini-AGI on none. The folded notes:

- explain each column;
- leave out MambaByte-972M, whose bits per byte appear only in a table
  of generation speeds;
- make no sliding-window claim, since Yu et al. score PerceiverAR with
  one.

The scaling paragraph's PG19 best-effort sentence moves into the table,
and the paragraph now points to the table. The replication notes no
longer quote 2.4496, a PG19 score from 376M characters, as "the
benchmark further down this page".

subject: readme: MambaByte by its best model, the 972M at 0.883
body:
The PG19 table and the scaling chart show MambaByte by its best model
only: MambaByte-972M, 0.883 bits per byte after 75B bytes at a context of
8,192, from Wang et al.'s Table 5 in the COLM 2024 paper. It replaces the
compute-matched 353M (0.930 after 30B, their Table 2), which the notes
still quote.

The notes add that the 972M scores 0.863 with a sliding window, and that
the table shows 0.883. They also say it went on to 150B bytes (Appendix C:
380,000 steps of 48 x 8,192), where the paper reports only word-level
perplexity.

Its cost is estimated the same way as the others: all 972M parameters on
every byte over 75B bytes is 4.4x10^20 FLOPs, about 970 A100-hours at
Lambda's $1.29, so about $1.3k. The table rounds that to ~$1k.

The chart moves the point to (75B, 0.883) and drops its "closest match:
same FLOPs/byte" label, which held only for the 353M. Its data-gap arrow
now runs to MambaByte's point, reading 29x. eval_pg19.py's printed
comparison changes to match.

subject: readme: PG19 training costs at AWS's A100 price, two significant figures
body:
The published PG19 models' costs were priced at Lambda's on-demand A100,
the cheapest uninterruptible rental of the time, which made them look
cheap beside the enwik9 table's list-price estimates. The estimate is
meant to be what the authors paid, which neither paper states. It now
uses what AWS charged on demand for an A100 when the papers came out:
$32.77 an hour for a p4d.24xlarge with eight, $4.10 each. The price was
the same on its pricing page in May 2023, December 2023 and April 2024,
and all three Internet Archive captures are linked. The compute estimate
is unchanged: 6ND on A100s at 40% utilisation, about 380 A100-hours for
Yu et al.'s three models and 970 for MambaByte-972M.

The rows become ~$1.6k (est.) for MegaByte-758M+262M, Transformer-320M
and PerceiverAR-248M, and ~$4k (est.) for MambaByte-972M. The notes say
these are best-effort estimates of what the authors paid. They add that
Lambda rented an A100 for $1.10 in May 2023, about a quarter as much, so
the real cost may have been lower. They also say mini-AGI's $0.081 is
the cheapest rental of its card, which no big cloud offers.

dollars() now gives the two significant figures its docstring promised.
Above $1k it had rounded to whole thousands, which would have shown
$1,561 as ~$2k. Every enwik9 row it prices stays as it was.

subject: benchmarks: the best efforts read everything they are scored on
body:
The best-effort measurements (tools/measure_enwik9_adapt.py --natural)
read an even spread of pages sized to the frozen pieces' 4 MB: 1,429 of
the enwik9 slice's 17,426 pages, and 10 of PG19's 100 test books. A best
effort should let the model try its best, so they now read everything by
default: every page of the 50 MB slice, and every book of the split. They
read it in order, as one stream the model goes on learning from.

The tactic is unchanged and is what makes this fair. Each 2,048-byte
chunk is scored with the weights as they stand and only then learned
from, so no byte is scored by weights that have seen it. What the model
learns carries into every page and book after it, so it can improve
while it sits the test, as a person might.

--budget still reads an even spread of that many bytes, for a quicker
look. Measurements of the spread are not reused for a whole read, so the
next ./measure_benchmarks.sh measures both best efforts again.

The README says which a measurement was. Over everything, enwik9's note
says every page of the slice, in order, with what it learns carried into
the rest. PG19's note says all 100 books, the frozen row's books, one
after another. A spread keeps its sample wording.

measure_benchmarks.sh's header now gives the times last night's sweep
measured, scaled to the whole sets: about 13 hours for enwik9's best
effort and 10 for PG19's. That makes about a day for everything, or 23
hours when only the best efforts need measuring.

subject: benchmarks: enwik9 on its 2,000 pieces only; the best effort is PG19's
body:
enwik9 is scored on the 2,000 pieces of 2,048 bytes and nothing else.
That is the text the published method reads, and the text the frozen,
dynamic-evaluation and GPT-2 rows read. The best-effort row read whole
pages of the slice instead, so it is gone, along with its ** note,
enwik9_natural() and the step in measure_benchmarks.sh, which had become
a 13-hour read of all 17,426 pages.

Nothing better is lost. Each piece is shorter than the model's window, so
reading it whole, scoring it, then learning from it is the most the model
can do with it. That is the dynamic-evaluation row, and its note now says
so: what the model learns from each piece carries into every piece after
it.

PG19 keeps its best effort over all 100 books. A sweep is now about half
a day: about 35 minutes for enwik9's pieces, an hour for PG19 frozen, and
ten hours for PG19's best effort.

The script was replaced as a new file rather than edited in place. A
sweep running from the old one reads it as it goes, and keeps reading the
old one unharmed.

subject: Revert "benchmarks: enwik9 on its 2,000 pieces only; the best effort is PG19's"
body:
This reverts commit "benchmarks: enwik9 on its 2,000 pieces only; the best effort is PG19's". the author had reverted that change on purpose:
the enwik9 best effort stays as it was, every page of the held-out slice
read in the model's native window, learning as it goes. Claude re-applied
the change by mistake. Every file it touched is back as it was in
"benchmarks: the best efforts read everything they are scored on".

subject: publish: measure_benchmarks.sh ships, with every script it runs and imports
body:
The README's enwik9 and PG19 tables are measurements, and anyone with the
weights should be able to repeat them. publish.sh now publishes
measure_benchmarks.sh and the six tools it runs: measure_heldout.py (to
refuse while a run trains), measure_enwik9.py, measure_enwik9_adapt.py,
eval_pg19.py, plot_scaling.py and refresh_readme.py. Everything those
import was published already: minagi/, train.py and
tools/plot_progress.py.

tests/test_publish_benchmarks.py keeps that true as the tools change. It
follows every script the benchmark script runs through every import in
this repo, and checks each file is in publish.sh's published set, tracked
and not withheld. It reads train.py as published, with the notifier's
block stripped by publish.sh's own pattern. The only import of the one
withheld module, minagi/notify.py, is in that block.

test_eval_pg19 checked that publish.sh never named the measuring tools.
It now checks that publish.sh never runs them.

subject: publish: measure_enwik9_gpt2.py ships too, for the enwik9 table's GPT-2 rows
body:
measure_benchmarks.sh does not run it, but it is what measured the four
GPT-2 rows the enwik9 table compares mini-AGI with, on the same 2,000
pieces. It needs only minagi/ (published), torch and transformers.
tests/test_publish_benchmarks.py follows its imports too.

subject: corpora: enwik9 builds the 50 MB slice the enwik9 table is scored on
body:
Nothing in the repo made data/enwik9/wikipedia/test.txt, so a reader
could not recreate the text the enwik9 rows are measured on.
`python3 -m corpora enwik9` now does. It downloads enwik9.zip from Matt
Mahoney's site (322,592,222 bytes), reads the slice straight out of it
without unpacking the billion bytes, and writes it only if its sha256 is
the one measured here. --zip uses a zip already on disk.

The slice is the last 50 MB of enwik9, bytes 950,000,000 to 1,000,000,000,
held out the way enwik8's test split is its last 5 MB. That was checked
against enwik9 itself: the slice's first bytes sit at offset 950,000,000,
the 50 MB from there match it by sha256 (fa616cef...), and enwik9 ends
where it ends. Cut by the new target from a fresh download, it is
byte-identical to the slice every enwik9 number was measured on.

The README's Benchmarks section ends with "Reproducing the benchmarks".
It covers the two corpora commands and ./measure_benchmarks.sh: about a
day on an RTX 3070 Laptop GPU, needing the GPU to itself, learning only
on a deleted copy of the weights, and rewriting the README's tables. It
also names tools/measure_enwik9_gpt2.py for the GPT-2 rows. corpora/ is
published whole, so the target ships with the scripts.

subject: governor: the learning rate's controller runs the same wherever the model learns
body:
The plasticity controller sets how fast the model adapts, so it is part
of the model. Until now only training ran it. Chat and the benchmarks'
learning (dynamic evaluation, best effort) started at training's rate but
took no held-out checks. The controller never moved, and the newborn
experts' rates never relaxed.

minagi/governor.py is now the one path all three take:
- At a session's start it reads the larger evaluation and the checks'
  blocks side by side, which set the level.
- At a check it reads the checks' blocks at that level. The controller
  observes their mean (Plasticity.observe), and every expert's own rate
  relaxes (relax_rates).

train.py takes its start, its check and its response through the
governor, and nowhere else. LiveLearner sets one up in for_run, runs the
session's evaluation, and takes a check whenever one is due after a
step, leaving the model in the mode it was in. A check the controller
would not count (fewer than MIN_STEPS steps since its last reading) is
not read, but rates still relax as training's round relaxes them. A
quiet conversation spends nothing on checks.

How often to check, on which held-out folder and how much of it comes
from the run. train.py now records them in the manifest (`checks`). Older
weights are read with the run's own settings: every 10 minutes, data/val,
60x512 and 240x512 characters. Held-out is read in training's chunks,
whatever the stream steps by. Without the folder the rate stays where the
run left it, and the learner says so. LiveLearner.save no longer relaxes
the rates itself when checks are doing it.

tools/measure_enwik9_adapt.py records how the rate went: the starting
rate (`lr`, as before), `lr_end`, the number of checks, their spacing and
their readings. It prints the course, and --held-out names another
folder. Only records taken with the controller working count as "already
measured", so the next sweep re-measures what learned at a fixed rate.
The README notes say where the controller took the rate; older records
keep their wording. serve.py reports each check in chat. The benchmark
script's header and the README's reproduction section mention data/val.

tests/test_governor.py covers the rules, and covers training and a
learner on a real model taking the same path. corpora/chat.py now reads
pool.balance with float(), as training does: "1e-5" without a decimal
point is a string to YAML.

subject: pool: A/B switches for how experts are chosen and mixed, and a harness that compares them
body:
Three switches, all off by default, read by build_paged from config.yaml:

- pool.gate_after: weight each character's chosen experts after their gates
  (probability x gate over the chosen total), so choosing an expert gated
  near zero no longer dilutes the strong ones; "scaled" keeps the gates'
  scale, so experts gated alike mix exactly as before.
- pool.route_bias / route_bias_offset: a per-expert offset added where
  experts are chosen (the card's vote and each character's top 8), never to
  the mixing weights or the loss, stepped by sign toward a 1/(rank+offset)
  share of training choices and centred as Moonlight centres DeepSeek-V3's.
  Saved with the weights, so reading and chat choose as training does.
- growth.birth_gate_parents: a newborn's gate as a share of its parents'.

MINAGI_CONFIG names the config file a run reads, so each arm of a comparison
has its own. train.py --loss-log writes every step's loss, the model's own
part of it (as held-out reads it, without the router's terms) and where it
was read, so runs over the same text compare chunk by chunk.

tools/ab_pool.py runs arms on copies of weights/, each reading the same
characters with the held-out checks off, then the same held-out blocks; it
reports paired differences, usage on held-out and while reading, and a chart.
Probes read held-out with a setting changed and nothing trained.

subject: optim: Muon for the weight matrices, as Liu et al. 2025 apply it (training.optimizer)
body:
minagi/muon.py builds the optimiser for training and for every learner
outside it (chat, the benchmarks' learning): AdamW as before, or Muon for
every weight matrix - attention's (query, key and value as three), the dense
MLPs', the adapter's, each expert's three and the router's - with AdamW for
the embedding, head, norms, halting unit, gates and depth embeddings.

As "Muon is Scalable for LLM Training" (arXiv 2502.16982) applies it:
Nesterov momentum 0.95, five Newton-Schulz steps with Jordan's coefficients,
decoupled weight decay, and each step scaled by 0.2 * sqrt(max(rows, cols))
so it has AdamW's typical size and lr, the controller and weight_decay keep
their meaning. Muon's momentum lives in AdamW's exp_avg, so the experts'
files and checkpoints carry it unchanged, a run moving from AdamW starts
from AdamW's momentum, and exp_avg_sq is left for a move back. An expert on
the card that no character chose is not stepped: Muon's step has full size
whatever its momentum's.

Growth and pruning keep a replaced router on Muon (muon.adopt in
_resync_opt). Default stays adamw.

subject: pool: the A/B chart draws the near arms again at their own scale when one is far off
pool: one learning rate for every expert; the newborn rate is gone
body:
A newborn expert no longer learns at its own multiple of the main rate:
every expert, its gate and its router rows step at the pool's rate, as
before training.newborn_lr. Turned off on a copy of the weights for 12M
characters it changed nothing measurable (held-out -0.0004 +/- 0.0003,
the same as the control run twice), so it goes for the simpler rule.

The governor no longer touches the pool, chat's learner sets no rates,
the dashboard draws the controller's rate alone, and dropping the
quietest keeps its tests in tests/test_drop_quietest.py. Weights saved
with per-expert rates load as before; the rates are ignored.

subject: optim: the run steps with Muon (training.optimizer: muon)
body:
From the same weights and the same 30M characters, Muon ended 0.0039
+/- 0.0004 nats lower on held-out than AdamW, better in all eight
subjects and still pulling away, at 8% fewer characters a second
(tools/ab_pool.py, two arms against a measured noise floor of 0.0005).
Chat and the benchmarks' learning take it from the same key.

subject: model, train: the largest attention logit, read at every check
body:
While a check reads its held-out blocks - the same blocks every check -
each attention keeps the largest score its softmax is taken of. The
sample log carries it before held-out, with each attention's own, the
check's line says it, and tools/export_history.py reads it into the
check's record. Under Muon that number can grow until a softmax
saturates on one key (Liu et al. 2025), so it is a series to watch.

It is computed in the dtype the kernel is handed, a block of queries at
a time with only the keys new to each block masked, and read from the
card once per check: about the cost of the scores themselves.

subject: corpora: the next stage's tool-use lanes, built by `python3 -m corpora agent`
body:
Three new lanes, nothing downloaded or built yet: tools (generated by
corpora/toolbox.py, every call run against its episode's world),
function-calls (xLAM, ToolACE, Hermes, When2Call, SmolTalk apigen-80k,
Glaive, tldr-pages) and trajectories (Toucan's SFT set, and TextWorld and
ALFWorld played by their own solvers in corpora/worlds.py).

Every source is rewritten into one protocol: the tools as JSON Schema
lines before the first turn, <call>{json}</call>, and the result inside
the same bot turn. Duplicates are dropped across sources, one record in a
hundred is held out by hash, downloads are kept under data/raw/agent, and
--check shows the plan without fetching anything. AgentInstruct states no
licence and is built only with --with agentinstruct.

subject: corpora: ARC lanes, whole datasets, and a build that asks for its space first
body:
Every dataset is now taken whole: Toucan's four sets (1.6M runs, 21.8 GB)
rather than its SFT subset, and tldr in every language it has. Toucan's
three big sets write a call as function_call with the result in a
`function` message; those are read now, where they would have been kept
as text alone.

ARC joins as four lanes:
- arc: ARC-AGI-2's and ARC-AGI-1's training tasks, ConceptARC and the
  community's sets, the hand-made ones copied 64 times turned, mirrored
  and recolored; plus RE-ARC.
- arc-synthetic: BARC, each problem also as its program, and Nemotron-RL.
- arc-traces: Nemotron-SFT's solving traces.
- arc-games: ARC-AGI-3's public games, played by a breadth-first search
  in corpora/arc3_play.py under its own Python 3.12, made with uv.

The public evaluation sets are copied to data/eval/arc-agi-1 and -2. A
guard keeps them out of training by task id and by grid content under
the eight symmetries and recoloring. That costs 376 of ARC-AGI-2's
training tasks, which are ARC-AGI-1's evaluation tasks;
--arc1-eval-for-training takes them instead. Every fifth public
ARC-AGI-3 game is held out.

A build now prints the disk it will keep and write and the memory it
will take, and asks before starting (--yes), instead of refusing when the
disk is short. Sources that state no licence are built only on request:
nvarc, nvarc-artifacts, arc-community-unlicensed, agentinstruct.

subject: memory: the project's history in one folder, for agents
body:
memory/ holds what an agent needs to pick the project up at any point:
state.md (where the run and the code stand), conventions.md (how work is
done here, and why), decisions.md (settled, reversed and rejected
choices), corrections.md (the run's in-flight measurement fixes, moved out
of the README), experiments.md (every test and A/B with its numbers and
verdict), history.md (dated, with commit refs) and changes.jsonl (the
commit log, written by tools/memory_changes.py). FINDINGS.md,
ARCHITECTURE.md and docs/adaptation.md move in as findings.md,
architecture.md and adaptation.md, each with a header saying what still
holds.

The README keeps today's held-out method and points at
memory/corrections.md instead of carrying both corrections' tables; its
Layout section names memory/ as history kept for agents. The generated
graph caption links there too.

publish.sh ships memory/ and rewrites changes.jsonl before it copies; a
commit of that file alone is left out of it, so committing it keeps it
current. The self-knowledge lane skips memory/: its history is full of
numbers that were true once (tests/test_self_knowledge.py checks it, and
fails with the skip removed). The lane changes only when it is rebuilt by
hand.

subject: memory: a glossary, the run's timeline, the lanes, and what was wrong in it
body:
glossary.md gives the project's words, units and markers, and reads a check
in runs/samples.txt line by line. timeline.md places every change that
reached the run at the first session that started after it, with the
author's uncommitted settings dated by when they were first seen, and lists
all 88 sessions with date, step, characters, experts, held-out (moved) and
the controller's scale.

The run began on 2026-09-16 from a fresh model, not "in early September":
the run before it (09-03 .. 09-16) re-read the same text after every
restart and is archived. state.md said the manifest holds the best
held-out; `read` saves at every check and every 5 minutes, so weights/ is
the latest state, and the "best state" and revert wording in the README
describes `train.py stream`.

state.md gains the lanes: sizes, shares and how much of each has been read.
The schedule pays credit per visit, and a visit is one file's passage, so a
lane's share of characters is its visit share times its mean visit length:
wikipedia has 29% of the visits and 9% of the characters, chess and
arithmetic 2.2x their share (E47). Not changed - it changes what the run
reads. Also there: the controller is at x0.0122 against its floor x0.01,
and what the next stage can change on these weights.

E46 records the 10-17 forecast of when the larger GPT-2s are reached;
conventions.md gains read_only for tools that open weights/, serve.py's
default learning, and a check for cost estimates; decisions.md corrects the
pruning and balance entries.

The commit log also leaves out a commit about the author's own material
and the sentences in other messages that name it, and names no local
settings file (tests/test_memory_changes.py, which fails with any of its
rules removed). The memory files lose the last such mentions.

subject: plasticity: the floor x0.01 -> x0.001, and the rate printed to three figures
body:
Easing is the controller's resting posture, so on a long plateau the rate
settles at the floor, and the run's had come within a fifth of it (x0.0122
on 10-29, ~9% lower a day). The floor goes to a tenth of what it was, at
the author's request, so the controller can keep easing where held-out
stops improving. The way back up is unchanged: a confirmed jump in
held-out doubles the rate, so from the new floor it takes about three more
doublings to reach x0.01 than it did.

The log printed the scale to three decimals, so 0.0095 read as x0.010 and
anything under 0.0015 as x0.001: below a hundredth it would hardly have
shown the rate going lower. Plasticity.shown gives three significant
figures and never an exponent (x0.00951), in the check line, the
controller's notes and its startup line; whatever reads "rate x" followed
by digits still reads it.

The README, config.yaml's comment and the self-knowledge answers state the
new floor (the answers formatted it as a whole percent, which would have
read 0%). tests/test_plasticity.py: a long flat run passes x0.01 and
settles at x0.001, and the printed scale keeps three figures.

It takes effect at the run's next start; until then the running session
stops at x0.01.

subject: memory: the controller's floor is x0.001 now, and what that means
body:
state.md, decisions.md, timeline.md, glossary.md and history.md record
"plasticity: the floor x0.01 -> x0.001, and the rate printed to three figures": the floor was x0.05 until 10-09, x0.01 until now, and is x0.001
from the run's next start. Since easing is the controller's resting
posture, a plateau ends at the floor, so the floor sets the plateau rate;
the way back up is still one doubling per confirmed jump. Whether the
lower rate helps is not measured at these rates: state.md names the
paired test that would say.

subject: memory: exact quotes only, and nothing more about private files
body:
A pre-publish audit of memory/ against the session records found a dozen
quotes of the author that did not match the messages they came from word
for word; inside quotation marks that is a misquote. Each is now a
paraphrase, and the six quotes left were checked against their messages.

Four commit refs pointed at the author's own material, which the
published commit log leaves out, so they led nowhere; they are gone.

The log generator also drops a sentence that names the private notifier,
the local settings file, or the author's script (UNSAID), as it already
did for the author's other material; tests/test_memory_changes.py covers
it.

subject: memory: the Public rules say the log drops sentences about private files too
readme: what a run saves, that nothing rolls back, and the modules the layout missed
body:
The README said weights/ holds the best state the model has reached and
that a diverging run repairs itself. Both are `train.py stream`'s; the run
uses `read`, which saves its latest state every five minutes, at every
held-out check and when it stops, and rolls nothing back. The weights
paragraph and the Initialization section now say that, and
minagi/store.py's best_val says which path keeps which.

The layout lists lanes.py, muon.py, governor.py and heldout.py, which it
had missed, and the files hold the optimiser's state rather than "Adam
moments": under Muon an expert's file carries the momentum Muon steps
with, where AdamW keeps its first moment.

subject: publish: the notifier ships as ordinary code, silent without its settings
body:
publish.sh no longer leaves out minagi/notify.py, strips its five lines
from the published train.py, or fails a publish that names it. The
notifier does nothing unless both of its settings are present, in the
environment or in a .env, which stays untracked and is never published
(the check that fails a publish with a .env in the destination stays).
The README does not mention it.

tests/test_notify.py points the module at a .env of its own (notify.py
gains ENV_FILE), so it holds the same with or without a configured
machine: no .env, a .env without the two settings, or only one of them
all leave it off. tests/test_publish_benchmarks.py reads train.py whole
and checks the notifier it imports is published with it.

subject: corpora: the self-description names the optimiser config.yaml sets
body:
The answers to "what optimiser do you use" said Adam with decoupled weight
decay; the run steps with Muon. They now say what training.optimizer and
training.muon_params set, through an {optimizer} fact, so they follow the
setting. One answer about precision said "Adam's moments" for what is now
the optimiser's.

_self_facts also loses an import of a facts module from a path that does
not exist, which always failed and fell through to an empty dict.

subject: memory: no commit hashes and none of the author's wording; the notifier is ordinary code
body:
This repository's git is not published, so a commit hash in memory/ leads
nowhere: every one is gone from the .md files, a change is named and dated
instead, and changes.jsonl records a commit by its date and subject. A hash
a commit message cites becomes the subject of the commit it names.

The author's wording is gone too, quoted or close to it: memory/ keeps the
intent of each decision and its reason, nothing more.

The notifier is no longer treated as private: the log no longer leaves out
its commits or the sentences about it, and conventions.md says how it
works, that the README does not mention it, and how an agent can help a
user set it up. Agents still never read .env.

tests/test_memory_changes.py checks the hashes, the subjects that replace
them, and that a sentence about the notifier now stays.

subject: release: refresh what the README reports and check the tree, without copying anything
body: The regeneration and checks publish.sh ran, for a repository that is its own public copy: held-out measured on the model as it is (refused while a run trains), the scaling chart and the architecture figure redrawn, the README's figures refreshed; then every tracked .py compiles, no .env is tracked, and every README link leads to something in the repository. It commits and pushes nothing. publish.sh stays until the move.

subject: release: publish.sh retired, with the commit-log generator it ran
body:
One repository now: what is tracked is what a push carries, and
release.sh refreshes the README's figures and checks the tree before
one. The three tests that read publish.sh hold release.sh to the same
things (it redraws the architecture figure, it runs none of the
day-long measurements), and the benchmark-closure test asks that
everything measure_benchmarks.sh runs and imports is tracked. The
tools that named publish.sh name release.sh or measure_benchmarks.sh,
whichever runs them.

memory/changes.jsonl stays as the log it last wrote.

subject: publish_weights: the Hugging Face clone is found beside the repository
body:
DEST defaulted to a path on one machine. It now defaults to
mini-AGI-undertrained in the directory that holds this repository, and
DEST still names any other clone; a missing clone says to set it. After
a push, README.md's new date is committed with the code, as there is no
second repository to copy it into. --help no longer prints the line
after the header.

subject: tools: comments and examples refer only to what the repository holds
body:
The animations call themselves animations, the loader's comments give
the reasons that still hold, and the scaling chart is written to
assets/ and runs/scaling/ only. rebuild_self_knowledge.py loses
SKIP_DIRS, which nothing read; the walk's own SKIP is unchanged, so the
lane would be rebuilt from the same files as before.

subject: tools: inspection tools read weights/ by default, and read-only
body:
Ten tools defaulted to weights_rows/, a directory the run left months
ago; they default to weights/ now. Five that read weights/ already
opened it writable - animate_routing, plot_routing, expert_grid,
latent_flow, depth_proposal - and paging an expert in marks it dirty,
so they could write expert files back under a running trainer. They
open it read-only now; animate_routing --learn steps the model in
memory only. collapse_depth's example writes its new model to a
directory of its own. animate_routing's docstring says animation, as
the other animations do.

subject: memory: one public repository
body:
The workshop is history now: the folder says what it was, that its
files moved into the public repository and its git history did not,
and that changes.jsonl is its frozen commit log. Hashes of this
repository's own commits on main may be cited; the workshop's never.
The conventions on commits (branch main, the author pushes), the
